United States 1946–89 Wiki
A narrative-research knowledge base on American history from the end of the Second World War through the close of the Cold War era — postwar reconversion and domestic Cold War order, suburbanization and mass consumption, civil rights and the Great Society, Vietnam and the political crises of the 1960s–70s, industrial and corporate restructuring, inflation and deregulation, and the rise of scaled retail, computing, biotechnology, and semiconductors through 1989.
Total pages: 32
Sources are processed from the period corpus. Entity, event, and concept pages will be built from those sources under a contemporary lens, without modern editorial framing.
Entities
People, places, and institutions of the United States, 1946–89.
(none yet)
Events
Elections, wars, strikes, legislation, crises, and other key occurrences.
(none yet)
Concepts
Broad themes, institutions, systems, and ideas.
(none yet)
Sources
The foundation of the wiki. Source pages summarize the primary and secondary texts used throughout.
Government / congressional investigations

church-committee-book-i-foreign-military-intelligence — [source] Foreign and Military Intelligence, Book I (Church Committee, 1976) — Senate Report 94-755 final report on U.S. foreign and military intelligence: postwar community history, NSC and DCI control, CIA charter and covert action, counterintelligence, domestic impact of clandestine operations, proprietaries, finished intelligence, State and Defense intelligence, budget secrecy, chemical and biological agent testing, and 1976 findings and recommendations. Read source page
church-committee-book-ii-rights-of-americans — [source] Intelligence Activities and the Rights of Americans, Book II (Church Committee, 1976) — Senate Report 94-755 final report on domestic intelligence: growth 1936–1976, COINTELPRO, CHAOS, Huston Plan, mail opening and NSA monitoring, seven major findings, and statutory recommendations to safeguard Americans’ rights. Read source page
church-committee-interim-assassination-plots — [source] Alleged Assassination Plots Involving Foreign Leaders (Church Committee Interim Report, 1975) — Senate Report 94-465 case studies on Congo/Lumumba, Cuba/Castro and MONGOOSE, executive action capability, Trujillo, Diem, Schneider/Chile, with findings, recommendations, and chronology. Read source page
church-committee-vol-5-nsa-fourth-amendment — [source] Hearings Vol. 5: NSA and Fourth Amendment Rights (Church Committee, 1975) — Public hearings Oct 29 and Nov 6, 1975: Director Lew Allen, SHAMROCK and MINARET as described on the record, and appendix documents. Read source page
church-committee-vol-6-fbi-hearings — [source] Hearings Vol. 6: Federal Bureau of Investigation (Church Committee, 1975) — Public hearings Nov 18–Dec 11, 1975 on COINTELPRO, informants (Cook, Rowe), Attorneys General Katzenbach, Clark, and Levi, Director Kelley, and large exhibits appendix. Read source page
church-committee-vol-7-covert-action-hearings — [source] Hearings Vol. 7: Covert Action (Church Committee, 1975) — Dec 4–5 hearings (Korry; Clifford/Vance panel) plus staff report Covert Action in Chile 1963–1973 and National Security Act / War Powers / Hughes–Ryan appendices. Read source page

Scholarly surveys / narrative histories

goldman-crucial-decade — [source] The Crucial Decade—and After: America, 1945–1960 (Goldman, 1960/1961) — Eric F. Goldman’s narrative survey of reconversion, Truman Fair Deal and Cold War mobilization, McCarthy-era politics, Eisenhower consensus, and the late-1950s turn toward the 1960s, with the “and after” frame carrying into the Kennedy threshold. Read source page
burns-crosswinds-of-freedom — [source] The Crosswinds of Freedom (Burns, 1989/2012) — James MacGregor Burns’s third volume of The American Experiment: leadership-centered political and intellectual history from FDR’s 1932 nomination through the late Reagan years, with wiki core on Cold War, civil rights, Vietnam, Watergate, and Carter–Reagan leadership. Read source page
leebaert-grand-improvisation — [source] Grand Improvisation: America Confronts the British Superpower, 1945–1957 (Leebaert, 2018) — Derek Leebaert’s Anglo-American history: no clean baton pass from British Empire to U.S. leadership; a dozen years of improvisation through sterling crisis, NATO, Korea, Middle East, and Suez until late-1950s American supremacy. Read source page
bird-sherwin-american-prometheus — [source] American Prometheus: The Triumph and Tragedy of J. Robert Oppenheimer (Bird and Sherwin, 2005/2006) — Pulitzer biography from childhood and Los Alamos through AEC politics and the 1954 security hearing; wiki core on postwar nuclear policy, the Super fight, and McCarthy-era destruction of Oppenheimer’s government role. Read source page
gabler-walt-disney — [source] Walt Disney: The Triumph of the American Imagination (Gabler, 2006) — Full-life Disney biography; wiki core on postwar studio recovery, Disneyland, television empire, and EPCOT-era utopia through 1966, with pre-1946 animation chapters as continuity. Read source page
nasaw-the-chief-hearst — [source] The Chief: The Life of William Randolph Hearst (Nasaw, 2000) — Full Hearst biography; wiki core on 1946–51 old age and San Simeon coda, with yellow press–Hollywood–New Deal arcs period-gated to earlier U.S. wikis. Read source page
murray-cox-apollo-race-to-the-moon — [source] Apollo: The Race to the Moon (Murray and Cox, 1989) — Oral-history narrative of Project Apollo through engineers and Mission Control: Space Task Group, Kennedy commitment, L.O.R./Saturn, Apollo 1 fire, Apollo 8–11, and Apollo 13 recovery. Read source page
duncan-rickover-struggle-for-excellence — [source] Rickover: The Struggle for Excellence (Duncan, 2001) — Francis Duncan’s Naval Reactors biography of Adm. Hyman G. Rickover: Oak Ridge to Nautilus and Shippingport, national-figure and nuclear-carrier fights, Thresher, two-year extensions, shipbuilding claims, Carter years, 1982 retirement, and engineering legacy; pre-1946 career as continuity. Read source page

Business memoirs / corporate autobiography

walton-made-in-america — [source] Sam Walton: Made in America — My Story (Walton with Huey, 1992) — Sam Walton’s first-person account of Ben Franklin variety stores and Wal-Mart’s rise from Bentonville and small-town discounting to national scale, covering family partnership, the 1970 IPO, associate culture, distribution technology, Kmart/Sears competition, Sam’s Clubs, and management rules. Read source page
iacocca-iacocca — [source] Iacocca: An Autobiography (Iacocca with Novak, 1984/2011) — Lee Iacocca’s account of immigrant Allentown origins, Ford rise through Mustang and the presidency, 1978 firing by Henry Ford II, and Chrysler turnaround with federal loan guarantees, K-car, and minivan. Read source page
welch-straight-from-the-gut — [source] Jack: Straight from the Gut (Welch with Byrne, 2001) — Jack Welch’s GE career from plastics through the chairmanship: no. 1 or no. 2 portfolio strategy, 1980s restructuring, Crotonville, boundaryless culture, and Work-Out, with post-1989 spill on services, Six Sigma, and succession. Read source page
sloan-my-years-with-general-motors — [source] My Years with General Motors (Sloan, 1964) — Alfred P. Sloan, Jr.’s corporate autobiography of GM organization, product policy, financial controls, annual model/styling/dealers/GMAC, defense and labor, with wiki weight on postwar dealer/defense/labor peace and mid-century management creed. Read source page
kroc-grinding-it-out — [source] Grinding It Out: The Making of McDonald’s (Kroc with Anderson, 1977) — Ray Kroc’s autobiography: 1954 San Bernardino deal, Des Plaines launch, Sonneborn real-estate financing, Turner operations, brother buyout, public growth, and Padres coda; Lily Tulip/Multimixer years as continuity. Read source page
turner-call-me-ted — [source] Call Me Ted (Turner with Burke, 2008) — Ted Turner’s autobiography: billboards after father’s 1963 suicide, WTCG/SuperStation, Braves, America’s Cup, CNN, Goodwill Games, CBS/MGM fights, cable-operator rescue, Jane Fonda and Montana land; 1990s–AOL chapters period-gated. Read source page
schroeder-snowball-warren-buffett — [source] The Snowball: Warren Buffett and the Business of Life (Schroeder, 2008) — Authorized Buffett biography: Graham/partnerships, Berkshire, See’s/GEICO/Washington Post, Susie/Astrid, 1980s deal culture; childhood and Salomon/philanthropy chapters period-gated. Read source page
trimble-overnight-success-federal-express — [source] Overnight Success: Federal Express and Frederick Smith (Trimble, 1993) — FedEx founding biography: hub-and-spoke overnight network, Falcon fleet, 1974 forgery crisis, first profits, Memphis hub scale-up, Flying Tiger global bid; Smith family fortune as continuity. Read source page

Business / technology histories

hughes-genentech — [source] Genentech: The Beginnings of Biotech (Hughes, 2011) — Sally Smith Hughes’s scholarly history of Genentech’s founding and early years: recombinant DNA, Swanson–Boyer partnership, insulin and growth-hormone races, IPO, and the biotech industry template in 1970s–80s California. Read source page
collins-built-to-last — [source] Built to Last: Successful Habits of Visionary Companies (Collins and Porras, 1994) — Six-year Stanford paired study of eighteen visionary U.S. companies versus comparison firms, deriving clock-building, core ideology, BHAGs, cult-like cultures, and home-grown management from founding eras through the early 1990s. Read source page
isaacson-steve-jobs — [source] Steve Jobs (Isaacson, 2011) — Authorized biography from adoption and Apple founding through Macintosh, ouster, NeXT/Pixar, and later return; wiki priority on U.S. personal-computing arcs through 1989 with hard period gate on post-1989 product chapters. Read source page
miller-chip-war — [source] Chip War: The Fight for the World’s Most Critical Technology (Miller, 2022) — Global semiconductor history from transistor and IC origins through Cold War military demand, Silicon Valley and Japanese rivalry, and later supply-chain geography; period-gated for U.S. arcs through 1989. Read source page
barlett-steele-empire-howard-hughes — [source] Empire / Howard Hughes: His Life & Madness (Barlett & Steele, 1979) — Copied from United States 1920–45: RKO, Culver City electronics revolt, TWA jets, Las Vegas, Air West, Watergate/Hughesgate, CIA Glomar, death and estate; Hollywood/WWII chapters period-gated. Read source page
foster-henry-j-kaiser — [source] Henry J. Kaiser: Builder in the Modern American West (Foster, 1989) — Copied from United States 1866–1919: Kaiser-Frazer Detroit, overseas ventures, aluminum, Permanente growth, Hawaii/Pacific, sunset years through 1967 death, and empire dispersal; dams/ships period-gated. Read source page
lyons-david-sarnoff — [source] David Sarnoff: A Biography (Lyons, 1966) — RCA/NBC chief from immigrant wireless operator to postwar “father of television” and color-TV triumph; wiki core on 1946–60s electronics leadership, with radio/WWII chapters period-gated to earlier U.S. wikis. Read source page
grove-only-the-paranoid-survive — [source] Only the Paranoid Survive (Grove, 1996/1999) — Intel CEO Andy Grove on strategic inflection points: 10X forces, PC-industry morph, memory-to-microprocessor exit; Internet/career chapters period-gated post-1989. Read source page
burrough-helyar-barbarians-at-the-gate — [source] Barbarians at the Gate (Burrough and Helyar, 1990) — WSJ reconstruction of the 1988 RJR Nabisco LBO: Ross Johnson, Shearson, KKR, Forstmann, First Boston, 30 November special committee. Read source page
mansfield-vision-saga-of-the-sky — [source] Vision: A Saga of the Sky (Mansfield, 1956) — Copied from United States 1920–45: postwar swept-wing B-47/B-52, Stratocruiser, tankers, 707 board decision, Bomarc missiles, and Cold War outlook (Books Four–Five); founding/WWII Fortress chapters period-gated. Read source page

sources/barlett-steele-empire-howard-hug.title: [source] Empire / Howard Hughes: His Life & Madness (Barlett & Steele, 1979)
sources/barlett-steele-empire-howard-hug.content:
Empire / Howard Hughes: His Life & Madness
Authors: Donald L. Barlett and James B. Steele
Published: 1979 (W. W. Norton & Company; originally Empire: The Life, Legend, and Madness of Howard Hughes; Norton paperback reissue 2004 as Howard Hughes: His Life & Madness)
Working text: Digital EPUB via Anna’s Archive (hash e52a0b470771df3e9e8152f929451816)
Raw extract: wiki/raw/barlett-steele-empire-howard-hughes.txt (EPUB via pandoc -t plain)
Extract stats: 36,061 lines · ~315,387 words · 1,925,679 bytes
Deploy note: Full-text raw is not deployed — wiki/.gitignore ignores *.txt; Quartz ignorePatterns includes raw.
Period-Overlap Note
This source has been copied from United States 1920-45 into the United States 1946–89 wiki because Chapters 6–25 (plus Epilogue) cover RKO, Hughes Aircraft’s electronics boom and Culver City revolt, Mormon aides, TWA jet financing and loss of control, Las Vegas empire-building, Air West, political influence, Watergate/Hughesgate, CIA Project Jennifer/Glomar Explorer, death in 1976, and the estate fight—core postwar material for this period. Mine first from Chs. 6–25. Use Chs. 1–5 (Hollywood, 1930s records, WWII contracting, 1947 Senate/Spruce Goose) only as continuity for stories that continue after 1945. Sister home page remains in United States 1920–45 for the wartime hinge.
Overview
Empire (1979; Norton 2004 reissue Howard Hughes: His Life & Madness) is Barlett and Steele’s four-year investigative biography of Howard Robard Hughes, Jr. (1905–1976), built from more than a quarter-million pages of scattered government, corporate, and court records rather than Hughes-company cooperation. The authors treat Hughes as a figure whose public legend—record aviator, Hollywood producer, defense contractor, reclusive billionaire—was sustained by secrecy, public relations, and decades of distorted repetition. The narrative runs from colonial Hughes family roots and Howard Hughes Sr.’s rock-bit invention through young Howard’s inheritance fight, Hollywood films (Hell’s Angels, Scarface), speed records and the 1938 around-the-world flight, wartime plywood bomber and flying-boat programs, the 1947 Brewster Senate hearings, and then postwar RKO, Hughes Aircraft’s electronics boom, TWA jet financing, breakdown and seclusion, Las Vegas empire-building, political influence, Watergate-era money trails, the Romaine Street burglary, CIA’s Glomar Explorer, death in Acapulco, and the Mormon-will fortune battle.
For this United States 1946–89 wiki the book covers Hughes’s postwar empire—RKO, Culver City electronics, TWA jets, Las Vegas, political machine, Watergate-era scandals, and CIA Glomar—through death and the fortune fight. Period-gate hard on Chs. 1–4 except as brief continuity; treat Ch. 5’s 1947 Senate/Spruce Goose as the opening hinge into the postwar narrative.
EPUB structure: Also-by list; title/copyright (1979 Empire / 2004 Norton reissue); Contents; Preface; Acknowledgments; Prologue; Chapters 1–25; Epilogue; Chronology; Appendices; Sources; Notes.
Narrative Source Flow
Front matter / TOC
Lines 1–315. Also-by Barlett/Steele titles; Norton 2004 reissue copyright and original 1979 Empire title; Library of Congress data; full Contents listing Preface through Notes with chapter subheads (Family, Rock Eater, Hate Hughes Club, Project Jennifer, etc.).
Preface
Lines 316–448. Frames Hughes as the most misunderstood figure of his era; recounts 1976 death fingerprint verification for Treasury/FBI; contrasts public legend with documented losses and secrecy; describes four years of research across fifty cities, fifty government offices, and a fifty-thousand-page document collection—the largest outside the Hughes organization.
Acknowledgments
Lines 449–538. Credits anonymous Hughes employees and associates, dozens of libraries and newspaper archives, court clerks, and research collaborators who supplied access to the scattered record on which the biography rests.
Prologue — Death in Mexico
Lines 539–876. Opens on Hughes’s final hours at the Acapulco Princess Hotel in April 1976—Waldron pouring water, erratic breathing, heart stopping at 1:27 P.M.—then flashes back through the reclusive endgame that preceded his last flight home to Texas.
Chapter 1 — The Early Years
Lines 877–2456. Traces the Hughes clan from colonial Virginia through Missouri law and Iowa respectability; Howard Hughes Sr.’s Spindletop-era oil-field work and 1909 two-cone rock-bit patent founding Hughes Tool; Allene Gano’s courtship and Houston life; young Howard’s mother-dominated childhood; parents’ deaths; and the teenage fight with relatives and executives for control of the tool company and his inheritance.
Chapter 2 — Hollywood
Lines 2457–3141. Hughes and Ella Rice move to Los Angeles in 1925; failed Swell Hogan and modest Everybody’s Acting; Caddo Film Company and Noah Dietrich as administrator; obsessive production of Hell’s Angels with real aerial combat footage; and the censorship battles over Scarface that established Hughes as a producer willing to fight the Hays Office.
Chapter 3 — Hero
Lines 3142–4549. Aviation supplants movies after 1932; Hughes streamlines the H-1 racer at Lockheed, founds Hughes Aircraft as a tool-company division, sets speed records, and in 1938 completes the around-the-world flight in a Lockheed 14—cementing the Lindbergh-era hero image while rarely visiting Houston kin again.
Chapter 4 — The War Years
Lines 4550–6051. Hughes seeks Wright Field contracts against the perceived “Hate Hughes Club”; wins wartime bomber and flying-boat programs using duramold plywood construction; navigates strange procurement bedfellows and cost overruns; and pushes the giant Hercules flying boat and XF-11 reconnaissance prototype even as management chaos grows at Culver City.
Chapter 5 — The Senate Investigation
Lines 6052–7328. After Chuck Perelle’s reforms fail against Hughes’s interference, the July 1946 XF-11 crash in Beverly Hills triggers Senator Owen Brewster’s hearings; Hughes testifies in Washington while the Spruce Goose remains unfinished; the committee’s political theater culminates in Hughes flying the Hercules at Long Beach in November 1947—the hinge between wartime contracting and postwar empire.
Chapter 6 — Movies, Missiles, and Communists
Lines 7329–8556. Post-hearing staff reorganization brings Frank Gay to Romaine Street; Hughes buys RKO in 1948 and runs it from seclusion; anti-Communist crusading and blacklist politics mesh with his need to purge troublesome stockholders and reshape the studio.
Chapter 7 — Revolt at Culver City
Lines 8557–9569. Hughes Aircraft’s 1950s electronics and Falcon-missile boom outgrows Culver City management; Tucson plant tax controversy; a 1953 executive revolt over charity fronts, political insurance, and Hughes’s remote control of a now-massive defense contractor.
Chapter 8 — Seeds of Disaster
Lines 9570–10441. Mormon aides rise in the inner circle; Hughes commits to a $400-million TWA jet fleet order without clear financing; Rockefeller and Zeckendorf are drawn into a secret sale that never closes—planting the seeds of the late-1950s financial crisis.
Chapter 9 — Breakdown
Lines 10442–11671. Secret 1957 Tonopah marriage to Jean Peters; deepening isolation, psychiatric crisis, and institutionalization rumors; showdown with Noah Dietrich and Wall Street lenders over TWA jet commitments and Hughes Tool collateral.
Chapter 10 — Retreat
Lines 11672–12984. December 1960 voting-trust agreement strips Hughes of TWA control; flight to Rancho Santa Fe with germ-phobia rituals; manhunt when he vanishes from the Beverly Hills Hotel; lenders take the airline while Hughes retreats from public business.
Chapter 11 — A New Career
Lines 12985–13954. Four-and-a-half-year seclusion ends with a train move to Boston’s Ritz-Carlton; medical-institute cover stories; transition planning through Bob Maheu toward a Nevada relocation and a new phase of hidden operations.
Chapter 12 — Lord of the Desert
Lines 13955–14963. 1967 Desert Inn purchase launches the Las Vegas casino-buying spree; public-relations blitz and masterplan for Strip dominance; Washington warnings about monopoly and hidden ownership as Hughes becomes “lord of the desert.”
Chapter 13 — Out of Control
Lines 14964–16515. Rival Kirk Kerkorian builds the International Hotel; Hughes lieutenants feud; conspiracy fears, press leaks, and the Boxcar nuclear-test shelter scheme expose how little Hughes actually controls his Nevada empire.
Chapter 14 — The $90-Million Mistake
Lines 16516–17308. Vietnam-era helicopter contract mispricing costs Hughes a fifth of his fortune; lobbying Lyndon Johnson; the “buy-in” and renegotiation fights that typify his postwar defense-industrial missteps.
Chapter 15 — The Billion-Dollar Deal
Lines 17309–18086. Hughes insists on “billionaire” press identity while secretly strapped; cornering TWA stock then selling out to become liquid—turning airline equity into cash for Las Vegas and Summa operations.
Chapter 16 — The Hijacking of Air West
Lines 18087–18918. 1970 hostile takeover of regional carrier Air West (Bonanza/Pacific/West Coast merger); squeeze tactics, overbooked holiday flights, and CAB/Washington rubber-stamping that Maheu and Raymond Cook botch—another Hughes airline adventure ending in federal scrutiny.
Chapter 17 — Gold Fever
Lines 18919–20196. 1967–68 precious-metals panic; Hughes buys hundreds of Nevada mining claims through Maheu; prospector parades, sting operations, and mining-stock swindles tied to the Hughes name and President’s brother subplot.
Chapter 18 — Turning Point
Lines 20197–21456. Jean Peters’s 1970 divorce announcement; Hughes ousted from effective control by Bill Gay, Chester Davis, and Nadine Henley; Summa Corporation hands change while Hughes remains a figurehead in exile.
Chapter 19 — The Political Connection
Lines 21457–22383. Two decades of IRS, CAB, Interior, and Pentagon favors; secret contributions and “I can buy any man” bravado; political machine that runs on the Hughes name regardless of who actually pulls levers.
Chapter 20 — Life in Exile
Lines 22384–23649. Clifford Irving hoax autobiography of 1971–72; Bahamas move; $350-million Howard Hughes Medical Institute giveaway; Hughes declared invalid as aides wall him off from the world.
Chapter 21 — Watergate
Lines 23650–24690. December 1973 flight to Freeport on Khashoggi’s plane; Hughes–Nixon money threads, Bebe Rebozo, and Larry O’Brien as “well-wired source”—connecting the reclusive billionaire to the scandal consuming Washington.
Chapter 22 — Hughesgate
Lines 24691–25540. June 1974 Romaine Street (“the Bastille”) burglary of Hughes archives; million-dollar ransom for stolen files linking Project Jennifer, Watergate, and Las Vegas operations.
Chapter 23 — The CIA’s Best-Kept Secret
Lines 25541–26252. Los Angeles Times leak of Hughes–CIA contract to raise Soviet submarine K-129; Glomar Explorer cover story; Mell Stewart problem and grand-jury aftermath of the stolen Romaine documents.
Chapter 24 — The Last Year
Lines 26253–27715. Hughes’s seventieth year contrasts profitable Hughes Aircraft with loss-ridden Summa; legacy reckoning; last fights among aides; Candyman and missing-will anxieties before the final move to Mexico.
Chapter 25 — The Fight for the Fortune
Lines 27716–29563. April 1976 body flown Houston to Methodist Hospital; autopsy and identity confirmation; cover-up of neglect; Mormon will surfaced in Las Vegas; fallout among heirs, executives, and courts over a billion-dollar estate.
Epilogue — A Summing Up
Lines 29564–30316. Argues Hughes’s legend outran his business acumen—passbook savings would have beat his empire-building; fame and control of image, not Midas touch, drove movies, aviation, and seclusion; public relations sustained the superman myth after repeated corporate failures.
Notes
Lines 30317–36061. Endnotes keyed to chapters; documentary citations from FBI, CIA, SEC, CAB, congressional hearings, court records, and newspaper archives supporting the narrative.
Coverage Guide
Early years, Tool Co., inheritance (continuity ← 1920–45)
Ch. 1: Hughes family, rock-bit invention, parents’ deaths, fight for company control—brief background only.
Hollywood and celebrity culture (continuity ← 1920–45)
Ch. 2: Hell’s Angels, Scarface, Caddo/Dietrich—continuity into the RKO takeover.
Aviation records and Hughes Aircraft origins (continuity ← 1920–45)
Ch. 3: H-1 racer, speed records, 1938 world flight—continuity into wartime/postwar aircraft empire.
World War II contracting and flying boat (continuity ← 1920–45)
Ch. 4: Wright Field/Hate Hughes Club, duramold bomber, Hercules flying boat, XF-11—brief continuity into Culver City and Senate aftermath.
1946–47 Senate hinge (wiki opening / continuity)
Ch. 5: XF-11 crash, Brewster committee, Spruce Goose flight—opening hinge into the postwar narrative; mine with Ch. 6+.
RKO through TWA crisis (wiki core)
Chs. 6–10: studio takeover, aircraft revolt, Mormon aides, jet order, TWA voting trust—postwar empire and breakdown.
Las Vegas, airlines, mining, political machine (wiki core)
Chs. 11–19: Boston exile, Desert Inn, Kerkorian rivalry, helicopters, TWA sale, Air West, gold claims, 1970 ouster, Washington influence.
Exile, Watergate, CIA, death, estate (wiki core)
Chs. 20–25 plus Epilogue: Irving hoax, Nixon money, Romaine burglary, Glomar Explorer, 1976 death, will fight, summing-up on legend vs. losses.

sources/bird-sherwin-american-prometheus.title: [source] American Prometheus: The Triumph and Tragedy of J. Robert Oppenheimer (Bird and Sherwin, 2005/2006)
sources/bird-sherwin-american-prometheus.content:
American Prometheus
Authors: Kai Bird and Martin J. Sherwin
Published: 2005 (Knopf); First Vintage Books edition, May 2006
Working text: Digital EPUB via Anna’s Archive (hash 422cbf640ccecea946b652ad85b730c8)
Raw extract: wiki/raw/bird-sherwin-american-prometheus.txt (EPUB via pandoc -t plain)
Extract stats: 35,044 lines · ~314,407 words · 1,953,744 bytes
Deploy note: Full-text raw is not deployed — wiki/.gitignore ignores *.txt; Quartz ignorePatterns includes raw.
Overview
American Prometheus is Kai Bird and Martin J. Sherwin’s biography of J. Robert Oppenheimer (1904–1967): theoretical physicist, builder of the Berkeley theoretical school, scientific director of Los Alamos, postwar government adviser and Institute for Advanced Study director, and the most prominent scientist destroyed by the McCarthy-era security system. Bird and Sherwin frame his life as triumph (quantum physics, wartime leadership, public intellectual stature) and tragedy (left associations, Chevalier episode, hydrogen-bomb opposition, Lewis Strauss’s vendetta, and the 1954 AEC hearing).
For this United States 1946–89 wiki the book is a core Cold War science-and-security spine: Trinity and Hiroshima aftermath, Acheson–Lilienthal / Baruch international control debates, AEC politics, FBI surveillance, the Super controversy, and the Gray Board hearing. Parts One–Two (childhood through 1942) are retained for continuity; Parts Three–Five plus Preface/Prologue/Epilogue are the wiki priority. Period-gate late family aftermath (Kitty, Toni, Frank’s Exploratorium) as post-career coda.
EPUB structure: Table of Contents; Title / Dedication / Praise; Preface; Prologue; Parts One–Five with Chapters One–Forty; Epilogue; Author’s Note and Acknowledgments (Sherwin); Notes; Bibliography; Illustration Credits; About the Authors / Also by; Vintage copyright block.
Narrative Source Flow
Front matter
Lines 1–208. TOC; title/dedication/praise; Knopf/Vintage front matter.
Preface
Lines 209–407. Opens on December 1953: Strauss hands Oppenheimer the AEC charges letter; the career-and-self-worth crisis that structures the biography’s tragic arc.
Prologue
Lines 408–551. Princeton funeral, 25 February 1967: six hundred mourners; “Oppie” as teacher, “father” of the bomb, national hero, then fallen figure—“Damn it, I happen to love this country.”
PART ONE
Lines 552–555. Part divider opening youth and scientific formation (Chs. 1–7).
Chapter One — “He Received Every New Idea as Perfectly Beautiful”
Lines 556–1427. Early-century science revolution; Oppenheimer childhood as “unctuous, repulsively good little boy”; Ethical Culture / New York Jewish milieu and first intellectual formation.
Chapter Two — “His Separate Prison”
Lines 1428–1933. Harvard 1922 enrollment; Standish Hall; extreme physique and social isolation; early adult “separate prison” temperament.
Chapter Three — “I Am Having a Pretty Bad Time”
Lines 1934–2580. Post-Harvard emotional crisis (1926 letter); Cambridge difficulties and near-disastrous psychological strain after the protective undergraduate shield falls away.
Chapter Four — “I Find the Work Hard, Thank God, & Almost Pleasant”
Lines 2581–3119. Move to Göttingen (1926); quantum mecca of Lower Saxony; hard, almost pleasant work and scientific maturation under Born’s circle.
Chapter Five — “I Am Oppenheimer”
Lines 3120–3649. End of Göttingen year; homesickness and American chauvinism (New Mexico deserts); self-assertion as Oppenheimer among European peers (Rabi contrast).
Chapter Six — “Oppie”
Lines 3650–4260. Zurich productivity; Perro Caliente rhythm—intense work then New Mexico horseback renewal; 1931 letter on a restless, uncompromising world.
Chapter Seven — “The Nim Nim Boys”
Lines 4261–4887. Parents’ 1930 Pasadena visit; Depression-era family fortune after Julius’s 1928 retirement; Berkeley/Caltech “Nim Nim Boys” circle and politics vs. truth/beauty question.
PART TWO
Lines 4888–4891. Part divider: politics, love, and wartime recruitment (Chs. 8–14).
Chapter Eight — “In 1936 My Interests Began to Change”
Lines 4892–5633. Meeting Jean Tatlock (spring 1936); courtship; political awakening tied to personal life (Serber: Jean as truest love).
Chapter Nine — “[Frank] Clipped It Out and Sent It In”
Lines 5634–6290. Julius’s death (20 Sept 1937); Chevalier friendship and ambiguous Communist Party membership claims; brother Frank’s Party card episode.
Chapter Ten — “More and More Surely”
Lines 6291–6711. Nazi–Soviet pact (24 Aug 1939) and Poland invasion; Weisskopf on a decisive weekend turning Oppenheimer away from the Party; letter to Willie Fowler.
Chapter Eleven — “I’m Going to Marry a Friend of Yours, Steve”
Lines 6712–7294. Break with Tatlock; engagement near-misses; courtship and marriage path to Kitty (Serber on her advancing Robert’s career).
Chapter Twelve — “We Were Pulling the New Deal to the Left”
Lines 7295–7869. Popular Front / New Deal left organizing; teachers’ union and related Bay Area political work pulling reform leftward.
Chapter Thirteen — “The Coordinator of Rapid Rupture”
Lines 7870–8532. Early fission program role—“Coordinator of Rapid Rupture”; recruitment into the wartime bomb project apparatus.
Chapter Fourteen — “The Chevalier Affair”
Lines 8533–8811. Haakon Chevalier approach and the security episode that will haunt every later clearance fight.
PART THREE
Lines 8812–8815. Part divider: Los Alamos and the gadget (Chs. 15–22).
Chapter Fifteen — “He’d Become Very Patriotic”
Lines 8816–9615. Wartime patriotism and lab leadership persona; building the Los Alamos community.
Chapter Sixteen — “Too Much Secrecy”
Lines 9616–10178. Secrecy regime, compartmentation tensions, and scientific communication under military control.
Chapter Seventeen — “Oppenheimer Is Telling the Truth …”
Lines 10179–10767. Security interrogations and truthfulness contests inside the project’s clearance culture.
Chapter Eighteen — “Suicide, Motive Unknown”
Lines 10768–11025. Jean Tatlock’s death and its personal/security repercussions.
Chapter Nineteen — “Would You Like to Adopt Her?”
Lines 11026–11589. Family life at Los Alamos; children and domestic strain under wartime secrecy.
Chapter Twenty — “Bohr Was God, and Oppie Was His Prophet”
Lines 11590–11964. Niels Bohr’s visits; internationalist open-world vision versus military secrecy; Oppie as Bohr’s prophet.
Chapter Twenty-one — “The Impact of the Gadget on Civilization”
Lines 11965–12527. Interim Committee / target and use debates; scientists’ reckoning with civilization-scale effects.
Chapter Twenty-two — “Now We’re All Sons-of-Bitches”
Lines 12528–13442. Trinity test; Bainbridge’s line; path to Hiroshima and Nagasaki use.
PART FOUR
Lines 13443–13446. Part divider: postwar fame, AEC politics, and approaching doom (Chs. 23–33).
Chapter Twenty-three — “Those Poor Little People”
Lines 13447–13900. Immediate Hiroshima aftermath; Oppenheimer’s reaction to Japanese victims and public celebrity.
Chapter Twenty-four — “I Feel I Have Blood on My Hands”
Lines 13901–14468. Truman encounter and blood-on-hands remark; early postwar guilt and policy voice.
Chapter Twenty-five — “People Could Destroy New York”
Lines 14469–15143. International control, Acheson–Lilienthal lineage, and urban-destruction warnings in the new nuclear order.
Chapter Twenty-six — “Oppie Had a Rash and Is Now Immune”
Lines 15144–15919. Security clearance scrapes and the sense (among allies) that he had survived and was “immune”—a false calm.
Chapter Twenty-seven — “An Intellectual Hotel”
Lines 15920–16867. Directorship of the Institute for Advanced Study; Princeton as intellectual hotel and public platform.
Chapter Twenty-eight — “He Couldn’t Understand Why He Did It”
Lines 16868–17544. Personal contradictions, relationships, and self-sabotaging episodes as political enemies gather.
Chapter Twenty-nine — “I Am Sure That Is Why She Threw Things at Him”
Lines 17545–17985. Kitty, domestic turbulence, and the private costs of public pressure (FBI awareness, wiretap lore).
Chapter Thirty — “He Never Let On What His Opinion Was”
Lines 17986–18659. GAC / Super debates; studied ambiguity and the political price of opposing the hydrogen bomb.
Chapter Thirty-one — “Dark Words About Oppie”
Lines 18660–19662. Campaign of dark words from Strauss, Teller circle, and security bureaucrats; Kennan as intellectual ally after the Super fight.
Chapter Thirty-two — “Scientist X”
Lines 19663–19975. FBI/HUAC/Justice closing in (1950); Weinberg estrangement; “Scientist X” spy-hunt shadow over Oppenheimer.
Chapter Thirty-three — “The Beast in the Jungle”
Lines 19976–21007. Henry James story as personal omen; 1953 “two scorpions in a bottle” image; premonition before Strauss’s letter.
PART FIVE
Lines 21008–21011. Part divider: the 1954 inquisition and after (Chs. 34–40).
Chapter Thirty-four — “It Looks Pretty Bad, Doesn’t It?”
Lines 21012–21493. Refusal to resign; Nichols/Green charges machinery; Kafka Trial epigraph for the American inquisition.
Chapter Thirty-five — “I Fear That This Whole Thing Is a Piece of Idiocy”
Lines 21494–22721. Gray Board proceedings skewed from the outset; Strauss’s fear of defection/passport and McCarthy interference.
Chapter Thirty-six — “A Manifestation of Hysteria”
Lines 22722–23414. Defense witnesses (Bethe, Kennan, McCloy, Bush, Conant, et al.); McCloy to Eisenhower on inquiring into a Newton or Galileo.
Chapter Thirty-seven — “A Black Mark on the Escutcheon of Our Country”
Lines 23415–23970. Waiting for Gray Board judgment; Lilienthal’s verdict on public-service wisdom; FBI wiretaps of Oppenheimer’s despair.
Chapter Thirty-eight — “I Can Still Feel the Warm Blood on My Hands”
Lines 23971–24612. Aftermath letters; Rabi: the hearing achieved opponents’ aim—it destroyed him; public and private wreckage.
Chapter Thirty-nine — “It Was Really Like a Never-Never-Land”
Lines 24613–24979. St. John exile from 1954; separate prison renewed in Virgin Islands beauty; Hiilivirta on his humility.
Chapter Forty — “It Should Have Been Done the Day After Trinity”
Lines 24980–25647. Partial rehabilitation under Kennedy/Johnson; Fermi Award (Dec 1963) and Oppenheimer’s charity/courage remark to LBJ.
Epilogue — “There’s Only One Robert”
Lines 25648–25761. Kitty and Serber; Kitty’s death (1972); Frank’s Exploratorium; Peter in New Mexico; Toni’s clearance denial, depression, and 1977 suicide; Oppenheimer Beach.
Author’s Note and Acknowledgments
Lines 25762–26072. Sherwin’s “Long Ride with Oppie” (1979 Perro Caliente research horseback start); twenty-five-year project; Bird partnership; research thanks.
Notes
Lines 26073–33181. Abbreviations (AEC, AIP, DDEL, etc.) and dense chapter notes; Bird/Sherwin collection disposition note.
Bibliography

Illustration Credits / About the Authors / Copyright

Coverage Guide
Formation and European training (pre-wiki continuity)
Chs. 1–7: childhood, Harvard, Cambridge crisis, Göttingen, Caltech/Berkeley “Oppie”—needed to read later loyalty and temperament arguments.
Left politics, Tatlock, Kitty, Chevalier (continuity into clearance fights)
Chs. 8–14: 1936–42 political and personal web that the 1954 hearing will weaponize—essential background for security-case pages.
Los Alamos and the bomb (1942–45 bridge into wiki period)
Chs. 15–22: lab leadership, secrecy, Bohr, Interim Committee, Trinity, use of the bombs—pair with Groves Now It Can Be Told where that source is available in adjacent wikis.
Postwar adviser, IAS, Super, and siege (wiki core)
Chs. 23–33: blood-on-hands politics, international control, Institute directorship, hydrogen-bomb fight, FBI/HUAC, Strauss campaign—central 1945–53 material.
1954 hearing and aftermath (wiki core)
Chs. 34–40 + Preface/Prologue: AEC inquisition, Gray Board, destruction of public role, St. John exile, Fermi Award rehabilitation—McCarthy-era science-and-security centerpiece.
Epilogue (period gate)
Family aftermath into the 1970s: summarize only where completing Oppenheimer’s legacy; do not expand Toni/Frank stories into primary entity pages unless separately sourced for the 1946–89 frame.

sources/burns-crosswinds-of-freedom.content:
The Crosswinds of Freedom
Author: James MacGregor Burns
Published: 1989 (The American Experiment, Vol. 3); Open Road Integrated Media digital edition 2012
Working text: Digital EPUB via Anna’s Archive (hash f147642a4f5c1f5c6029137769e0279c)
Raw extract: wiki/raw/burns-crosswinds-of-freedom.txt (EPUB clean plain text)
Extract stats: 49,341 lines · ~393,555 words · 2,540,679 bytes
Overview
The Crosswinds of Freedom is the third volume of Burns’s American Experiment trilogy, a leadership-focused political and intellectual history of the United States from Franklin D. Roosevelt’s 1932 nomination flight to Chicago through the late Reagan years. Burns organizes the book around contested meanings of freedom—economic security, majority rule, wartime survival, Cold War “imperium,” civil rights and liberation struggles, and late-century cultural and constitutional disarray—tracing how presidents, second-cadre leaders (King, RFK, movement organizers), interest groups, and constitutional structure enable or block transformative leadership.
For this United States 1946–89 wiki the volume is a long-arc scholarly narrative survey: New Deal and wartime baselines (Parts I–II opening chapters) feed directly into Cold War containment and McCarthy-era suspicion (Ch. 5), postwar prosperity and global “freedom” ideology (Chs. 6–7), civil rights, Great Society, Vietnam, and Sixties culture (Chs. 8–10), Nixon–Carter foreign policy and Watergate morality (Chs. 11–12), science/economy/space culture (Ch. 13), and Carter–Reagan leadership decline, party realignment, and constitutional reform debate (Chs. 14–15). Pre-1946 chapters are retained for continuity; the wiki core is Chapters 5–15 plus the personal epilogue.
EPUB structure: front matter and dedication; Contents (PARTS I–V, Chapters 1–15 with subheads, Memories of the Future, Notes, Acknowledgments, Index); King epigraph (Letter from Birmingham Jail); PARTS I–V body; Memories of the Future: A Personal Epilogue; Notes; Acknowledgments; Index; publisher back matter.
Narrative Source Flow
PART I — What Kind of Freedom?
Lines 219–222. Part divider opening the New Deal–era inquiry into freedom, leadership, and majority rule.
Chapter 1 — The Crisis of Leadership
Lines 223–1865. Opens with FDR’s July 2, 1932 Ford Trimotor flight to accept the Democratic nomination in person; campaign strategy between programmatic coherence (Tugwell) and expedience; Hundred Days action; divided progressive/conservative legacies; early New Deal leadership and the question of “discipline and direction under leadership.” Subheads in TOC: The Divided Legacy; The “Hundred Days” of Action; “Discipline and Direction under Leadership”?
Chapter 2 — The Arc of Conflict
Lines 1866–4088. Depression hardship vignettes; NRA and racial/class meanings in the South and North; labor schism (AFL craft unions vs. industrial unionists Lewis, Hillman, Dubinsky); 1936 “we have only just begun to fight” rhetoric; class war, middle paths between Lenin and Christ, politics of tumult, and appeal to the people. Subheads: Class War in America; “Lenin or Christ” or a Path Between?; The Politics of Tumult; Appeal to the People.
Chapter 3 — The Crisis of Majority Rule
Lines 4089–6801. 1936 landslide and the problem of sustaining liberal majorities; court-packing and the “switch in time”; failed congressional purge; 1937–38 return of interest-group deadlock; wage-hour and reorganization fights; cultural left (Waiting for Lefty) and fission of ideas. Subheads: Court-Packing: The Switch in Time; Congress-Purging: The Broken Spell; Deadlock at the Center; The Fission of Ideas; The People’s Art.
PART II — Strategies of Freedom
Lines 6802–6805. Part divider turning from domestic New Deal conflict to war, Cold War, and global strategies of freedom.
Chapter 4 — Freedom Under Siege
Lines 6806–9555. April 1939 Roosevelt appeals to Hitler and Mussolini; zigzag road to war; Lend-Lease and Battle of the Atlantic; production of war; rainbow coalition under strain; Yalta aftermath and FDR’s failing health toward Warm Springs. Subheads: The Zigzag Road to War; The War of Two Worlds; The Production of War; The Rainbow Coalition Embattled.
Chapter 5 — Cold War: The Fearful Giants
Lines 9556–11948. FDR’s February 1945 Yalta report to Congress; death and succession; Kennan’s Long Telegram premises on Soviet official and “subterranean” policy; spiral of fear through Truman–Eisenhower years; price of suspicion; closes through Eisenhower’s military-industrial complex warning, U-2, and claim of having “kept the peace” as stalemate. Subheads: The Death and Life of Franklin D. Roosevelt; The Long Telegram; The Spiral of Fear; The Price of Suspicion.
Chapter 6 — The Imperium of Freedom
Lines 11949–13661. Late-1950s U.S.–Soviet force balances and nuclear arsenals; American economic primacy; technology of freedom; Luce’s “American Century” and critics (Niebuhr, Wallace); language and dilemmas of Freedom versus Autocracy; Khrushchev–Reuther clash over can-can “freedom.” Subheads: The Technology of Freedom; The Language of Freedom; Dilemmas of Freedom.
Chapter 7 — The Free and the Unfree
Lines 13662–15532. Global majority outside the freedom debate—peasant poverty, illiteracy, caloric subsistence; domestic and hemispheric unfree: Boston Irish mobility path, southern poor and TVA as planning complex by 1960, “invisible Latins,” revolutionary Asia; Bowles’s critique of Kennedy-era Third World “realism.” Subheads: The Boston Irish; The Southern Poor; The Invisible Latins; The Revolutionary Asians.
PART III — Liberation Struggles
Lines 15533–15536. Part divider for 1960s civil rights, Vietnam/Great Society upheaval, and women’s liberation.
Chapter 8 — Striding Toward Freedom
Lines 15537–17436. Grassroots black, student, and women leadership versus prior top-down New Deal/Truman policy making; Freedom Rides (Rock Hill, Anniston bus burning); Christian nonviolence to Black Power schism (NAACP vs. CORE 1966); media images of dogs, clubs, and prayer. Subheads: Onward, Christian Soldiers; Marching to War; We Shall Overcome.
Chapter 9 — The World Turned Upside Down
Lines 17437–19419. Johnson’s 1965 legislative flood (Medicare, Voting Rights, HUD, arts/humanities, immigration, water/air quality, school aid); LBJ persuasion techniques; Vietnam escalation, limited war, and failed Indochinese Great Society; generational revolt and Sixties songs (Solidarity Forever displaced by “Yellow Submarine”). Subheads: People of This Generation; Rolling Thunder; Into the Quicksand; Songs of the Sixties.
Chapter 10 — Liberty, Equality, Sisterhood
Lines 19420–20760. Eleanor Roosevelt’s late public role and Kennedy Commission on the Status of Women; younger-branch women’s liberation (Firestone, Freeman, New York Radical Women) versus NOW; personal-is-political organizing; left’s failure of staying power by 1972 contrasted with rising conservative movements and Nixon’s reelection night. Subheads: Breaking Through the Silken Curtain; The Liberation of Women; The Personal is Political.
PART IV — The Crosswinds of Freedom
Lines 20761–20764. Part divider for Nixon–era diplomacy, Watergate virtue politics, and workshop culture.
Chapter 11 — Prime Time: Peking and Moscow
Lines 20765–22178. Opaque Nixon persona; China opening and Moscow summit diplomacy; 1972 Easter Offensive, mining Haiphong, bombing resumed; Vietnam “peace without peace”; catalogue of faltering U.S. foreign-policy experiments since 1932 and the missing sustained comprehensive détente strategy. Subheads: Finding China; Peace Without Peace; Foreign Policy: The Faltering Experiments.
Chapter 12 — Vice and Virtue
Lines 22179–24156. Vietnam’s moral and strategic scars versus earlier wars; Watergate as failed moral leadership and cover-up rationalizations (Magruder); crime and punishment of the Nixon circle; Carter’s arc of morality and human-rights language; gun-and-Bible cultural politics; hypocrisy as evidence of stable justice norms (Walzer). Subheads: Watergate: A Morality Tale; Crime and Punishment; Carter: The Arc of Morality; Gun and Bible.
Chapter 13 — The Culture of the Workshop
Lines 24157–26233. 1960s–70s American science Nobels in medicine, physics, chemistry; Nixon economic phases, wage-price controls, and 1971–74 freeze disasters; rich/poor and land/sky crossways; space program and grounded Hubble as symbol of intellectual failure by late 1980s. Subheads: The Dicing Game of Science; The Rich and the Poor; Crossways, Land and Sky.
PART V — The Rebirth of Freedom?
Lines 26234–26237. Part divider asking whether leadership and freedom can be renewed after the 1970s–80s crises.
Chapter 14 — The Kaleidoscope of Thought
Lines 26238–28108. Carter’s July 1979 Camp David “crisis of confidence” consultations and malaise politics; habits of individualism; Southern California kinesis and Hollywood writers; superspectatorship; New York intellectual life; conservative mall and left’s under-attention to constitutional veto traps as Reagan era dawned. Subheads: Habits of Individualism; Kinesis: The Southern Californians; Superspectatorship; The New Yorkers; The Conservative Mall.
Chapter 15 — The Decline of Leadership
Lines 28109–29898. 1987 Constitutional bicentennial under Iran-Contra and deficit deadlock; Reagan compared unfavorably with Thatcher and Gorbachev; dependent U.S. economy; Republicans waiting for Mr. Right; structure of disarray in separated powers; realignment and “waiting for Lefty”; proposals linking party renewal to constitutional modernization for governable majorities. Subheads: Republicans: Waiting for Mr. Right; The Structure of Disarray; Realignment? Waiting for Lefty; A Rebirth of Leadership?
Memories of the Future: A Personal Epilogue
Lines 29899–30372. Burns from his Berkshire study under Mount Greylock—Thoreau, Melville, Hawthorne, Frost, Williams College—linking local landscape and war memory to the American freedom experiment; closes with space probes, a planned platform named Freedom, and “My Country, ’Tis of Thee.”
Notes
Lines 30373–42120. Extensive chapter notes and citations (primary collections, newspapers, monographs) supporting the narrative from FDR through the 1980s.
Acknowledgments
Lines 42121–42218. Trilogy method: stress on second- and third-cadre leadership; stronger presidential agency assigned to FDR through early LBJ than to late LBJ, Nixon, Ford, Carter, and most of Reagan; corrections to volume 2; research thanks.
Index
Lines 42219–end. Alphabetical index and residual Open Road publisher matter.
Coverage Guide
New Deal baselines and majority-rule problem (pre-wiki continuity)
Chapters 1–3 establish Burns’s leadership frame—FDR nomination and Hundred Days, labor/class conflict, 1936 majority and court/Congress deadlock—needed to read later majority and realignment arguments.
World War II into early Cold War
Chapters 4–5 carry freedom under siege through Yalta, FDR’s death, Kennan, and the spiral of suspicion to Eisenhower’s stalemate peace—core for 1945–60 foreign-policy and domestic-fear chapters in the wiki period.
Postwar imperium, ideology, and global unfree
Chapters 6–7 cover 1950s military-economic power, American Century language, TVA/planning, and Third World/unfree populations—use for prosperity, ideology, and North–South asymmetry.
Liberation movements, Great Society, Vietnam
Chapters 8–10 are the 1960s spine: civil rights tactics and schisms, LBJ legislative peak and Vietnam quicksand, women’s liberation branches, and the 1972 turning point toward conservative mobilization.
Nixon–Carter diplomacy, scandal, and moral politics
Chapters 11–12 treat China/Moscow triangular diplomacy, Vietnam endgame, Watergate, and Carter human-rights/morality arcs—central for 1969–80 political history.
Workshop culture, Carter–Reagan leadership, constitutional structure
Chapters 13–15 and the epilogue document science/economy/space culture, malaise and Iran-Contra-era decline of leadership, party/constitutional reform debate, and Burns’s personal coda.

Barbarians at the Gate
Authors: Bryan Burrough and John Helyar
Published: Harper & Row, 1990; this working text HarperBusiness Essentials / PerfectBound EPUB, September 2003
Working text: Anna’s Archive EPUB hash 26de569c72ed7f0b20075ac0a134bc57

Completeness
Complete as this EPUB: dedications; epigraphs (Adolphus Green; F. Ross Johnson; Jackie Mason on LBOs); Contents; Introduction; The Players; Prologue; numbered chapters 1–18 (unheaded in the EPUB; first-line titles); Authors’ Note; Index; About the Authors; Praise; HarperBusiness Essentials list; Copyright. Pandoc wraps many lines short; body is clean digital English. confidence: high is a quoting-readability cue.
Overview
The book reconstructs the October–November 1988 contest for RJR Nabisco, from Wall Street Journal coverage plus 100+ interviews (January–October 1989). Cast: F. Ross Johnson’s management group with Shearson Lehman Hutton (Peter Cohen, Tom Hill) and later Salomon; Kohlberg Kravis Roberts (Henry Kravis, George Roberts, Paul Raether) with Drexel and Merrill; Ted Forstmann; First Boston (Jim Maher); special committee at Skadden Arps (Charlie Hugel, Peter Atkins). Backstory: Standard Brands, Nabisco, Reynolds Tobacco, Winston-Salem, 19 October 1987 crash. Close: 30 November boardroom. Authors’ Note (2003) on the HBO film and History Channel is post-1989 spill.
Wiki core: 1980s LBO market and this deal. Period-gate Authors’ Note reception after 1989.
Narrative Source Flow
Introduction
Lines 173–214. WSJ fight Oct–Nov 1988; 100+ interviews; Kravis/Roberts/Raether >20 hours; Johnson 36 hours (Atlanta cigarillos; New York pizza). Dialogue reconstructed; italics = the person’s thought.
The Players
Lines 215–396. Management group (Johnson, Horrigan, Robinson, Henderson, Welch, Martin, Sage, Benevento, Goldstone, Bason); American Express (James D. Robinson III); Shearson (Cohen, Hill, Stern); KKR; third parties (Forstmann Little, First Boston); special committee.
Prologue
Lines 397–590. Florida porch: Steve Goldstone as devil’s advocate to Johnson before the LBO is unleashed.
Chapter 1
Lines 591–1094. Spring 1976: Johnson tailed for Henry Weigl at Standard Brands; expense accounts; coup among the young renegades.
Chapter 2
Lines 1095–1752. Winston-Salem as Reynolds company town (1929 HQ as Empire State prototype; Wachovia; Womble Carlyle). Tobacco cash and the modest skyline.
Chapter 3
Lines 1753–2240. Johnson CEO Nabisco 1984, merger 1985, CEO RJR Nabisco 1986; $1 billion tobacco cash; keeps Horrigan; Ferrari in Winston-Salem.
Chapter 4
Lines 2241–2802. 19 October 1987 crash: RJR from mid-sixties to low forties; food stocks recover, tobacco multiple sticks; Johnson eyes Pillsbury.
Chapter 5
Lines 2803–3306. Metropolitan Museum party: Henry Kravis and Carolyne Roehm ($10 million gift); Midori; LBO society New York.
Chapter 6
Lines 3307–3948. 8 October: Peter Cohen’s Gulfstream into Atlanta to meet Johnson; Shearson data; whether Johnson will do the LBO.
Chapter 7
Lines 3949–4370. Johnson the morning after; the management bid taking shape.
Chapter 8
Lines 4371–5210. Friday: Tom Hill in a Pillsbury meeting while the RJR situation moves.
Chapter 9
Lines 5211–5466. Ted Forstmann’s East River duplex breakfast; Forstmann Little as the third-party critic of junk.
Chapter 10
Lines 5467–6442. Shearson Monday pandemonium (Audubon prints); war room after the news breaks.
Chapter 11
Lines 6443–7088. Peace talks off; Kravis 90 tender; Shearson “napalms” planes, penthouses, Premier, clubs, Atlanta HQ; PIK preferred ~11 / $2.5 billion of the KKR bid.
Chapter 12
Lines 7089–8432. LBO as buying a house with someone else’s down payment; mechanics of the auction.
Chapter 13
Lines 8433–9068. 7 November, Skadden Arps: directors sullen; New York Times management-agreement details; Vernon Jordan, John Macomber, Marty Davis, Charlie Hugel.
Chapter 14
Lines 9069–9784. Monday upstairs conference at Skadden; auction process continues.
Chapter 15
Lines 9785–10258. Joke bids by fax (126, 127, Toronto $123 with director payoffs); Atkins and Mike Mitchell for courtroom rules.
Chapter 16
Lines 10259–11180. Stillness on the Street as bids sit.
Chapter 17
Lines 11181–11810. Shearson camp high; Cohen’s anniversary dinner; wait on First Boston’s Maher scheme vs KKR.
Chapter 18
Lines 11811–13082. 30 November, 7:45 a.m., Skadden 35th floor: Atkins “as clear and thoughtful as any day ever spent in a boardroom”; Hugel, Davis, Anderson, Butler, Macomber, Schaeberle, Kreps, Jordan, Medlin; Dillon Read and Lazard; secrecy; the decision.
Authors’ Note
Lines 13083–end matter. Written 1989 in eight months; Harper & Row the only interested house; Pearlstine/Steiger leave; Bryan M&A, John Atlanta; HBO 1993; History Channel 2002. Period-gate this reception block.

Foreign and Military Intelligence (Church Committee Book I)
Author / body: U.S. Senate Select Committee to Study Governmental Operations with Respect to Intelligence Activities (Frank Church, Chairman; John G. Tower, Vice Chairman)
Published: April 26 (legislative day, April 14), 1976 — U.S. Government Printing Office, Washington
Working text: Internet Archive ChurchCommittee — Church Committee Book I - Foreign and Military Intelligence_djvu.txt
Raw extract: wiki/raw/church-committee-book-i-foreign-military-intelligence.txt (IA /download/ full-book OCR)
Extract stats: 41,493 lines · ~305,915 words · 2,244,787 bytes
Citation form: Senate Report No. 94-755, Book I
Overview
Book I is the Church Committee’s principal public final report on foreign and military intelligence. Transmitted by Chairman Frank Church after the fifteen-month inquiry opened under Senate Resolution 21 (27 January 1975), it pairs a structural history of the postwar U.S. intelligence community with institutional chapters on the President and National Security Council, the Director of Central Intelligence, the CIA’s statutory charter and practices, covert action, counterintelligence, the domestic footprint of foreign clandestine work (academia, media, religion), proprietaries, finished intelligence production, internal legal and inspector-general controls, the Department of State, the Department of Defense intelligence apparatus, budget disclosure, chemical and biological agent testing, and a long summary of findings and recommendations. Appendices treat congressional authorization of covert action, outside recommendations on covert action, and Soviet/Eastern European intelligence operations against the United States; members’ additional, separate, and supplemental views and a glossary close the volume.
For this United States 1946–89 wiki the report is a primary institutional source on the Cold War intelligence state as Congress described it in 1975–76: National Security Act of 1947 and CIA Act of 1949 foundations; Korea and “protracted conflict” expansion; third-world covert competition and nuclear crisis; technology and tragedy (including the 1960s–70s crises that forced public investigation); and the mid-1970s demand for permanent oversight under the Constitution. The lens is the Committee’s own: constitutional checks and balances, secrecy versus open government, and the claim that effective foreign intelligence remains necessary while past practices required legislative and executive remedy. Companion Church Committee books (domestic intelligence, assassination interim report, supplementary staff studies, Kennedy assassination agency performance, hearings volumes) are separate works in the same IA collection and are not covered on this page.
OCR note: the IA _djvu.txt is continuous and complete through staff list and GPO imprint, with typical government-scan spacing and occasional character errors (e.g. “PRANK CHURCH,” “INTEODUCTION,” “COXSTITUTIOXAL”). Structure and pagination below follow the printed Contents and body openers.
Front matter
Title page, imprint, and membership
Senate Report No. 94-755, 94th Congress, 2d Session: Foreign and Military Intelligence, Book I, Final Report of the Select Committee to Study Governmental Operations with Respect to Intelligence Activities, United States Senate, together with additional, supplemental, and separate views. Date line April 26 (legislative day, April 14), 1976; GPO Washington 1976; stock no. 052-071-00470-0. Committee roster: Frank Church (Idaho), Chairman; John G. Tower (Texas), Vice Chairman; Philip A. Hart, Walter F. Mondale, Walter D. Huddleston, Robert Morgan, Gary Hart; Howard H. Baker, Jr., Barry Goldwater, Charles McC. Mathias, Jr., Richard S. Schweiker. Staff leadership named: William G. Miller, Staff Director; Frederick A. O. Schwarz, Jr., Chief Counsel; Curtis R. Smothers, Counsel to the Minority; Audrey Hatry, Clerk.
Letter of Transmittal (Church)
Church presents Book I as the foreign-and-military volume of the Final Report after fifteen months’ work. The inquiry arose from allegations of abuse and improper intelligence activity and from public demand that Congress bring the agencies within the constitutional framework. He thanks Tower, Huddleston’s Foreign and Military Subcommittee (with Mathias, Gary Hart, and Goldwater), and the staff under Senate Resolution 21. Despite security limits on public release, he presents the volume as a reasonably complete picture of U.S. intelligence activities and the problems they pose for constitutional government, with Findings and Recommendations at the end.
Contents
Printed table of contents for Parts I–XVIII, Appendices I–III, additional/separate/supplemental views, glossary, national intelligence charts, Senate Resolution 21, and staff list, with page references used below as the printed spine of the book.
Narrative Source Flow
I. Introduction (p. 1)
Opens the Final Report as the first major congressional intelligence inquiry since World War II, driven by allegations of substantial wrongdoing inside the “national intelligence” system and by the duty to review community structure and performance since 1945. Affirms that extensive national intelligence has been vital since 1941 for foreign policy, early warning, arms-limitation verification, counterintelligence, and related missions, while concluding that secrecy’s adverse effects and weak congressional oversight left accountability inadequate. Subsections set mandate (A), purpose of findings and recommendations (B), focus, scope, and obstacles including classification (C), historical context of the inquiry (D), and the dilemma of secrecy versus open constitutional government (E), including the Brandeis warning on well-meaning zeal without understanding.
II. The Foreign and Military Intelligence Operations of the United States: An Overview (p. 15)
Historical overview: America long improvised intelligence in crisis and let it fallow in peace until Pearl Harbor forced permanent institutions. Traces Joint Committee on the Pearl Harbor Attack recommendations (1946), the National Security Act of 1947 as basic charter, and the incomplete treatment of secrecy, accountability, and clandestine missions in that founding moment. Subsections move through secrecy and democracy (A); scope of the Select Committee’s foreign/military inquiry (B); intelligence process theory versus reality (C); evolution of the community (D); origins of the postwar system (E); response to the Soviet threat (F); Korea as turning point (G); “protracted conflict” (H); third-world competition and nuclear crisis (I); technology and tragedy (J); the 1970s (K); and the task ahead (L).
III. The Constitutional Framework for Intelligence Activities (p. 31)
Argues that although the Constitution does not name “intelligence,” foreign-affairs and national-defense allocations create joint legislative–executive responsibility under separation of powers and checks and balances (Madison’s “partial mixture of powers”; Brandeis on precluding arbitrary power). Covers historical practice of secret foreign intelligence (B) and Congress’s constitutional power to regulate foreign intelligence activity (C), grounding later recommendations in shared rather than presidential-only authority.
IV. The President’s Office (p. 41)
Positions intelligence as historically the President’s province—information to classify or share, instruments to use and sometimes abuse—while stressing that the President is the only elected official in the chain of command and is ultimately accountable to Congress and the public. Investigates executive oversight under S. Res. 21 through the National Security Council (A); authorization and control of covert activities (B); providing intelligence required by policymakers (C); advising the President on intelligence issues, including the President’s Foreign Intelligence Advisory Board (D); and allocating intelligence resources, including the Office of Management and Budget (E).
V. The Director of Central Intelligence (p. 71)
From Truman’s January 1946 National Intelligence Authority directive through the 1947 Act’s coordination charge and the DCI as principal foreign intelligence adviser. Examines the unresolved tension among three roles: producer of national intelligence (A); coordinator of community activities without clear command over departmental services (B); and director of the CIA as an agency (C). Frames the DCI problem as structural ambiguity left by a statute written primarily to unify the armed services.
VI. History of the Central Intelligence Agency (p. 97)
Organizational history against the myth of an unfettered monolith: the Agency shaped by international events, pressures from other agencies, and internal norms across twenty-nine years. Periodization: Central Intelligence Group and CIA, 1946–1952 (A); the Dulles era, 1953–1961 (B); change and routinization, 1961–1970 (C); the recent past, 1971–1975 (D); conclusion (E). Stated purposes: explain present structure and illuminate possibilities and obstacles for reform.
VII. The Central Intelligence Agency: Statutory Authority (p. 127)
Close reading of National Security Act §102(d) powers and duties—advise and recommend to the NSC, correlate and evaluate national intelligence, bar on police/subpoena/law-enforcement/internal-security functions, protect sources and methods, services of common concern, and other functions the NSC directs. Applies the charter to clandestine collection (A), covert action (B), and domestic activities (C), testing practice against the 1947 text and later enactments.
VIII. Covert Action (p. 141)
Defines covert action in CIA usage as clandestine operations designed to influence foreign governments, organizations, persons, or events in support of U.S. foreign policy so that U.S. involvement is not apparent. Surveys public controversy (Iran, Chile, Tibet, Guatemala, Libya, Laos, Greece, Indonesia; allegations of assassination, coups, vote buying, economic warfare) and Clark Clifford’s observation that the United States is blamed for nearly every internal difficulty abroad. Treats evolution of covert action (A), congressional oversight including the path to Hughes–Ryan-style reporting (B), and findings and conclusions (C). S. Res. 21’s charge on the extent and necessity of overt and covert activities frames the chapter.
IX. Counterintelligence (p. 163)
Defines counterintelligence as activity to discover hostile foreign intelligence operations and destroy their effectiveness—protection against infiltration, control and manipulation of adversary services, and analysis of inimical clandestine activity—a “secret war” against antagonistic services. Introduction and definition (A); current issues (B); conclusions (C). (Body heading style in the OCR: “IX. CIA COUNTERINTELLIGENCE.”)
X. The Domestic Impact of Foreign Clandestine Operations: The CIA and Academic Institutions, the Media, and Religious Institutions (p. 179)
Documents how foreign-theater clandestine work used American citizens and institutions: university officials and professors providing leads and introductions; scholars and journalists collecting intelligence; journalists devising and placing propaganda; U.S. publications as cover. Traces origins to early Cold War perceptions of a communist threat to international organizations, mass communications, and culture, and records later doubts whether a democracy should secretly use free institutions in ways that blur the difference claimed between systems. Subsections: covert use of academic and voluntary organizations (A); covert relationships with the U.S. media (B); covert use of U.S. religious groups (C).
XI. Proprietaries (p. 205)
Defines proprietaries as CIA-owned business entities that operate or appear to operate as private firms—an “arsenal of tools” whose Vietnam-era scale raised questions about competition with legitimate business (including airlines), secret “back door” funding of covert operations, domestic-impact risks relative to the Agency’s charter, favored treatment by IRS/CAB and others, unknown size, and disposal. Structure covers overview (A), structure (B), operation (C), disposal (D), financial aspects (E), and general considerations (F).
XII. CIA Production of Finished Intelligence (p. 257)
Treats finished intelligence for the President, chief advisers, and Congress as the main purpose of the system; notes policymakers’ perpetual dissatisfaction and the absence of purely objective quality standards. Focuses on the Directorate of Intelligence (DDI) as core of national finished production—strongest analytical organization in government, with acknowledged shortcomings. Subsections on evolution of the Intelligence Directorate (A); the directorate “today” (B); intelligence–policy relationship (C); limits of intelligence (D); personnel (E); recruitment and training (F); analytical culture and bias (G); consensus versus competition (H); “current events” syndrome (I); innovation (J); overload on analysts and consumers (K); quality control (L); consumer guidance and evaluation (M); congressional role (N).
XIII. The CIA’s Internal Controls: The Inspector General and the Office of General Counsel (p. 279)
Reviews General Counsel (A) and Inspector General (B) as instruments for legality and performance under the Director, with internal and external review of the IG office (C). Drawn from interviews, depositions, and a detailed questionnaire; Committee concludes both offices must be maintained and strengthened. Ties the review to S. Res. 21 charges on coordination failures, domestic conformity to charter, sources-and-methods versus the police-powers ban, and information exchange.
XIV. The Department of State (p. 305)
Casts intelligence as service to more effective foreign policy, while noting clandestine activity sometimes became an end insulated from policy oversight. State and the Foreign Service as chief producers and consumers of political and economic intelligence, active in interagency collection/production mechanisms, yet without Defense-like command over clandestine activities essential to mission. Subsections: origins of State intelligence (A); command and control (B); support communications (C); production of intelligence (D). Highlights Foreign Service competition with the Clandestine Service in the field.
XV. Department of Defense (p. 319)
Defense as primary consumer of intelligence, controller of nearly ninety percent of national intelligence spending, and operator of most technical collection systems. Limits public detail for security but presents central findings on national (versus purely tactical) intelligence. Covers objectives and organization of the defense intelligence community (A); defense intelligence budget (B); management problems (C); agencies and activities of special interest (D); military counterintelligence and investigative agencies (E); chemical and biological activities (F); meeting future needs (G). Notes new technology blurring national/tactical boundaries.
XVI. Disclosure of Budget Information on the Intelligence Community (p. 367)
States that aggregate intelligence spending and individual CIA, NSA, and certain Defense intelligence budgets are classified not only from the public but from most Members of Congress. Argues concealment prevents priority judgments, hides funds in other agencies’ open appropriations, and conflicts with the Appropriations Clause’s “regular Statement and Account.” Treats the present budgetary process and consequences (A); constitutional requirement (B); alternatives to total concealment (C); national-security effects of varying disclosure levels (D); slippery-slope and foreign-practice arguments (E–F); summary and conclusion (G).
XVII. Testing and Use of Chemical and Biological Agents by the Intelligence Community (p. 385)
Under the Committee mandate, studies intelligence-agency CB programs: defensive origins against hostile use; shift toward materials to obtain information from or gain control over enemy agents; late 1940s–early 1950s research progressing from witting subjects to unwitting, non-volunteer human testing. Public chapter emphasizes rationale, monitoring and control, and interagency/private relationships; detailed program descriptions reserved to a separately published appendix. Subsections: programs investigated (A); CIA drug testing programs (B); covert testing on human subjects by military intelligence groups (C); cooperation and competition among agencies and with other institutions (D).
XVIII. Summary: Findings and Recommendations (p. 423)
Agenda for remedial legislative and executive action to rebuild consensus on the proper scope of foreign and military intelligence under law and to restore confidence after abuse allegations, press revelations, and the fifteen-month inquiry. Frames the fundamental issue as balancing democratic requirements against necessary secrecy. Structured recommendations and findings: general findings (B); 1947 National Security Act and related legislation (C); NSC and Office of the President (D); DCI (E); CIA (F); reorganization of the intelligence community (G); CIA relations with U.S. institutions and private citizens (H); proprietaries and cover (I); intelligence liaison (J); General Counsel and Inspector General (K); Department of Defense (L); Department of State and ambassadors (M); oversight and the intelligence budget (N); chemical and biological agents (O); general recommendations (P).
Appendix I — Congressional Authorization for the CIA to Conduct Covert Action (p. 475)
Legal-historical brief: covert action not listed as a mission in the 1947 National Security Act or 1949 CIA Act; examines claimed authorities and later statutory hooks. Subparts: National Security Act of 1947 (A); CIA Act of 1949 (B); congressional provision of funds (C); Holtzman and Abourezk Amendments of 1974 (D); Hughes–Ryan Amendment (E); conclusion (F).
Appendix II — Additional Covert Action Recommendations (p. 511)
Collected external statements and recommendations: Clark M. Clifford (A); Cyrus Vance (B); David A. Phillips (C); Morton H. Halperin prepared statement (D); Harvard Institute of Politics Study Group on Intelligence Activities (E); House Select Committee on Intelligence recommendations on covert action (F); Harry Rositzke, “America’s Secret Operations: A Perspective,” Foreign Affairs (G); Tom Braden, “What’s Wrong with the CIA?,” Saturday Review (H); Murphy Commission (Commission on the Organization of the Government for the Conduct of Foreign Policy) recommendations on covert action (I).
Appendix III — Soviet Intelligence Collection and Operations Against the United States (p. 557)
Committee description of large-scale Soviet espionage and “active measures” against the “main enemy,” executed by KGB and GRU and by Soviet-influenced Eastern European services. Targets include U.S. officials and business, scientific, political, youth, journalist, and trade communities. Subparts: introduction (A); organization and structure (B); the GRU (C); scope and methods of KGB/GRU anti-U.S. operations (D); Eastern European security and intelligence services (E).
Additional, separate, and supplemental views
Member statements following the main report and appendices, including additional views of Senator Frank Church; additional views of Senators Walter F. Mondale, Gary Hart, and Philip Hart; introduction to separate views of Senators John G. Tower, Howard H. Baker, Jr., and Barry M. Goldwater; separate views of Tower; individual views of Goldwater; separate views of Baker; supplemental views of Charles McC. Mathias, Jr.; additional views of Richard S. Schweiker. These record concurrence, emphasis, and dissent on the Committee’s recommendations and factual framing (including national-security caution about unduly restrictive recommendations).
Glossary, charts, Senate Resolution 21, staff list
Glossary of selected intelligence terms and abbreviations; national intelligence charts; text of Senate Resolution 21 creating the Select Committee; staff list. Closes with GPO imprint.
Coverage Guide
Founding charter and presidential control (1946–1950s core)
Parts II–VII and Appendix I are the spine for CIG/CIA origins, National Security Act 1947, CIA Act 1949, NSC machinery, DCI ambiguity, and Dulles-era expansion. Use for early Cold War institutional design.
Covert action, third world, and oversight crisis
Parts II (I–K), IV.B, VIII, and Appendices I–II for evolution of covert action, alleged country cases as the Committee frames public controversy, Hughes–Ryan and 1974 amendments, and mid-1970s oversight politics.
Domestic society and private institutions under foreign clandestine programs
Part X (academia, media, religion) and XI (proprietaries) for how foreign intelligence touched universities, press, churches, airlines, and corporate cover inside the United States.
Defense, budget secrecy, and technical collection
Parts XV–XVI for DoD dominance of spending and technical systems, management problems, and the constitutional argument over classified intelligence budgets.
Chemical/biological programs and human testing
Part XVII (with pointer to separate detailed appendix) for late-1940s onward drug and CB programs, CIA and military intelligence testing, and control failures—as stated by the Committee in 1976.
Reform agenda as of April 1976
Part XVIII plus member views for the contemporary reform package: statute rewrite, NSC/DCI/CIA reorganization themes, IG/GC strengthening, State/ambassador roles, budget oversight, CB prohibitions/controls, and residual disagreements among senators.
