Steve Jobs
Author: Walter Isaacson
Published: 2011 (Simon & Schuster)
Working text: Digital EPUB via Anna’s Archive (hash 439c6e1e78297b64eb08b22094143049)
Raw extract: wiki/raw/isaacson-steve-jobs.txt (pandoc plain from EPUB)
Extract stats: 26,109 lines · ~231,174 words · 1,356,383 bytes
Overview
Steve Jobs is Isaacson’s full-life authorized biography, drawn from more than forty interviews with Jobs over two years plus more than a hundred interviews with family, friends, adversaries, and colleagues. Jobs encouraged candor, waived control over the manuscript, and did not read it in advance. The book is a continuous chronological narrative: Characters list; Introduction on how the book came to be; Chapters 1–42 from childhood adoption through legacy, spanning Apple’s founding, the Macintosh, the 1985 ouster, NeXT and Pixar, the 1996–97 return, consumer-electronics reinvention, illness, and death-adjacent reflection.
For this United States 1946–89 wiki the highest-value material is Chapters 1–18 (and related personal chapters): Paul and Clara Jobs in the postwar Bay Area, Homestead High and Wozniak, counterculture and Reed, Atari, Homebrew and Apple I/II, Markkula and the 1980 IPO, Xerox PARC and Lisa, Mac development and the 1984 launch, Sculley, Gates, and the 1985 board crisis, then NeXT’s late-1980s founding. Pixar purchase (1986) and early animation technology sit at the period edge. Chapters 19–42 carry substantial post-1989 spill (Toy Story 1995, Apple restoration 1997+, iMac, stores, iPod/iTunes, iPhone, iPad, cancer). Use post-1989 chapters only for continuity, later consequences of pre-1990 choices, or explicitly marked spill; prioritize pre-1990 U.S. personal-computing, Silicon Valley culture, and corporate-conflict arcs.
EPUB structure: Characters; Introduction; Chapters 1–42; residual notes/back matter in the extract tail of Chapter 42.
Narrative Source Flow
Characters
Lines 278–447. Dramatis personae spanning Jobs’s life: Al Alcorn, Gil Amelio, Bill Atkinson, Chrisann Brennan, Lisa Brennan-Jobs, Nolan Bushnell, Bill Campbell, Edwin Catmull, Kobun Chino, Lee Clow, Debi Coleman, Tim Cook, Eddy Cue, Andrea Cunningham, Michael Eisner, Larry Ellison, through Burrell Smith, Avie Tevanian, James Vincent, Ron Wayne, and Stephen Wozniak. Quick-reference cast for the continuous narrative.
Introduction: How This Book Came to Be
Lines 448–654. Isaacson recounts Jobs’s 2004 biography request after the Franklin and Einstein books; walks as Jobs’s preferred serious conversation; initial demurral then full cooperation with no manuscript control. New Year’s Eve 2009 Palo Alto call with Mona Simpson; cancer context; Henry V muse-of-fire frame opening a tale of two sets of parents and Silicon Valley.
Chapter 1 — Childhood: Abandoned and Chosen
Lines 655–1402. Paul Jobs leaves Coast Guard after WWII, marries Clara Hagopian in March 1946; adopts Steve; Mountain View/Los Altos craftsmanship upbringing; real-estate setback and family strain; school rebellion; Homestead High electronics and lasers. Abandoned-and-chosen theme structures the adoption story.
Chapter 2 — Odd Couple: The Two Steves
Lines 1403–1754. Friendship with Wozniak; Paul Jobs’s deal-making versus Jerry Wozniak’s Caltech/Lockheed engineering ethos. Garage work with Bill Fernandez; Blue Box phreak device establishes the template—Woz invents, Jobs packages and sells—for the Apple partnership.
Chapter 3 — The Dropout: Turn On, Tune In …
Lines 1755–2168. Chrisann Brennan romance; fruitarian diets, unblinking stare, LSD; Reed College path with Daniel Kottke; Zen and Eastern books (Suzuki, Yogananda, Trungpa). Later credits psychedelics and Zen with prioritizing creation and consciousness over money.
Chapter 4 — Atari and India: Zen and the Art of Game Design
Lines 2169–2656. February 1974 Atari job under Nolan Bushnell and Al Alcorn; Bushnell mentors acting in control. India pilgrimage for Neem Karoli Baba; illness and recovery; return with driven entrepreneurial attitude fusing games, Zen, and showmanship.
Chapter 5 — The Apple I: Turn On, Boot Up, Jack In …
Lines 2657–3203. Bay Area fusion of military electronics, hackers, LSD research (Engelbart), hippies, Free Speech politics, and self-fulfillment movements. Homebrew sharing ethic; Woz designs Apple I to give away; Jobs commercializes. Atlantic City fair; SOL-20 contrast teaches finished packaging.
Chapter 6 — The Apple II: Dawn of a New Age
Lines 3204–3729. Vision of fully packaged PC for non-hobbyists; Woz color/board genius; Mike Markkula joins with finance and distribution skill. McKenna: without Jobs the machine stays in hobby shops. Apple II as Woz masterpiece pushing Jobs toward a machine of his own.
Chapter 7 — Chrisann and Lisa: He Who Is Abandoned …
Lines 3730–3951. On-and-off Brennan relationship; pregnancy; Jobs’s denial and cold disengagement; Lisa born 1978. Barren Los Gatos house with Einstein and Maharaj-ji images; Halloween-as-Jesus. Personal abandonment theme mirrored in family life.
Chapter 8 — Xerox and Lisa: Graphical User Interfaces
Lines 3952–4311. Apple II sales boom; Apple III flop (May 1980). Xerox PARC bitmapping/GUI; Raskin advocacy. September 1980 reorganization strips Jobs of Lisa and R&D VP role—non-executive chairman, feels abandoned by Markkula and Scott.
Chapter 9 — Going Public: A Man of Wealth and Fame
Lines 4312–4506. 1977 valuation about 5,309 to December 1980 IPO (most oversubscribed since Ford 1956); 1.79 billion year-end value. Kottke denied options. Shares 22 to 29; Jobs worth $256 million at twenty-five. Sixties idealism versus later careerism.
Chapter 10 — The Mac Is Born: You Say You Want a Revolution
Lines 4507–4811. Raskin’s mass-computer project renamed Macintosh; clash with Jobs over mouse, icons, power. Atkinson sides with Jobs; Raskin loses project. Scott’s layoffs; Markkula interim; Jobs gains full Mac rein.
Chapter 11 — The Reality Distortion Field: Playing by His Own Set of Rules
Lines 4812–5098. Tribble coins reality distortion field (Star Trek) for Jobs’s persuasion and impossible schedules. Hero/shithead binary; idea-appropriation pirouettes; A-player culture; abuse alongside fierce loyalty (Coleman).
Chapter 12 — The Design: Real Artists Simplify
Lines 5099–5466. Eichler modernism, car styling, Sony brochures, Aspen/Italian design influence. Case lines (Porsche not Ferrari); Mercedes detail model. Forty-five signatures engraved inside each Mac; work framed as art.
Chapter 13 — Building the Mac: The Journey Is the Reward
Lines 5467–5946. IBM PC August 1981 dissected and mocked; Welcome IBM ad. Time profile harshness and Lisa Brennan exposure. Engineers defy Jobs on disk drive (Sony vs Alps); he thanks them for disobeying.
Chapter 14 — Enter Sculley: The Pepsi Challenge
Lines 5947–6326. Markkula seeks president; Jobs not ready; Sculley courtship after Estridge unavailable. Pepsi/Apple visits; Mac price raised against team—Jobs later blames high price for slow sales and Microsoft’s rise. Control struggle begins.
Chapter 15 — The Launch: A Dent in the Universe
Lines 6327–6764. 1983 Dating Game with Gates predicting Mac software revenue while Microsoft shifts to IBM PC OS. Ridley Scott 1984 Super Bowl ad. Mac ships; Jobs scorns market research. Neither Raskin nor committees could have made the Mac.
Chapter 16 — Gates and Jobs: When Orbits Intersect
Lines 6765–7084. Binary-star rivalry of two 1955 dropouts; backgrounds contrasted. Mac demos; Gates doubts software cursor elegance. Jobs on Microsoft’s lack of taste; best products do not always win.
Chapter 17 — Icarus: What Goes Up …
Lines 7085–8236. Post-launch celebrity (Warhol, Haring, Jagger); unfurnished mansions. Board crisis; Sculley alliance collapses; spring 1985 showdown and ouster. Russia trip; exile mood—hibernate and reemerge thinking differently.
Chapter 18 — NeXT: Prometheus Unbound
Lines 8237–9224. Paul Berg gene-splicing talk sparks academic workstation company. Rand logo fight over yellow e. Beautiful costly hardware; Gates refuses software and parodies launch. 1989 sales about 400/month vs factory for 10,000; cash burn.
Chapter 19 — Pixar: Technology Meets Art
Lines 9225–9642. 1985 Kay walk to Lucasfilm computer division; Catmull and Lasseter; Jobs buys after Apple refuses. RenderMan limited; Disney CAPS. Wrong hardware bet, right art-plus-digital animation instinct.
Chapter 20 — A Regular Guy: Love Is Just a Four-Letter Word
Lines 9643–10248. Joan Baez romance and Dylan link; sister Mona Simpson reunion (Miyake box, later novel A Regular Guy); Tina Redse spiritual regret. Personal life in wilderness years.
Chapter 21 — Family Man: At Home with the Jobs Clan
Lines 10249–10870. October 1989 Stanford lecture; Laurene Powell front-row meet; marriage. Sparse bachelor party; children; Ellison as rich friend; anti-ostentation Buddhist lesson and no CEO security detail.
Chapter 22 — Toy Story: Buzz and Woody to the Rescue
Lines 10871–11207. Katzenberg partners Pixar for feature; 1993 half-film disaster and rewrite; later equal branding fight with Disney. Jobs on building brands/companies (Apple and Pixar). Primary events post-1989.
Chapter 23 — The Second Coming: What Rough Beast, Its Hour Come Round at Last …
Lines 11208–11643. NeXT hardware fails vs Sun; 1992 NeXTSTEP license. Apple Copland vaporware under Amelio; Be vs NeXT. Acquisition path; Jobs seeks Lasseter blessing to help Apple. 1996-97 reentry.
Chapter 24 — The Restoration: The Loser Now Will Be Later to Win
Lines 11644–12473. Post-forty flourishing; Ellison strategy of board seat until Amelio stumbles. Stock-sale flap; Microsoft detente speech; one-day 33 percent stock jump, about $830 million cap—back from the grave. 1997 center.
Chapter 25 — Think Different: Jobs as iCEO
Lines 12474–12929. Lee Clow and Think Different; crazy ones; Dreyfuss voice chosen over Jobs. Counterculture brand restored; one more thing; Think Profit; FY1998 profit $309 million.
Chapter 26 — Design Principles: The Studio of Jobs and Ive
Lines 12930–13220. Jony Ive nearly quits; great-products philosophy retains him. Craftsman father; simplicity as conquered complexity. Credit tensions; Jobs drives design through resistance.
Chapter 27 — The iMac: Hello (Again)
Lines 13221–13549. May 1998 all-in-one consumer iMac about $1,200; design/engineering unity; Jobs fury over tray button. Translucent Bondi blue hit; slot-vs-tray choice delays rip-burn then forces music leap.
Chapter 28 — CEO: Still Crazy after All These Years
Lines 13550–13889. Operational focus: cut lines, outsource manufacturing, crush inventory. Tim Cook hired 1998. Miyake uniform fails; turtleneck remains. Drops interim title to ovation.
Chapter 29 — Apple Stores: Genius Bars and Siena Sandstone
Lines 13890–14241. Control retail experience vs big-box spiffs; Ron Johnson; Drexler prototype advice; secret Cupertino store lab. Glass cube minimalism. 2000s spill.
Chapter 30 — The Digital Hub: From iTunes to the iPod
Lines 14242–14818. Top 100 retreats; pick three priorities. 2001 digital hub; iTunes; iPod; Gates ‘only for Macintosh?’ Post-1989 music-device arc.
Chapter 31 — The iTunes Store: I’m the Pied Piper
Lines 14819–15456. Legal downloads vs Napster-era piracy; label talks; Iovine on Apple turnkey versus Sony silos. iTunes Store and trusted payments platform. 2002-03+ spill.
Chapter 32 — Music Man: The Sound Track of His Life
Lines 15457–15985. iPod-as-identity culture; Jobs’s library; Dylan boxed set; Yo-Yo Ma Bach and funeral promise. Music as lifelong aesthetic core.
Chapter 33 — Pixar’s Friends: … and Foes
Lines 15986–16642. Jobs lets Lasseter lead at calm Pixar vs volatile Apple. Eisner wars; Iger merger; Catmull/Lasseter at Disney animation. Building great companies. Late spill.
Chapter 34 — Twenty-first-century Macs: Setting Apple Apart
Lines 16643–16935. iBook clam, G4 Cube (MoMA); Motorola fight; secret Intel switch planning. $1 salary versus large grants; handicapped-parking contradiction of rebel and tycoon.
Chapter 35 — Round One: Memento Mori
Lines 16936–17408. 2003 pancreatic shadow on kidney scan; delay and diets; Stanford commencement (dots, love, death). Integrated versus modular philosophy; weak partnering DNA admission.
Chapter 36 — The iPhone: Three Revolutionary Products in One
Lines 17409–17780. Phone threat to iPod; ROKR failure; multi-touch from tablet work; P1/P2 paths. iPhone as three products in one; Kay Dynabook note. 2005-07 spill.
Chapter 37 — Round Two: The Cancer Recurs
Lines 17781–18312. 2008 progression, pain, weight loss, diet obsession. Board/SEC disclosure issues. Brief recovery and product push toward iPad year.
Chapter 38 — The iPad: Into the Post-PC Era
Lines 18313–19069. Tablet ambitions deferred for phone multi-touch; 2010 launch; closed ecosystem; textbooks and publishers. Post-PC consumer computing spill.
Chapter 39 — New Battles: And Echoes of Old Ones
Lines 19070–19587. Android/Google betrayal rant; open vs closed; Flash ban; app control controversies; Beatles on iTunes. Echoes of 1980s platform control fights.
Chapter 40 — To Infinity: The Cloud, the Spaceship, and Beyond
Lines 19588–20066. iPad 2; magnetic cover; yacht as anti-death project; Laurene anniversary; Andrea Cunningham ‘journey is the reward’—Jobs says he learned some things.
Chapter 41 — Round Three: The Twilight Struggle
Lines 20067–20879. Reed’s graduation as goal; family; Obama Valley dinner planning; medical leave; Cook succession. ‘I’ve done all that I can do.‘
Chapter 42 — Legacy: The Brightest Heaven of Invention
Lines 20880–end. Personality-product unity: intensity, end-to-end integration, hero/shithead binary, perfectionism, artistry, control. From 1984 Mac to iPad as one philosophy. Closing legacy judgment; notes/back matter in extract tail.
Coverage Guide
Postwar Bay Area youth and counterculture-to-electronics path (pre-1990 priority)
Chapters 1–4: adoption and Paul/Clara Jobs after 1946, Homestead High, Wozniak partnership, Reed dropout, Zen/LSD, Atari, India. Core for Silicon Valley social history and the human capital of the personal-computer industry.
Apple founding through IPO and Lisa/Mac origins (pre-1990 priority)
Chapters 5–12: Homebrew, Apple I/II, Markkula, Chrisann/Lisa personal crisis, Xerox PARC GUI narrative, 1980 IPO, Raskin Mac project, reality distortion field, industrial design. Spine of U.S. personal-computing business history 1976–84.
Macintosh launch, IBM/Microsoft rivalry, Sculley, ouster (pre-1990 priority)
Chapters 13–17: IBM PC response, Sculley courtship, 1984 ad and Mac launch, Gates relationship, 1985 crisis and departure. Essential for 1980s computer industry structure and celebrity-entrepreneur culture.
NeXT and Pixar beginnings (period edge)
Chapters 18–19: NeXT workstation bet (mid/late 1980s into 1989 sales failure); Lucasfilm computer division purchase and early Pixar hardware/CAPS path. Pre-1990 corporate facts usable; animation triumphs are later.
Personal life across the divide
Chapters 7, 20–21: Brennan/Lisa; Baez, Mona Simpson, Tina Redse; Laurene Powell (from 1989). Use for biography and family dimensions of tech entrepreneurship; marriage and children continue past 1989.
Post-1989 spill (continuity only)
Chapters 22–42: Toy Story and Disney wars; Amelio/NeXT acquisition; Think Different, Ive, iMac; retail stores; iPod/iTunes; iPhone/iPad; cancer; legacy. Mine only when tracing consequences of integrated hardware-software philosophy, design culture, or platform control doctrines formed before 1990. Do not treat 2000s product narrative as primary 1946–89 evidence.

sources/kroc-grinding-it-out.content:
Grinding It Out: The Making of McDonald’s
Author: Ray Kroc with Robert Anderson (Preface by Paul D. Paganucci)
Published: 1977 (Contemporary Books); St. Martin’s Griffin ebook edition August 2016; Afterword © 1987 Robert Anderson
Working text: Digital EPUB via Anna’s Archive (hash 5e2271eadd452dd8a590286782db4dde)
Raw extract: wiki/raw/kroc-grinding-it-out.txt (EPUB via pandoc -t plain)
Extract stats: 6,899 lines · ~70,549 words · 396,704 bytes
Deploy note: Full-text raw is not deployed — wiki/.gitignore ignores *.txt; Quartz ignorePatterns includes raw.
Period-Overlap Note
Wiki core is Chapters 1–2 and 6–16 + Afterword (1954 San Bernardino contract and Des Plaines launch through Sonneborn/Turner, brother buyout, public growth, personal life, Padres, mid-1970s company scale)—inside United States 1946–89. Chapters 3–5 (Florida real-estate interlude, Lily Tulip paper-cup years 1927–37, Multimixer entrepreneurship from 1938) are pre-McDonald’s apprenticeship; the adapted sister page in United States 1920-45 mines those chapters first. Ch. 6’s opening on 1930s California drive-ins is brief continuity before the San Bernardino/Des Plaines hinge.
Overview
Grinding It Out is Ray A. Kroc’s first-person account of building McDonald’s Corporation from a Multimixer salesman’s 1954 visit to the McDonald brothers’ San Bernardino stand into a national (then international) fast-food system. Written with Robert Anderson near the company’s first billion-dollar revenue year, it is salesman autobiography and franchise-operations creed: QSC (quality, service, cleanliness), real-estate leverage via Harry Sonneborn, operations schooling under Fred Turner, friction with the founding brothers, and Kroc’s own marriages, baseball ownership, and “green and growing” philosophy.
For this United States 1946–89 wiki the book is a spine for postwar franchising, standardized food service, and Sun Belt / suburban consumer markets: Des Plaines prototype, Franchise Realty, insurance-company financing, operator culture, 1960s store-count and public-company growth, and the Padres coda. Pre-1954 Lily Tulip / Multimixer chapters supply continuity only here.
EPUB structure: Macmillan front matter; dedication and jacket blurb; Preface (Paganucci, June 1976); Chapters 1–16 (untitled numbered chapters); Afterword (1976 company stats + blurbs); About the Author; Copyright.
Narrative Source Flow
Front matter / dedication / blurb
Lines 1–65. Cover; St. Martin’s ebook notices; dedication with wife Joni to the McDonald’s family; jacket line on Kroc as hamburger salesman, moneymaker, and storyteller (including San Diego Padres P.A. scolding).
Preface (Paul D. Paganucci)
Lines 66–172. Tuck School entrepreneurship frame; Kroc’s 1974 and 1976 Dartmouth visits with Fred Turner; “grinding it out” as thirty-year sales apprenticeship before the 1954 opportunity at age fifty-two; 1976 as McDonald’s first billion-dollar revenue year compared with IBM/Xerox timelines; industry impact on speed, price, fries, and cleanliness expectations. Dated Hanover, N.H., 29 June 1976.
Chapter 1
Lines 173–432. Philosophy of personal responsibility; Lily Tulip and Multimixer flashbacks; news of a San Bernardino stand running eight Multimixers; flight west; meeting Dick and Mac McDonald; Speedee Service System, limited menu, and assembly-line kitchen; Kroc’s offer to franchise additional units—“Well, what about me?”
Chapter 2
Lines 433–778. 1954 return to Chicago with signed contract at age fifty-two (diabetes, arthritis, prior surgeries); gray Chicago landing as omen; early life sketch closing the chapter—piano work, Ethel, Lily Tulip paper cups as America’s direction, father’s assent to marriage.
Chapter 3
Lines 779–1250. Early-1920s Florida underwater-lot boom as winter escape from seasonal cup selling; Kroc as salesman defending honest operators against “alligator lot” folklore; nightclub/piano work; Palm Island; Capone and later Latin Quarter notes; departure before the boom’s collapse.
Chapter 4
Lines 1251–1951. 1927–37 “decade of destiny” in paper cups; John Clark / Sanitary Cup and Service; full-time selling vow; disillusionment and the bargain that pushed Kroc toward Multimixer independence; formation of Prince Castle Sales with corporate capital terms that became an “anchor.”
Chapter 5
Lines 1952–2264. Entrepreneurship credo (Dartmouth 1976 aside); early Multimixer road years from 1938; Frejlack / capital squeeze and Arlington Heights mortgage; sleep discipline as “grinding it out”; stories of the McDonald brothers’ eight-mixer volume pull him west at fifty-two.
Chapter 6
Lines 2265–2653. 1930s Southern California drive-in context; McDonald brothers’ innovation; Kroc’s first Des Plaines store and obsessive standards (fries, cleanliness, detail fights with partner Ed); perfection as non-negotiable.
Chapter 7 — Harry Sonneborn
Lines 2654–2994. May 1955: Tastee-Freeze veteran Harry Sonneborn offers himself after watching Des Plaines; Franchise Realty / site-control logic; June Martino; funding strain while Prince Castle still bankrolls the franchise launch.
Chapter 8 — Fred Turner
Lines 2995–3401. February 1956: twenty-three-year-old Fred Turner answers a franchise ad with Joe Post; $1/hour Des Plaines apprenticeship; rise into corporate operations; seed of the later president/chairman path and operator training culture.
Chapter 9
Lines 3402–3812. Clem Bohr mechanic’s-lien crisis on East Coast sites; Sonneborn’s scramble; Milton Goldstandt path to a $1.5 million loan from three insurance companies for ~22½ percent of stock—financial bridge for expansion.
Chapter 10
Lines 3813–4249. Art Trygg as companion; meeting organist Joni Smith in St. Paul; divorce settlement with Ethel; McDonald brothers’ buyout demand (~$2.7 million / “a million apiece after taxes”); struggle to finance the purchase of name and rights.
Chapter 11
Lines 4250–4577. 1959: Sonneborn named president/CEO after the insurance loan; Kroc as chairman focused on retail/operations; California move and marriage to Jane; brief, jarring call from Joni.
Chapter 12
Lines 4578–4897. Beverly Hills years and 1963–64 construction/earnings surge (110 stores in 1963; 2.1 million net on 129.6 million sales cited for the following year); commuting to Chicago; Sonneborn studying a public offering; coming fight over building redesign.
Chapter 13
Lines 4898–5260. Final confrontation and Sonneborn’s resignation; loneliness at the top; operators’ convention and renewed interest in Roland and Joni Smith of Winnipeg / Rapid City.
Chapter 14
Lines 5261–5883. Reunion with Joni at San Diego Western Region Operators Convention; divorce from Jane and marriage to Joni; impulse to buy the San Diego Padres (“What on earth is that, a monastery?”).
Chapter 15
Lines 5884–6217. 1974 Padres ownership; P.A. microphone blast at opening home game; press and Joni’s reaction; defense of McDonald’s against cheap shots; Truman kitchen line—still not hanging up the spatula.
Chapter 16
Lines 6218–6623. Reincarnation joke about the 1929 Cubs; Kroc Foundation (medical science, not tax shelter); free-enterprise / pioneer-risk closing creed.
Afterword
Lines 6624–6814. Omissions apology; end-1976 snapshot—4,177 stores in the U.S. and 21 other countries; system-wide sales over 3 billion; corporate revenue over 1 billion; net earnings over 100 million; net worth 500 million; still “green and growing”; review blurbs.
About the Author / Copyright
Lines 6815–6899. Author note and Macmillan copyright block (© 1977 Ray A. Kroc; Afterword © 1987 Robert Anderson; Griffin 2016; eISBN 9781250127518). Publisher “About the Author” date line is garbled in this EPUB packaging—use Chronology from the narrative (1902 birth; career through mid-1970s; death 1984 outside this text’s close).
Coverage Guide
Lily Tulip / Multimixer apprenticeship (continuity → 1920–45 sister)
Chs. 3–5: Florida interlude, paper-cup decade, Multimixer independence—brief background here.
San Bernardino to system build (wiki core)
Chs. 1–2, 6–10: 1954 contract, Des Plaines, Sonneborn realty model, Turner operations, Bohr crisis, insurance loan, brother buyout.
Public growth, personal life, Padres (wiki core)
Chs. 11–16 + Afterword: Sonneborn presidency/exit, store surge and IPO path, Joni, Padres, 1976 scale stats.

sources/leebaert-grand-improvisation.title: [source] Grand Improvisation: America Confronts the British Superpower, 1945–1957 (Leebaert, 2018)
sources/leebaert-grand-improvisation.content:
Grand Improvisation
Author: Derek Leebaert
Published: 2018 (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, first edition)
Working text: Digital MOBI via Anna’s Archive (hash 5a15aa457e91e45abcc51e66f9bb5bd3)
Raw extract: wiki/raw/leebaert-grand-improvisation.txt (MOBI → HTML via mobi unpack, then pandoc -t plain)
Extract stats: 26,208 lines · ~217,543 words · 1,396,810 bytes
Overview
Grand Improvisation is a diplomatic and strategic history of Anglo-American relations from the end of World War II through the late 1950s. Leebaert’s central claim is that the familiar “American Century” succession story—Britain too weak to continue, America confidently assuming leadership of a U.S.-led international order—is a myth. Britain did not want out; the United States did not suddenly shed continental insularity. For roughly a dozen years the two powers improvised together and against each other—sterling and Marshall aid, Middle East oil and bases, NATO and rearmament, Korea and Indochina, Iran and Egypt, Churchill’s return and Eden’s Suez—until Washington’s late-1950s break amounted to a practical declaration of independence from British influence.
For this United States 1946–89 wiki the book is a dense early-period spine: Truman–Eisenhower foreign policy, the British Empire/Commonwealth as America’s “outer fortress,” the Korean War as the true push into world political-military power, and the Suez/Hungary/Sputnik hinge into explicit U.S. supremacy. Pre-1946 wartime baselines appear for continuity; post-1957 material is mostly Conclusion spill (later Cold War misunderstandings, China rise, NASA/Webb coda) and should be period-gated.
MOBI structure: Kindle front matter and piracy notice; dedication (Michelle Nyama Kingue / Angela Lindsay Kingue); epigraph from Katharine Lee Bates, “America the Beautiful”; Introduction; Parts I–V with Chapters 1–20; Conclusion; Notes (by chapter); Acknowledgments; Index; Also by / Note About the Author; Macmillan newsletter and copyright block; trailing Contents list.
Narrative Source Flow
Front matter
Lines 1–59. Farrar, Straus and Giroux ebook boilerplate; personal-use / piracy notice; dedication; Bates epigraph (“Confirm thy soul in self-control…”).
Introduction
Lines 60–237. Attacks the baton-passing myth of British collapse and instant American leadership; argues Britain remained a historic military-imperial power covering a quarter of the world’s land and that the United States remained a self-contained continental island-state. Frames the book as a world without American “grand strategy,” every Washington move a desperate improvisation, ending with Sputnik-era dread and Kennedy’s struggle-for-supremacy rhetoric as the later drive that still shapes policy.
PART I — They Thought It Was Peace
Lines 238–246. Part divider (photo caption: FDR and Vice President-elect Truman, 1944).
Chapter 1 — The Three in 1945
Lines 247–1094. Opens with Nat Gubbins’s 1946 sketch of Britain mute in austerity, Russia enormous and suspicious, America a nervous girl with a hand grenade; Hitler’s death and European war’s end; refugee masses; the three victors’ self-images and early postwar dispositions of power, occupation, and peace expectations.
Chapter 2 — Keynes & Co.
Lines 1095–1943. Keynes epigraph on Britain’s refusal to surrender and the price to follow; U.S. wartime boom versus fear of a peace bust / Depression return; Truman reassurances after Japan’s surrender; Anglo-American financial negotiation, Lend-Lease abruptness, and the sterling–dollar settlement struggle that opens the economic half of the improvisation.
Chapter 3 — Entering the Middle East
Lines 1944–2827. Imperial fable of communal conflict as frame; U.S. and British stakes in Middle Eastern oil, bases, and local politics as Washington steps into a region long treated as British imperial ground.
Chapter 4 — False Starts
Lines 2828–3939. Bevin on shocking Americans into consciousness (Feb 1947); Marshall’s China mission failure (Nanjing to Hickam); U.S. democracy/aid experiments ridiculed in the Foreign Office; false starts in China and related early Cold War initiatives that do not yet produce coherent American world policy.
PART II — A Chilling World
Lines 3940–3950. Part divider (Marshall, Bevin, and Ambassador Lewis Douglas, 1947).
Chapter 5 — Warfare States
Lines 3951–4952. Yeager / sound-barrier vignette as American technological swagger; simultaneous 1947 sterling crisis talks (Snyder, Clayton, Yorkshire miners) and Pentagon staff talks on Anglo-American military cooperation—finance and warfare-state building as twin tracks.
Chapter 6 — Year of the Offensive
Lines 4953–5770. 1938 Fascist-offensive analogy applied to Stalin’s 1948 pressure on Czechoslovakia and Berlin; Bevin’s 22 January 1948 Commons speech as a riveting step toward a remade Western order; year of Soviet offensive and Western response.
Chapter 7 — Defending the West
Lines 5771–6767. Bevin in Berlin May 1949 wanting Europe “settled for a couple of hundred years”; U.S. realization that Empire and Commonwealth are vital to protecting non-Soviet Europe; political-economic union and military cohesion seen to depend on Britain; Kremlin denunciations of “Marshallizing Europe in the British manner”; NATO-era Western defense architecture.
Chapter 8 — The Outer Fortress: Protecting the Middle East, Africa, and Asia
Lines 6768–7595. Hubert Humphrey (Sept 1949) calling the British Empire America’s outer fortress; renewed talk of British “bankruptcy” and fear that imperial collapse would pull down European economies before NATO allies could rearm; Middle East, Africa, and Asia as the fortress perimeter.
PART III — Chips on the Table
Lines 7596–7604. Part divider (Truman with Treasury Secretary John Wesley Snyder, 1949).
Chapter 9 — Auditing an Empire
Lines 7605–8450. Harriman’s complaint that America cannot say “No” to Britain; Bevin’s September 1949 Washington mission through early Korean War; Acheson and Snyder scramble to inventory British Empire strengths and weaknesses amid years of collapse talk in editorials and on Capitol Hill.
Chapter 10 — Pivoting to Asia and into Vietnam
Lines 8451–9142. MacArthur’s later claim that America’s existence was entwined with Asia; late-1949 U.S. rescinding of Middle East force commitments as bitter surprise to Bevin and to Admiral Conolly in London; pivot of scarce American “shots” toward Asia and the Indochina/Vietnam problem.
Chapter 11 — War on the Rim
Lines 9143–10032. Chip Bohlen: Korea, not World War II, made the United States a world political-military power; June 1950 Oxford Union regret at U.S. dominance; outbreak and early course of the Korean War as the hinge that forces global U.S. military engagement.
Chapter 12 — Asia’s Three Fighting Fronts
Lines 10033–10899. Acheson 1951: not enough shots to scatter worldwide; Fortress America habits persist despite Korea spending surge and labor strikes delaying buildup; stalemate replaces Dunkirk-evacuation fear; Korea, Indochina, and related Asian fronts as simultaneous drains.
PART IV — The Ground Changes
Lines 10900–10908. Part divider (Acheson and Eden, 1952).
Chapter 13 — “Holding the Ring” in Iran and Egypt
Lines 10909–11727. Ambassador Grady on British expectation that America follow British Middle East policy; Korea’s casualty scale versus expanding global commitments; Iran and Egypt crises as Britain “holding the ring” while seeking U.S. strength for British aims.
Chapter 14 — Churchill Is Back
Lines 11728–12639. Churchill quoting Cromwell to Truman on being versus well-being; 26 October 1951 return to office; cabinet of older men at Hyde Park Gate; renewed personal Anglo-American summit diplomacy under a second Churchill premiership.
Chapter 15 — Stemming the Tide
Lines 12640–13446. Churchill ready to learn if not always to be taught; Oliver Franks’s claim that Americans never have grand strategies—only ad hoc decisions under domestic stress; 1952 efforts to stem Communist and imperial-tide problems without a settled U.S. design short of outright war; Malaya (Templer, herbicides) and Kenya/Mau Mau as British colonial wars on a different scale from Korea.
Chapter 16 — Coronations and Crises
Lines 13447–14353. Eisenhower on leadership as getting others to want what you want; Eden’s pre-election plea that Ike not appoint Dulles; coronation-year politics and overlapping Middle East / European crises as Eisenhower–Dulles diplomacy begins.
PART V — A New Supremacy
Lines 14354–14367. Part divider (Eisenhower and Churchill at Bermuda 1953; Dulles 1954).
Chapter 17 — The Break Points of 1954
Lines 14368–15296. Dulles on success as not facing the same problem twice; Eisenhower’s January 1954 State of the Union inventory (Korea halt, Indochina aid, Europe unity, Iran “victory,” Middle East impartial friendship); 1954 as a cluster of break points that test whether America yet holds strategic initiative.
Chapter 18 — Ordering Chaos
Lines 15297–16220. Churchill warning that U.S. isolation would doom Europe and Britain; mid-1954 to early-1956 surge of American wealth, population, Fortune 500 earnings, and resolve relative to the Empire; attempts to order post-Korea, European, and Middle Eastern chaos from a position of growing material supremacy.
Chapter 19 — No End of a Lesson
Lines 16221–17272. Dulles refusing to champion the status quo; New Year 1956 review (Baghdad Pact, West Germany in NATO); Suez crisis and the harsh education of British (and French) power against American opposition—no end of a lesson in who now sets limits.
Chapter 20 — What Happened Next
Lines 17273–18172. Eisenhower on the psychological advantage of putting “the thing” up without hysteria (Oct 1957); post-Suez and Hungary sense that America’s world place had shifted more than in the late 1940s; from improvising into NATO and failing to impose liberal trade on Britain, through Korea’s push to global power, toward Sputnik-era recognition that only Washington and Moscow compete at the highest level.
Conclusion
Lines 18173–18573. Avoids casual “Cold War” label; argues each continent/decade had its own cold war and that late-century myths about how the conflict ended are as flawed as early ones; Bevin and Churchill’s effort to dispel American insularity; China rise analogy; remembrance of forgotten operators (Snyder, Douglas, MacDonald) versus James Webb’s NASA/civil-rights/graduate-education legacy and the James Webb Space Telescope coda on science as America’s historic advantage.
Notes
Lines 18574–23264. Chapter-by-chapter endnotes (Introduction through Conclusion) with archival citations (FO 371, HSTL, DDEPL, RG 59, ADST, etc.).
Acknowledgments
Lines 23265–23375. Research and institutional thanks.
Index
Lines 23376–25926. Alphabetical index.
Back matter
Lines 25927–26208. Also by Derek Leebaert; A Note About the Author (Knowledge Exchange site); Macmillan newsletter signup; copyright page (© 2018 Leebaert; maps © Jeffrey L. Ward; First edition 2018; e-book ISBN 978-0-374-71406-2); residual footnote-style asterisks; trailing Contents list.
Coverage Guide
Myth-busting frame and 1945 baselines
Introduction + Ch. 1 set the wiki’s early Cold War interpretive problem: no clean baton pass; three victors, austerity, and American unreadiness.
Sterling, Marshall, and the economic improvisation
Ch. 2 and Parts of Chs. 5, 7–9 cover Keynes/settlement, 1947 crisis, Marshallizing Europe “in the British manner,” and empire audit—core for postwar political economy pages.
Middle East as contested imperial ground
Chs. 3, 8, 10 (retrenchment), 13 (Iran/Egypt), 16–19 (to Suez) are the densest Middle East sequence for 1946–57 entity/event work.
Western defense and NATO
Chs. 5–7 carry warfare-state cooperation, 1948 offensive year, Berlin, and defending the West—use beside Church Committee and Burns for institutional Cold War pages.
Asia pivot, Korea, Indochina
Chs. 10–12 (and Malaya material in Ch. 15) document the shot-scattering problem and Korea as world-power hinge—priority for Korean War and early Vietnam commitment pages.
Churchill–Eden–Eisenhower–Dulles endgame
Chs. 14–20 cover the second Churchill government through Suez, Hungary, and Sputnik-era supremacy—wiki core for 1951–57 diplomacy.
Conclusion (period gate)
Use sparingly for later Cold War / China / NASA echoes; do not let 1960s–2020s coda drive entity pages outside the book’s 1945–57 spine unless completing a story already opened inside the period.

sources/lyons-david-sarnoff.title: [source] David Sarnoff: A Biography (Lyons, 1966)
sources/lyons-david-sarnoff.content:
David Sarnoff: A Biography
Author: Eugene Lyons
Published: 1966 (Harper & Row, New York; first edition)
Working text: Digital PDF via Anna’s Archive (hash e30c54dd944dfea91261cdfdaf2d8e20)
Raw extract: wiki/raw/lyons-david-sarnoff.txt (pdftotext -layout)
Extract stats: 15,099 lines · ~159,840 words · 1,028,553 bytes
Deploy note: Full-text raw is not deployed — wiki/.gitignore ignores *.txt; Quartz ignorePatterns includes raw.
OCR note: Scan OCR (pdftotext -layout); frequent hyphenation and name garbling (Samoff for Sarnoff, Bom for Born).
Overview
David Sarnoff is Eugene Lyons’s life of the RCA chief—immigrant childhood through electronics leadership: ghetto childhood in Russia; New York slums and Marconi messenger/operator years (including Titanic survivor traffic); commercial manager and “radio music box” prophecy; creation of the Radio Corporation of America; NBC networks and talkie/phonograph alliances; Depression research stubbornness and the fight for television; World War II mobilization and European theatre service; postwar “father of television,” color-TV triumph, setbacks, public-figure roles, and still-active eighth decade as of the mid-1960s.
For this United States 1946–89 wiki the core is Chapters 20–26: postwar TV industry leadership, color struggle, corporate succession (Robert Sarnoff), failed crusades, public-figure honors, and 1950s–60s electronics stature. Chapters 1–19 are continuity from earlier U.S. period wikis (especially 1920–45). Period-gate hard on pre-1946 narrative except where needed to finish stories already under way after 1945.
PDF structure: jacket/title/copyright; dedication; Contents (Chs. 1–26 + Index); Chapters 1–26; Index; residual jacket blurbs.
Narrative Source Flow
Front matter
Lines 1–301. Jacket copy; title; books by Lyons; Harper & Row 1966 copyright (LC 66-10632); dedication to grandchildren; Contents.
Chapter 1 — Success Story
Lines 302–766. Frames Sarnoff as rags-to-riches classic of the electronic age—radio, TV, satellites, gadgetry—rather than merely another fortune tale.
Chapter 2 — Twin of the Electron
Lines 767–1286. Birth of wireless as long scientific arc; Sarnoff’s life paired with the electron’s industrial coming-of-age.
Chapter 3 — Boyhood in the Promised Land
Lines 1287–1901. Immigrant arrival; New York “promised land” boyhood and early American weeks.
Chapter 4 — The Formative Years
Lines 1902–2497. Marconi Wireless Telegraph Company apprenticeship; formative wireless-operator years.
Chapter 5 — The Titanic and the Music Box
Lines 2498–3191. 1912 voting-age year; Titanic wireless traffic fame; early “radio music box” vision for broadcasting.
Chapter 6 — The Radio Corporation Is Born
Lines 3192–3774. Commercial manager role; RCA’s birth from Marconi/GE wartime communications complex.
Chapter 7 — “Sarnoff’s Folly”
Lines 3775–4380. Early RCA push for broadcasting dismissed as folly; Sarnoff’s energy inside the new corporation.
Chapter 8 — The Self-Appointed Leader
Lines 4381–4875. After age thirty (May 1921), self-assertion as industry leader.
Chapter 9 — Prophet with Honor
Lines 4876–5517. Forecasts of industry growth; forums with Hoover-era figures; prophet reputation.
Chapter 10 — Networks and Talkies
Lines 5518–5995. Private life (Lizette; sons Robert, Edward, Thomas) beside network building and phonograph/talkie alliances.
Chapter 11 — A New President Is Born
Lines 5996–6593. Phonograph–radio “marriage”; path to RCA presidency.
Chapter 12 — Double Trouble
Lines 6594–7119. Presidency amid Depression dual crises for radio industry and company.
Chapter 13 — The Roosevelt Years
Lines 7120–7908. Depression research as first ballast to cut—Sarnoff refuses to jettison R&D under bookkeeping pressure.
Chapter 14 — Quest for Quality
Lines 7909–8535. September 1937 board/quality drive; programming and technical standards agenda.
Chapter 15 — Struggle for Television
Lines 8536–9219. Prewar and wartime TV development fight; antenna forest as postwar symbol introduced retrospectively.
Chapter 16 — At the Half-Century Mark
Lines 9220–9648. WWII decorations and half-century career mark framing.
Chapter 17 — Another World War
Lines 9649–10037. 7 Dec 1941 offer of RCA facilities to FDR; electronics switch to military radio, radar, tubes, navigation.
Chapter 18 — In the European Theatre
Lines 10038–10528. Near age fifty-one; wartime service in the European theatre.
Chapter 19 — D Day and After
Lines 10529–11031. Allied invasion and Sarnoff’s wartime communications role through war’s end.
Chapter 20 — Father of Television
Lines 11032–11646. Dec 1944 Television Broadcasters Association award of the title “Father of Television”; postwar TV push—wiki core begins.
Chapter 21 — Roster of Setbacks
Lines 11647–12291. Late-1940s setbacks (Newsweek Dec 1949 cover era); competitive and regulatory bruises.
Chapter 22 — Triumph for Color
Lines 12292–12716. Color television hammered out at Princeton labs; 1951 forty-five-year association celebration.
Chapter 23 — Tribute in Gold
Lines 12717–13230. Dec 1955: Robert Sarnoff named RCA president/CEO; succession tribute.
Chapter 24 — The Crusade That Failed
Lines 13231–13575. Firm opinions on domestic/world problems; a public crusade that fails.
Chapter 25 — The “Public Figure”
Lines 13576–14173. FDR-era request beginnings of public-service persona; postwar public-figure stature.
Chapter 26 — In the Eighth Decade
Lines 14174–14638. 1961 Capitol Hill luncheon honor (55th anniversary with radio); still-active eighth decade as Lyons writes.
Index
Lines 14639–end. Index and residual jacket blurbs.
Coverage Guide
Immigrant wireless years through RCA birth (continuity → 1866–1919 / 1920–45)
Chs. 1–6: Russia/NY boyhood, Marconi, Titanic, RCA founding—mine primarily in earlier sister wikis.
Radio networks, Depression, TV struggle, WWII (continuity → 1920–45)
Chs. 7–19: “folly,” NBC era, Roosevelt-years research, television fight, Dec 1941–D-Day service—primary for 1920–45.
Postwar TV, color, succession, public figure (wiki core)
Chs. 20–26: Father of Television title, setbacks, color triumph, Robert Sarnoff succession, failed crusade, public honors into the 1960s—primary for this wiki.

sources/mansfield-vision-saga-of-the-sky.title: [source] Vision: A Saga of the Sky (Mansfield, 1956)
sources/mansfield-vision-saga-of-the-sky.content:
Vision: A Saga of the Sky
Author: Harold Mansfield
Published: 1956 (Duell, Sloan and Pearce, New York; First Edition; Library of Congress 56-9591; copyright © 1956 by Harold Mansfield)
Working text: Scanned PDF via Anna’s Archive (hash 519b658d106d9c0ea1aa2c7341cff4c2; OCLC 1151666232)
Raw extract: wiki/raw/mansfield-vision-saga-of-the-sky.txt (pdftotext -layout from scanned PDF)
Extract stats: 14,780 lines · ~130,567 words · 794,842 bytes
Deploy note: Full-text raw is not deployed — wiki/.gitignore ignores *.txt; Quartz ignorePatterns includes raw.
Period-Overlap Note
This source has been copied from United States 1920-45 into the United States 1946–89 wiki because Books Four–Five cover swept-wing jet bomber studies, Stratocruiser, B-47/B-52, tankers, the 707 board decision, Bomarc missiles, and Cold War outlook—core postwar Boeing for this period. Mine those books first. Use Books One–Three (founding through WWII Fortress/Superfortress) only as continuity from the 1920–45 sister page.
Overview
Vision: A Saga of the Sky is Harold Mansfield’s thematic company saga of Boeing—not a formal corporate history but a narrative built on scores of interviews, records, and rechecks with participants (research assisted by Reynolds Phillips of Boeing Magazine). Mansfield centers engineering progress and individual vision (Egtvedt, Johnson, Allen, Wells, Schairer, Beall, Eddie Allen) rather than manufacturing detail. The frame is engineer John Haberlin preparing a speech at a 1950s thirty-year-awards banquet, looking back forty years from fabric-covered machines to the 707 jet and pilotless-aircraft work.
For this United States 1946–89 wiki the book is the principal near-contemporary Boeing jet-age account: postwar design leap, Stratocruiser bet, B-47/B-52, tanker-transport bridge to the 707, missiles/Bomarc, and Bill Allen–era commercial jet decisions. Period-gate Books One–Three to continuity except where needed to complete a postwar story.
Book structure: Foreword; Book One — THE CHALLENGE (10 chs.); Book Two — THE INSPIRATION (10 chs.); Book Three — THE TEST (8 chs.); Book Four — THE REALIZATION (11 chs.); Book Five — THE OUTLOOK (5 chs.); airplane timeline plates; illustrations lists.
OCR caveat: Raw text is pdftotext -layout from a scanned first edition. Expect hyphenation noise (¬), form-feeds, running headers (“VISION”), garbled chapter numerals/titles, and medium confidence on fine orthography; high confidence on overall structure and line-range anchors below.
Narrative Source Flow
Front matter / airplane timeline plates / title
Lines 1–122. OCR-noisy Boeing airplane timeline plates (1915–1955 types from B&W through 707 and Bomarc); title page Vision: A Saga of the Sky; Duell, Sloan and Pearce imprint; copyright © 1956; LC 56-9591; First Edition; Van Rees Press.
Contents
Lines 123–203. Five-book table of contents: Book One The Challenge through Book Five The Outlook with chapter titles from “Just Forty Years?” through “Vision.”
Illustrations lists
Lines 204–263. Photo plates (Model C, PW-9, 247, Fortress, Superfortress, B-47, 707, Bomarc, etc.) and in-text illustration page references.
Foreword
Lines 264–306. Mansfield disclaims official Boeing endorsement; states the book is factual but interpretive, engineering-centered, and focused on selected individuals; credits Reynolds Phillips’s research assistance.
Book One — THE CHALLENGE (lines 307–3326)
Chapter 1 — Just Forty Years?
Lines 312–397. Opens in the 1950s with Haberlin watching a 707 fly over Seattle while assigned to pilotless-aircraft work; his banquet-speech assignment triggers a forty-year lookback at aviation’s acceleration from ~70 mph to jet speeds.
Chapter 2 — Meant to Fly
Lines 398–809. Bill Boeing at Dominguez Field (1910), thwarted by Louis Paulhan and Wright patent litigation; Westervelt partnership; early Seattle flying; Wong’s Model C stability innovations; Herb Munter’s test flights on Lake Union; Navy interest as America nears WWI entry.
Chapter 3 — Learning Things
Lines 810–1067. Wong applies Eiffel wind-tunnel thinking to Model C inherent stability; Navy school-plane competition; Munter’s control disputes; first flight November 1916; growing wartime production pressure.
Chapter 4 — Out of the Storm Cellar
Lines 1068–1319. Model C trials at Pensacola—Munter’s high-angle low-speed technique, rough-water tests; Navy acceptance; Boeing’s reputation as a serious designer amid fragile early aviation.
Chapter 5 — Production Needed
Lines 1320–1679. Armistice letter: Navy may halve HS-2L orders; Boeing urges flying-boat commercial development and side furniture/fixture work; B-1 flying boat; Vancouver airmail flight March 1919; postwar slump and payroll strain.
Chapter 6 — Airplanes, Not Cement Sidewalks
Lines ~1680–1841 (approximate). Egtvedt’s plea to keep engineering alive (“airplanes, not cement sidewalks”); Boeing backs R&D; Billy Mitchell’s GAX armored attack triplane; McCook Field contracts; MB-3A pursuit order brings production holiday to Seattle shops.
Chapter 7 — The Pursuit
Lines 1842–2564 (Ch. 8 Trials overlaps this band in OCR). MB-3A license production vs. original design frustration; metal-wood joint experiments and arc welding; PW-9 pursuit lineage; Navy fighter competitions; Haberlin’s crossed-wire fix wins forty-plane order.
Chapter 8 — Trials
Lines ~2183–2564 (OCR fuzzy—digest from TOC and pursuit/mail thread). NB trainer spin crises and Mitscher flight tests; tail-surface redesign battles with the Navy; production backlog and reputation risk before 1925 reorganization.
Chapter 9 — Much to Be Discovered
Lines 2565–2856. Boeing resumes presidency; Egtvedt chief engineer; PW-9C combat competition; Wasp engine breakthrough; experimental organization under Monteith; auto-rotation/spin research culture.
Chapter 10 — Flying the Mail
Lines 2857–3326. Hubbard’s Chicago–San Francisco airmail bid; Model 40 mail plane; Boeing Air Transport; Admiral “Bull” Reeves’s carrier-deck lecture on battleship vs. airplane striking power—stimulus for bigger, better aircraft.
Book Two — THE INSPIRATION (lines 3327–6600)
Chapter 1 — The All-Metal Idea
Lines ~3354–3717. Egtvedt visits Admiral Reeves (1928); Eddie Hubbard’s hotel-room sketch for an all-metal low-wing monoplane mail plane; Monteith’s cantilever/flutter fears; commitment to smooth monocoque skin.
Chapter 2 — Bomber Experiment
Lines 3718–4134. European tour (Dornier Do-X); Egtvedt launches Boeing bomber design; B-9 monoplane bomber; Martin B-10 competition politics; lessons on enclosed cockpits, speed, and Army procurement.
Chapter 3 — Why Not a Twin-engine Transport?
Lines ~4135–4568. Model 247 lineage after B-9 loss to Martin; United Air Lines pressure; February 1933 first flight—“they’ll never build ’em any bigger”; Mansfield’s “diminishing returns” vs. progress theme.
Chapter 4 — Project A
Lines ~4429/4569–4780. XB-15 “Project A” long-range bomber—30-ton, 5,000-mile ambition; Pratt/Wright Field politics; parallel four-engine transport studies; engineering of passageways, turrets, and unprecedented scale.
Chapter 5 — Flying Fortress
Lines 4781–5058. Model 299 (B-17 prototype) nonstop Seattle–Dayton flight; Wright Field competition vs. B-12/B-18; October 1935 crash from locked control surfaces; Army buys thirteen YB-17s despite disaster.
Chapter 6 — The Transoceanic Step
Lines 5059–5965. Beall’s dining-table Clipper sketches from XB-15 wings; Pan American 314 contract; Eddie Allen’s transoceanic flight tests; June 1939 Clipper first flight amid press and engineering drama.
Chapters 7–9 — Over the Weather / Running Ahead / Extremity
Lines ~5220–6440 (grouped; OCR chapter breaks fuzzy). Army GHQ bombardment procurement debates over B-17 after Dayton crash; XB-15 as symbol of “running ahead”; Stratoliner pressurization; Clipper weight/CG and sea-handling extremes before proving long-range flying boats.
Chapter 10 — Lightning Strikes
Lines 6441–6600. Eddie Allen proposes permanent combined flight-test and wind-tunnel research department reporting outside line engineering; Model 341 superbomber mock-up tube crawl; Phil Johnson’s RFC refinancing and Plant Two planning as war looms in Europe.
Book Three — THE TEST (lines 6601–9708)
Chapter 1 — Mounting Pressure
Lines 6613–~6775. Phil Johnson returns; RFC loan and stock issue wipe deficit; B-17 option fights with War Department; French Douglas-bomber license; mounting European crisis; “superbomber” word enters public imagination (1939).
Chapter 2 — Superbomber Crisis
Lines ~6776–7393 (no clean OCR chapter head; flows from Mounting Pressure). Model 345 submission; Blitzkrieg accelerates requirements; Echols demands B-17E armament; B-29 contract and 990-plane schedule; XB-29 structure and pressurization engineering.
Chapter 3 — War
Lines ~7394–7876. December 7, 1941; 19th Bombardment Group in Philippines—Kelly, O’Donnell, Wheless Fortress actions; retreat through Java and Australia; Rangoon raids; B-29 as distant hope; Eddie Allen flight-test group under wartime strain.
Chapter 4 — Around the Clock
Lines 7877–8290. Eddie Allen’s collaborative flight-test philosophy; 8th Air Force buildup; Ira Eaker to England; Knudsen production surge; Fortress modification for combat; shift to around-the-clock Seattle output.
Chapter 5 — Red Streak Program
Lines 8291–~8515. Summer 1943 8th Air Force offensive; August 17, 1943 Regensburg–Schweinfurt double mission planning; LeMay leads; “Flying Fortress against Fortress Europe.”
Chapter 6 — Fortress Against Fortress
Lines ~8516–8881. Deep-penetration losses (16% on August 17); Schweinfurt/Regensburg results; bomber-escort math; continuing Eaker/Anderson pressure to hit German aircraft industry.
Chapter 7 — Battle of Kansas
Lines 8882–~9299. B-29 engine and field-modification crisis; Salina/Pratt modification centers; first China-based raids on Japan; typhoon ditching lessons; Hap Arnold’s urgency to make Superfortress combat-ready.
Chapter 8 — Victory
Lines ~9300–9708. LeMay’s low-altitude incendiary gamble over Tokyo; production transition from B-17 to B-29 lines; XC-97 flight previews postwar transport; Beall’s Pacific tour; Bill Allen’s presidency notes; war’s end and reconversion anxiety.
Book Four — THE REALIZATION (lines 9709–13702; period gate → 1946–89)
Opening / jet-bomber studies / swept wing (Ch. 1 area)
Lines 9709–~9921. Post-VJ-Day jet and turboprop bomber studies; compressibility/Mach tunnel work; Phase One contract; Schairer–Tsien transatlantic slide-rule session discovers swept-wing drag advantage (May 1945).
Chapter 2 — Bet on the Stratocruiser
Lines 9922–~10174. September 1945 board meeting; Allen elected president; B-29 cutbacks vs. Model 377 Stratocruiser commercial bet; peacetime employment cliff.
Chapters 3–9 — B-47 through tankers (grouped; OCR titles fuzzy)
Lines ~10175–12864. XB-47 Stratojet development and first flight; range/compressibility dilemmas; Wichita production struggles (“second Battle of Kansas”); XB-52/YB-52; KC-97/KC-135 tanker competition; Allen’s price-first sales philosophy; Soviet threat driving jet bomber schedules.
Chapter 10 — The Case for the 707
Lines 12865–~13268. April 1952 board unanimously approves jet transport prototype; tanker-transport crossover design; B-52 first flight and 707 business case meeting (Barton, Pennell, Schairer, Wood).
Chapter 11 — Missiles and Nuclear Weapons
Lines 13269–13702. Post-707 prototype organization; Bomarc/GAPA missile lineage; nuclear-age defense framing; engineering shift toward electronics and materials.
Book Five — THE OUTLOOK (lines 13703–~14780; period gate → 1946–89)
Chapter 1 — Air Force First
Lines 13724–~13944. “Under God” Pledge of Allegiance episode; Allen defers commercial jet sales until KC-135 tanker decision; military production priority over Stratoliner.
Chapter 2 — Bomarc on the Track
Lines 13945–~14136. Bomarc ramjet test success; Wood’s vision of automated air defense; telemetry and H-bomb deterrence context.
Chapter 3 — The Open Mind
Lines 14137–~14183. Allen’s reverse-pricing for 707; Renton plant evidence for parallel tanker/commercial production; engineers on titanium, rockets, and outer-space horizons.
Chapter 4 — Progress and Principle
Lines 14580–~14592 (OCR jumps; section spans ~14184–14579). Peacetime competition as source of great Boeing designs; LeMay on SAC deterrence; Wells on moon-shot feasibility with funding and unity.
Chapter 5 — Vision
Lines ~14593–end plates. Haberlin’s banquet speech—challenge/inspiration/test/realization/outlook cycle; tension between technical progress and human peace; closing timeline plates and library stamp.
Coverage Guide
Founding through WWII (continuity ← 1866–1919 / 1920–45)
Books One–Three: brief background only.
Postwar jets, Stratocruiser, B-47/B-52 (wiki core)
Book Four Chs. 1–9: swept wing, Stratocruiser, Stratojet, B-52, tankers/transports.
707 and missiles (wiki core)
Book Four Chs. 10–11 + Book Five: Case for the 707, Bomarc/nuclear weapons, Air Force–first policy, open-mind/pricing, progress and principle, Haberlin banquet close.
