sources/miller-chip-war.content:
Chip War: The Fight for the World’s Most Critical Technology
Author: Chris Miller
Published: 2022 (Scribner / Simon & Schuster)
Working text: Digital EPUB via Anna’s Archive (hash bf71a2befb21c6232b081ed68aadc036)
Raw extract: wiki/raw/miller-chip-war.txt (pandoc plain from EPUB)
Extract stats: 11,910 lines · ~106,759 words · 691,649 bytes
Overview
Chip War is Chris Miller’s synthetic history of semiconductors as strategic technology: from the transistor and integrated circuit through Cold War military and NASA demand, Fairchild and Intel, Japanese memory competition, Korean and Taiwanese manufacturing ascent, personal-computer and fabless shifts, and twenty-first-century U.S.–China rivalry over advanced logic and lithography. Miller writes in short chapters grouped into parts, mixing firm-level stories with state policy and supply-chain geography.
For this United States 1946–89 wiki, period-gate hard: prioritize Introduction and early parts on U.S. invention, Pentagon/offset demand, Silicon Valley founding firms, Soviet copying limits, Japan’s 1980s challenge, and the beginnings of offshore assembly and Taiwan’s foundry path as they appear through 1989. Later parts on 1990s–2020s globalization, China’s rise, ASML EUV, and export controls are continuity/spill only—do not treat them as primary evidence for 1946–89 without clear backward linkage. The book’s presentist frame is external to the wiki’s contemporary lens; mine what actors did and said in-period.
EPUB structure: Introduction; PARTS I–VIII with Chapters 1–54; Conclusion; Acknowledgments; Notes; Index. Part titles in this extract mapping: Cold War Chips; The Circuitry of the American World; Leadership Lost?; America Resurgent; Integrated Circuits, Integrated World?; Offshoring Innovation?; China’s Challenge; The Chip Choke.
Narrative Source Flow
Introduction
Lines 175–537. Introduction The destroyer USS Mustin slipped into the northern end of the Taiwan Strait on August 18, 2020, its five-inch gun pointed southward as it began a solo mission to sail through the Strait and reaffirm that these international waters were not controlled by China-at least not yet. A stiff southwestern breeze whipped across the deck as it steamed south. High clouds cast shadows on the water that seemed to stretch all the way to the great port cities of Fuzhou, Xiamen, Hong Kong, and the other harbors that dot the South China coast. To the east, the island of Taiwan rose in the distance, a broad, densely settled coastal plain giving way to tall peaks hidden in clouds. Today, no firm fabricates chips with more precision than the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, better known as TSMC. In 2020, as the world lurched between lockdowns driven by a virus whose diameter measured around one hundred nanometers-billionths of a meter-TSMC’s most advanced facility, Fab 18, was carving microscopic mazes of tiny transistors, etching shapes smaller than half the size of a coronavirus, a hundredth the size of a mitochondria. on research in historical archives on three continents, from Taipei to Moscow, and over a hundred interviews with scientists, engineers, CEOs, and government officials, this book contends that semiconductors have defined the world we live in, determining the shape of international politics, the structure of the world economy, and the balance of military power.
PART I — Cold War Chips
Lines 538–539. Part/section divider.
Chapter 1 — From Steel to Silicon
Lines 540–708. CHAPTER 1 From Steel to Silicon Japanese soldiers described World War II as a “typhoon of steel.” It certainly felt that way to Akio Morita, a studious young engineer from a family of prosperous sake merchants. Morita only barely avoided the front lines by getting assigned to a Japanese navy engineering lab. But the typhoon of steel crashed through Morita’s homeland, too, as American B-29 Superfortress bombers pummeled Japan’s cities, destroying much of Tokyo and other urban centers. Adding to the devastation, an American blockade created widespread hunger and drove the country toward desperate measures. Morita’s brothers were being trained as kamikaze pilots when the war ended. Across the East China Sea, Morris Chang celebrated the war’s end and Japan’s defeat with a prompt return to a leisurely teenaged life of tennis, movies, and card games with friends. In Hungary, Andy Grove and his mother slowly crept out of their bomb shelter, though they suffered as much during the Soviet occupation as during the war itself.
Chapter 2 — The Switch
Lines 709–813. CHAPTER 2 The Switch William Shockley had long assumed that if a better “switch” was to be found, it would be with the help of a type of material called semiconductors. Shockley, who’d been born in London to a globe-trotting mining engineer, had grown up amid the fruit trees of the sleepy California town of Palo Alto. An only child, he was utterly convinced of his superiority over anyone around him-and he let everyone know it. He went to college at Caltech, in Southern California, before completing a PhD in physics at MIT and starting work at Bell Labs in New Jersey, which at the time was one of the world’s leading centers of science and engineering. He hypothesized that placing a piece of semiconductor material like silicon in the presence of an electric field could attract “free electrons” stored inside to cluster near the edge of the semiconductor. If enough electrons were attracted by the electric field, the edge of the semiconductor would be transformed into a conductive material, like a metal, which always has large numbers of free electrons.
Chapter 3 — Noyce, Kilby, and the Integrated Circuit
Lines 814–948. CHAPTER 3 Noyce, Kilby, and the Integrated Circuit The transistor could only replace vacuum tubes if it could be simplified and sold at scale. Theorizing and inventing transistors was simply the first step; now, the challenge was to manufacture them by the thousands. Brattain and Bardeen had little interest in business or mass production. They were researchers at heart, and after winning the Nobel, they continued their careers teaching and experimenting. Shockley’s ambitions, by contrast, only grew. He wanted not only to be famous but also to be rich. He told friends he dreamed of seeing his name not only in academic publications like the Physical Review but in the Wall Street Journal, too. During World War II, the company had been drafted by the U.S. Navy to build sonar devices to track enemy submarines. After the war, TI executives realized this electronics expertise could be useful in other military systems, too, so they hired engineers like Kilby to build them. Kilby arrived in Dallas around the company’s July holiday period, yet he’d accumulated no vacation time so he was left alone in the lab for a couple of weeks.
Chapter 4 — Liftoff
Lines 949–1078. CHAPTER 4 Liftoff Three days after Noyce and Moore founded Fairchild Semiconductor, at 8:55 p.m., the answer to the question of who would pay for integrated circuits hurtled over their heads through California’s nighttime sky. Sputnik, the world’s first satellite, launched by the Soviet Union, orbited the earth from west to east at a speed of eighteen thousand miles per hour. “Russ ‘Moon’ Circling Globe,” declared the headline in the San Francisco Chronicle, reflecting Americans’ fears that this satellite gave the Russians a strategic advantage. Four years later, the Soviet Union followed Sputnik with another shock when cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin became the first person in space. By November 1962, Charles Stark Draper, the famed engineer who ran the MIT lab, had decided to bet on Fairchild chips for the Apollo program, calculating that a computer using Noyce’s integrated circuits would be one-third smaller and lighter than a computer based on discrete transistors. It would use less electricity, too. The computer that eventually took Apollo 11 to the moon weighed seventy pounds and took up about one cubic foot of space, a thousand times less than the University of Pennsylvania’s ENIAC computer that had calculated artillery trajectories during World War II.
Chapter 5 — Mortars and Mass Production
Lines 1079–1268. CHAPTER 5 Mortars and Mass Production Jay Lathrop pulled into Texas Instruments’ parking lot for his first day of work on September 1, 1958, just as Jack Kilby’s fateful summer spent tinkering in TI’s labs was coming to a close. After graduating from MIT, where he’d overlapped with Bob Noyce, Lathrop had worked at a U.S. government lab where he was tasked with devising a proximity fuse that would enable an 81mm mortar shell to detonate automatically above its target. Like engineers at Fairchild, he was struggling with mesa-shaped transistors, which were proving difficult to miniaturize. The slabs of silicon that Kilby’s integrated circuits required had to be ultra-pure, beyond what any company sold. TI therefore also began producing its own silicon wafers. Mass production works when everything is standardized. General Motors plugged many of the same car parts into all the Chevrolets that rolled off its assembly lines. When it came to semiconductors, companies like TI lacked the tools to know whether all the components of their integrated circuits were the same.
Chapter 6 — “I… WANT… TO… GET… RICH”
Lines 1269–1391. CHAPTER 6 “I… WANT… TO… GET… RICH” The computers that guided the Apollo spacecraft and the Minuteman II missile provided the initial liftoff for America’s integrated circuit industry. By the mid-1960s, the U.S. military was deploying chips in weaponry of all types, from satellites to sonar, torpedoes to telemetry systems. Bob Noyce knew that military and space programs were crucial for Fairchild’s early success, admitting in 1965 that military and space applications would use “over 95% of the circuits produced this year.” But he always envisioned an even larger civilian market for his chips, though in the early 1960s no such market existed. Though the military bought chips from Fairchild, the Defense Department was more comfortable working with big bureaucracies than nimble startups. As a result, the Pentagon underestimated the speed at which Fairchild and other semiconductor startups would transform electronics. A Defense Department assessment from the late 1950s had praised radio giant RCA for having “the most ambitious microminiaturization program underway” while dismissively noting that Fairchild had only two scientists working on the company’s leading circuit program.
PART II — The Circuitry of the American World
Lines 1392–1393. Part/section divider.
Chapter 7 — Soviet Silicon Valley
Lines 1394–1548. CHAPTER 7 Soviet Silicon Valley A couple months after Bob Noyce invented his integrated circuit at Fairchild Semiconductor, an unexpected visitor arrived in Palo Alto. In fall 1959, two years after Sputnik first orbited the earth, Anatoly Trutko, a semiconductor engineer from the Soviet Union, moved into a Stanford University dormitory called Crothers Memorial Hall. Though Cold War competition was near its peak, the two superpowers had agreed to begin student exchanges, and Trutko was one of a handful of students selected by the USSR and vetted by the U.S. State Department. He spent his year at Stanford studying America’s most advanced technology with the country’s leading scientists. He produced his prototype integrated circuit in 1962. Osokin and his colleagues knew they were at the cutting edge of Soviet science. They spent their days tinkering in labs and their evenings debating the theory of solid-state physics, with Osokin occasionally breaking out his guitar to accompany his colleagues in song. They were young, their work was exciting, Soviet science was rising, and several of the USSR’s Sputnik satellites were orbiting overhead, visible to the naked eye whenever Osokin put down his guitar and looked up into the night sky.
Chapter 8 — “Copy It”
Lines 1549–1665. CHAPTER 8 “Copy It” Around the same time that Nikita Khrushchev declared his support for building Zelenograd, a Soviet student named Boris Malin returned from a year studying in Pennsylvania with a small device in his luggage-a Texas Instruments SN-51, one of the first integrated circuits sold in the United States. A thin man with dark hair and deep-set eyes, Malin was one of the Soviet Union’s leading experts on semiconductor devices. He saw himself as a scientist, not a spy. Yet Alexander Shokin, the bureaucrat in charge of Soviet microelectronics, believed the SN-51 was a device the Soviet Union must acquire by any means necessary. Unlike their Soviet counterparts, they could draw on the expertise of other companies making advanced optics, chemicals, purified materials, and other production machinery. If no American companies could help, Fairchild and TI could turn to Germany, France, or Britain, each of which had advanced industries of their own. The Soviet Union churned out coal and steel in vast quantities but lagged in nearly every type of advanced manufacturing.
Chapter 9 — The Transistor Salesman
Lines 1666–1864. CHAPTER 9 The Transistor Salesman When Japanese prime minister Hayato Ikeda met French president Charles de Gaulle amid the splendor of the Elysée Palace in November 1962, he brought a small gift for his host: a Sony transistor radio. De Gaulle was formalistic and ceremonious, a tradition-minded military man who saw himself as the incarnation of French grandeur. Ikeda, by contrast, thought his country’s voters were straightforwardly materialistic, and promised to double their incomes within a decade. Japan was nothing but an “economic power,” de Gaulle declared, huffing to an aide after the meeting that Ikeda behaved like a “transistor salesman.” Morita’s physics degree proved useful in postwar Japan, too. In April 1946, with the country still in ruins, Morita partnered with a former colleague named Masaru Ibuka to build an electronics business, which they soon named Sony, from the Latin sonus (sound) and the American nickname “sonny.” Their first device, an electric rice cooker, was a dud, but their tape recorder worked well and sold better.
Chapter 10 — “Transistor Girls”
Lines 1865–2010. CHAPTER 10 “Transistor Girls” “Their clothing was of the West, but their love rites were founded in the ancient pleasures of the East,” read the cover of The Transistor Girls, a trashy Australian novel from 1964. The plot involved Chinese gangsters, international intrigue, and women assembly line workers who “added to their incomes by extracurricular night-time activity.” The image on the front cover of The Transistor Girls showed a young Japanese woman, scantily clad, with a silhouette of a pagoda in the background. The back cover revealed a woman amid more orientalist imagery but with even less clothing. I brought this competence to my new employer.” Many companies wouldn’t have described a strategy of labor relations that culminated in management getting burned in effigy as “competent.” But in Silicon Valley, unions were weak, and Sporck was committed to keeping it that way. He and his colleagues at Fairchild were “dead set” against unions, he declared.
Chapter 11 — Precision Strike
Lines 2011–2146. CHAPTER 11 Precision Strike About halfway on the flight between the company’s semiconductor plants in Singapore and Hong Kong during the early 1970s, Texas Instruments employees would occasionally peer out their aircraft window and look down on puffs of smoke rising from the battlefields on Vietnam’s coastal plains. TI’s staff across Asia were focused on making chips, not on the war. Many of their colleagues in Texas, however, thought about nothing else. TI’s first major contract for integrated circuits had been for massive nuclear missiles like the Minuteman II, but the war in Vietnam required different types of weapons. He’d just concluded a yearlong stint aboard a Navy ship gathering data for a new TI-developed sonar, an assignment that was mind-numbingly monotonous, but that demonstrated how much data military systems could collect with the right sensors and instrumentation. As early as the mid-1960s, Word was already envisioning using microelectronics to transform the military’s kill chain.
Chapter 12 — Supply Chain Statecraft
Lines 2147–2276. CHAPTER 12 Supply Chain Statecraft Though Texas Instruments executive Mark Shepherd had served in the Navy in Asia during World War II, Morris Chang quipped that his expertise in the region didn’t extend beyond “bars and dancing girls.” The son of a Dallas police officer, Shepherd had assembled his first vacuum tube at age six. He’d played a central role in building TI’s semiconductor business, including supervising the division Jack Kilby worked in when the first integrated circuit was invented. With broad shoulders, a starched collar, slicked-back hair, and a taut smile, Shepherd looked like the Texas corporate titan that he was. The 1960s had been a good decade for Taiwan’s economy but disastrous for its foreign policy. The island’s dictator, Chiang Kai-shek, still dreamed of reconquering the mainland, but the military balance had shifted decisively against him. In 1964, Beijing tested its first atomic weapon. A thermonuclear weapon test shortly followed. Facing a nuclear China, Taiwan needed American security guarantees more than ever.
Chapter 13 — Intel’s Revolutionaries
Lines 2277–2440. CHAPTER 13 Intel’s Revolutionaries The year 1968 seemed like a revolutionary moment. From Beijing to Berlin to Berkeley, radicals and leftists were poised to tear down the established order. North Vietnam’s Tet Offensive tested the limits of American military power. Yet it was the Palo Alto Times that scooped the world’s biggest newspapers by reporting on page 6 what, in hindsight, was the most revolutionary event of the year: “Founders Leave Fairchild; Form Own Electronics Firm.” The rebellion of Bob Noyce and Gordon Moore didn’t look like the protests in California’s East Bay, where Berkeley students and Black Panthers plotted violent uprisings and dreamt of abolishing capitalism. But rather than relying on wires and rings, DRAM circuits were carved into silicon. They didn’t need to be weaved by hand, so they malfunctioned less often and could be made far smaller. Noyce and Moore bet that their new company, Intel, could take Dennard’s insight and put it on a chip far denser than a magnetic core could ever be.
Chapter 14 — The Pentagon’s Offset Strategy
Lines 2441–2628. CHAPTER 14 The Pentagon’s Offset Strategy No one benefitted more from Noyce and Moore’s revolution than a cornerstone of the old order-the Pentagon. Upon arriving in Washington in 1977, William Perry felt “like a kid in a candy store.” For a Silicon Valley entrepreneur like Perry, serving as undersecretary of defense for research and engineering was, he said, the “best job in the world.” No one had a larger budget to buy technology than the Pentagon. And hardly anyone in Washington had so clear a view of how microprocessors and powerful memory chips could transform all the weapons and systems the Defense Department relied on. The U.S.-facing pressure at home to cut military spending-simply couldn’t keep up. Strategists like Marshall knew the only answer to the Soviet quantitative advantage was to produce better quality weapons. But how? As early as 1972, Marshall wrote that the U.S. needed to take advantage of its “substantial and durable lead” in computers. “A good strategy would be to develop that lead and to shift concepts of warfare in ways that capitalize on it,” he wrote.
PART III — Leadership Lost?
Lines 2629–2630. Part/section divider.
Chapter 15 — “That Competition Is Tough”
Lines 2631–2750. CHAPTER 15 “That Competition Is Tough” “Ever since you’ve written that paper, my life has been hell!” one chip salesman grumbled to Richard Anderson, a Hewlett-Packard executive tasked with deciding which chips met HP’s stringent standards. The 1980s were a hellish decade for the entire U.S. semiconductor sector. Silicon Valley thought it sat atop the world’s tech industry, but after two decades of rapid growth it now faced an existential crisis: cutthroat competition from Japan. When Anderson took the stage at an industry conference at Washington, D.C.’s historic Mayflower Hotel on March 25, 1980, the audience listened carefully, because everyone was trying to sell him their chips. The lowest failure rate of the three American firms was 0.09 percent-which meant four-and-a-half times as many U.S.-made chips were malfunctioning. The worst U.S. firm produced chips with 0.26 percent failure rates-over ten times as bad as the Japanese results. American DRAM chips worked the same, cost the same, but malfunctioned far more often. So why should anyone buy them?
Chapter 16 — “At War with Japan”
Lines 2751–2921. CHAPTER 16 “At War with Japan” “I don’t want to pretend I’m in a fair fight,” complained Jerry Sanders, CEO of Advanced Micro Devices. “I’m not.” Sanders knew something about fights. At age eighteen, he’d almost died after a brawl on Chicago’s South Side, where he grew up. After his body was found in a garbage can, a priest administered last rites, though he miraculously emerged from a coma three days later. He eventually landed a job in sales and marketing at Fairchild Semiconductor, working alongside Noyce, Moore, and Andy Grove before they left Fairchild to found Intel. Toshiba, the Japanese industrial conglomerate that by the mid-1980s was a world-leading DRAM producer, spent years fighting claims-true, it turned out-that the company sold the Soviets machinery that helped them build quieter submarines. There was no direct link between Toshiba’s Soviet submarine deal and the company’s semiconductor business, but many Americans saw the submarine case as further evidence of Japanese dirty dealing.
Chapter 17 — “Shipping Junk”
Lines 2922–3106. CHAPTER 17 “Shipping Junk” As the Japanese juggernaut tore through America’s high-tech industry, it wasn’t only companies producing DRAM chips that struggled. Many of their suppliers did, too. In 1981, GCA Corporation was being celebrated as one of America’s “hottest high-technology corporations,” growing rapidly by selling equipment that made possible Moore’s Law. In the two decades since physicist Jay Lathrop had first turned his microscope upside down to shine light on photoresist chemicals and “print” patterns on semiconductor wafers, the process of photolithography had become vastly more complicated. Long gone were the days of Bob Noyce driving up and down California’s Highway 101 in his old jalopy in search of movie camera lenses for Fairchild’s makeshift photolithography equipment. Such a “stepper” would be far more accurate than the existing scanners. Though a stepper had never been devised, GCA’s engineers believed they could create one, providing higher-resolution imaging and thus smaller transistors. Several years later, in 1978, GCA introduced its first stepper. Sales orders began rolling in. Before the stepper, GCA had never made more than $50 million a year in revenue on its military contracts, but now it had a monopoly on an extraordinarily valuable machine.
Chapter 18 — The Crude Oil of the 1980s
Lines 3107–3247. CHAPTER 18 The Crude Oil of the 1980s On a chilly spring evening in Palo Alto, Bob Noyce, Jerry Sanders, and Charlie Sporck met under a sloping, pagoda-style roof. Ming’s Chinese Restaurant was a staple of the Silicon Valley lunch circuit. But America’s tech titans weren’t at Ming’s for its famous Chinese chicken salad. Noyce, Sanders, and Sporck had all started their careers at Fairchild: Noyce the technological visionary; Sanders the marketing showman; Sporck the manufacturing boss barking at his employees to build faster, cheaper, better. A decade later they’d become competitors as CEOs of three of America’s biggest chipmakers. But shouldn’t the government find a way to help its struggling semiconductor firms? In the 1970s, Silicon Valley firms had forgotten about the government as they replaced defense contracts with civilian computer and calculator markets. In the 1980s, they crawled sheepishly back to Washington. After their dinner at Ming’s, Sanders, Noyce, and Sporck joined other CEOs to create the Semiconductor Industry Association to lobby Washington to support the industry.
Chapter 19 — Death Spiral
Lines 3248–3443. CHAPTER 19 Death Spiral “We’re in a death spiral,” Bob Noyce told a reporter in 1986. “Can you name a field in which the U.S. is not falling behind?” In his more pessimistic moments, Noyce wondered whether Silicon Valley would end up like Detroit, its flagship industry withering under the impact of foreign competition. Silicon Valley had a schizophrenic relationship with the government, simultaneously demanding to be left alone and requesting that it help. Noyce exemplified the contradiction. He’d spent his earliest days at Fairchild avoiding Pentagon bureaucracy while benefitting from the Cold War−era space race. threatened tariffs. America’s chip industry lodged a series of formal complaints against Japanese firms for “dumping” cheap chips in the U.S. market. The claim that Japanese firms were selling below production cost was hard to prove. U.S. firms cited Japanese competitors’ low cost of capital; Japan responded by saying that interest rates were lower across Japan’s economy.
Chapter 20 — The Japan That Can Say No
Lines 3444–3649. CHAPTER 20 The Japan That Can Say No After decades of making millions by selling Americans electronics, Sony’s Akio Morita began to detect “a certain arrogance” in his American friends. When he first licensed transistor technology in the 1950s, the U.S. was the world’s tech leader. Since then, America had faced crisis after crisis. The disastrous war in Vietnam, racial tension, urban unrest, the humiliation of Watergate, a decade of stagflation, a gaping trade deficit, and now industrial malaise. After each new shock, America’s allure dimmed. On his first trip abroad in 1953, Morita had seen America as a country “that seemed to have everything.” In parliament, Ishihara agitated for Japan to assert itself internationally and to change the country’s constitution, which had been dictated by U.S. occupation authorities after World War II, to let Tokyo build a powerful military. It was hard to imagine a more provocative coauthor for Morita to have chosen as he lectured the United States about its internal crises.
PART IV — America Resurgent
Lines 3650–3651. Part/section divider.
Chapter 21 — The Potato Chip King
Lines 3652–3852. CHAPTER 21 The Potato Chip King Micron made “the best damn widgets in the whole world,” Jack Simplot used to say. The Idaho billionaire didn’t know much about the physics of how his company’s main product, DRAM chips, actually worked. The chip industry was full of PhDs, but Simplot hadn’t finished eighth grade. His expertise was potatoes, as everyone knew from the white Lincoln Town Car he drove around Boise. “Mr. Spud,” the license plate declared. Yet Simplot understood business in a way Silicon Valley’s smartest scientists didn’t. As America’s chip industry struggled to adjust to Japan’s challenge, cowboy entrepreneurs like him played a fundamental role in reversing what Bob Noyce had called a “death spiral” and executing a surprise turnaround. Transistors and capacitors didn’t mean much to Simplot, who was as close to the opposite of a Silicon Valley venture capitalist as you could get. He’d later preside over impromptu Micron board meetings each Monday at 5:45 a.m. at Elmer’s, a local greasy spoon that served stacks of buttermilk pancakes for $6.99. However, as all of Silicon Valley’s tech titans were fleeing DRAM chips amid the Japanese onslaught, Simplot instinctively understood that Ward and Joe Parkinson were entering the memory market at exactly the right time.
Chapter 22 — Disrupting Intel
Lines 3853–3997. CHAPTER 22 Disrupting Intel “Look, Clayton, I’m a busy man and I don’t have time to read drivel from academics,” Andy Grove told Harvard Business School’s most famous professor, Clayton Christensen. When the two of them made the cover of Forbes several years later, Christensen-six feet, eight inches tall-towered over Grove, whose balding head barely reached Christensen’s shoulder. But Grove’s intensity outshone that of everyone around him. He was a “butt-kicking Hungarian,” his longtime deputy explained, “chewing on people’s ankles, and yelling at them, and challenging them, and pushing as hard as he could.” More than anything else did, Grove’s tenacity saved Intel from bankruptcy and made it one of the world’s most profitable and powerful companies. IBM contracted with a young programmer named Bill Gates to write software for the computer’s operating system. On August 12, 1981, with the ornate wallpaper and thick drapes of the Waldorf Astoria’s grand ballroom in the background, IBM announced the launch of its personal computer, priced at $1,565 for a bulky computer, a big-box monitor, a keyboard, a printer, and two diskette drives.
Chapter 23 — “My Enemy’s Enemy”: The Rise of Korea
Lines 3998–4130. CHAPTER 23 “My Enemy’s Enemy”: The Rise of Korea Lee Byung-Chul could make a profit selling almost anything. Born in 1910, just a year after Jack Simplot, Lee launched his business career in March 1938, a time when his native Korea was part of Japan’s empire, at war with China and soon with the United States. Lee’s first products were dried fish and vegetables, which he gathered from Korea and shipped to northern China to feed Japan’s war machine. Korea was an impoverished backwater, with no industry or technology, but Lee was already dreaming of building a business that would be “big, strong, and eternal,” he declared. South Korea was already an important location for outsourced assembly and packaging of chips made in the U.S. or Japan. Moreover, the U.S. government had helped fund the creation in 1966 of the Korea Institute of Science and Technology, and a growing number of Koreans were graduating from top U.S. universities or being trained in Korea by U.S.-educated professors.
Chapter 24 — “This Is the Future”
Lines 4131–4315. CHAPTER 24 “This Is the Future” The rebirth of America’s chip industry after Japan’s DRAM onslaught was only possible thanks to Andy Grove’s paranoia, Jerry Sanders’s bare-knuckle brawling, and Jack Simplot’s cowboy competitiveness. Silicon Valley’s testosterone and stock option−fueled competition often felt less like the sterile economics described in textbooks and more like a Darwinian struggle for the survival of the fittest. Lines 9785–10100. CHAPTER 54 The Taiwan Dilemma “Are your customers concerned,” one financial analyst asked TSMC chairman Mark Liu, when China from time to time threatens “a war against Taiwan?” CEOs are used to tough questions on quarterly earnings calls, but they’re usually about missed profit targets or product launches gone wrong. At the time of this call, July 15, 2021, TSMC’s financials looked fine. The company had weathered the sanctioning of its second-largest customer, Huawei, with scarcely any impact on its performance. TSMC’s share price was near a record high. The global semiconductor shortage had made its business even more lucrative. However, it’s easy to imagine a way that an accident, like a collision in air or at sea, could spiral into a disastrous war that neither side wants. It’s also perfectly reasonable to think China might conclude that military pressure without a full-scale invasion could decisively undermine America’s implicit security guarantee and fatally demoralize Taiwan. Beijing knows that Taiwan’s defense strategy is to fight long enough for the U.S. aircraft from the Longtian and Huian airbases on the Chinese side of the Strait, from which it’s only a seven-minute flight to Taiwan. Not coincidentally, in 2021, these airbases were upgraded with new bunkers, runway extensions, and missile defenses. A new Taiwan Strait crisis would be far more dangerous than the crises of the 1950s.
Conclusion
Lines 10101–10423. Conclusion It was only five days after People’s Liberation Army forces began shelling the Taiwanese-held Quemoy Island in 1958 that, amid the sweltering Dallas summer, Jack Kilby demonstrated to his colleagues that all the components of a circuit-transistors, resistors, and capacitors-could be made from semiconductor materials. Four days after that, Jay Lathrop pulled into the Texas Instruments parking lot for the first time. He’d already filed for a patent on the process of making transistors via photolithography but had yet to receive the Army prize that enabled him to buy a new station wagon. Several months earlier, Morris Chang had left his job at a Massachusetts electronics firm and moved to Texas Instruments, earning a reputation for a nearly magical ability to eliminate errors from TI’s semiconductor fabrication processes. And in the future China’s deluge of subsidies will profoundly reshape the semiconductor supply chain, whether China achieves its goal of semiconductor supremacy or not. There’s no guarantee, of course, that chips will remain as important as they’ve been in the past. Our demand for computing power is unlikely ever to diminish, but we could run out of supply. x86 chips continue to dominate the PC business. (AP Photo/Paul Sakuma) [Image] In what proved to be a colossally bad decision, Intel turned down Steve Jobs’s proposal to build chips for Apple’s mobile phones. “I couldn’t see it,” Intel CEO Paul Otellini would later say.
Acknowledgments
Lines 10424–10571. Acknowledgments Fabricating a cutting-edge chip involves hundreds of process steps and a supply chain that stretches across multiple countries. Writing this book was only slightly less complex than making a chip. I’m grateful to the many people, in many countries, who have helped along the way. For making archival material available, especially amid the restrictions of the pandemic, I thank the librarians and archivists at the Library of Congress, Washington, D.C.; Southern Methodist University; Stanford University; the Hoover Institution; the Archive of the Russian Academy of Sciences; and Academica Sinica in Taiwan. I am equally grateful for the opportunity to have conducted well over one hundred interviews with semiconductor experts from industry, academia, and government. Terry Daly, an industry veteran, was extraordinarily generous with his time, and I’m grateful for his guidance. Bob Loynd and Craig Keast at MIT’s Lincoln Labs were kind enough to give me a tour of their microelectronics facility. I also benefitted from guidance through FinFETs, high-k materials, and many other details of the science underlying semiconductors by a technical reviewer in the industry who wishes to remain anonymous.
Notes
Lines 10572–10685. Index

Clicking on a page number will take you to the ebook location that corresponds to the beginning of that page in the print edition. sources/murray-cox-apollo-race-to-the-mo.title: [source] Apollo: The Race to the Moon (Murray & Cox, 1989/2004)
sources/murray-cox-apollo-race-to-the-mo.content:
Apollo: The Race to the Moon
Authors: Charles Murray & Catherine Bly Cox
Published: 1989 (Simon & Schuster); 2004 South Mountain Books reprint; 2010 ebook
Working text: Digital EPUB via Anna’s Archive (hash 22042598e015adb0fa0c0b4d4ed6d0a6)
Raw extract: wiki/raw/murray-cox-apollo-race-to-the-moon.txt (EPUB via pandoc -t plain)
Extract stats: 19,859 lines · ~194,254 words · 1,154,733 bytes
Deploy note: Full-text raw is not deployed — wiki/.gitignore ignores *.txt; Quartz ignorePatterns includes raw.
Period-Overlap Note
This source belongs entirely in United States 1946–89 (Space Task Group 1958 through Apollo 11/13 and early-1970s program close). No copy to 1866–1919, 1920–45, or 1990–present.
Overview
Apollo: The Race to the Moon is a narrative history of how the American manned lunar program was engineered, managed, and flown, told through the people who stayed on the ground. Murray and Cox (interview-based, with extensive NASA and contractor access) follow the Space Task Group from its 1958 origins through Kennedy’s 1961 commitment, the mode and hardware decisions (L.O.R., Saturn V, command/service module, lunar module), the Apollo 1 fire and recovery, Mueller’s all-up testing, Mission Control’s evolution, and the flights through Apollo 11, 12, and 13. The book explicitly is not astronaut biography and not a comprehensive institutional history—it is an “epic captured in miniature” through engineers, managers, and flight controllers (Gilruth, Faget, Shea, Low, Petrone, Kraft, Kranz, Lunney, Houbolt, and dozens of trench-level figures).
For this United States 1946–89 wiki the entire narrative sits inside the period: Space Task Group formation (1958), Kennedy decision (1961), fire and rebuild (1967), Saturn V and Apollo 8 (1968), landing (1969), and Apollo 13 (1970), with epilogue and program-close material through the early 1970s. Use beside astronaut memoir sources (e.g. Built to Last) for the ground-operations complement; no copy needed to 1866–1919, 1920–45, or 1990–present.
EPUB structure: review blurbs; title/copyright (1989 / 2004 / 2010); Foreword to the 2004 Edition; Acknowledgments; Apollo Abbreviations; Prologue; Book I — Gathering (Chs. 1–5); Book II — Building (Chs. 6–17); Book III — Flying (Chs. 18–30); Epilogue; Notes; glossary/index material in back matter.
Narrative Source Flow
Front matter / blurbs / title
Lines 1–62. Contemporary review quotes (Collins, Sheffield, Petit, Mallon, etc.); title page; copyright blocks (© 1989 Cox and Murray, Inc.; 2004 South Mountain Books; 2010 ebook); ISBN 0-976008-0-6; dedication to Apollo workers and families.
Foreword to the 2004 Edition
Lines 63–155. Authors on modest 1989 sales but strong reception among Apollo veterans; republication with cosmetic changes only; deliberate anachronisms (CRT Mission Control, computer-capacity comparisons); Apollo 13 film vs. real displays; argument that Apollo was engineered excellence, not impetuous gamble; timeline from Space Task Group (Nov 5, 1958, forty-five people) to Apollo 11 (July 20, 1969).
Acknowledgments
Lines 156–254. Jack Trombka and agent Amanda Urban as origin; Simon & Schuster editors (Mayhew, Shipley); Robert Sherrod archive; NASA center public-affairs and history offices; interview contributors; long list of “unsung” helpers; Apollo Abbreviations note on insider pronunciation and period rules (N.A.C.A., L.O.R., NASA, DPS).
Prologue. May 25, 1961
Lines 255–447. Kennedy’s joint-session speech framed through Washington spring 1961 and Cape weather; reactions at Hangar S and in transit (Petrone, Preston, Simpkinson, Beddingfield, Koos, Gilruth “aghast”); book’s scope—ground workers who put men on the moon and brought them back, not the astronauts themselves.
Chapter 1 — “That famous Space Task Group is akin to the Mayflower”
Lines 448–1083. Owen Maynard’s April 1959 drive from Canada to Hampton/Langley; Peninsula isolation and STG culture; Gilruth’s forty-five-person shop; early engineer migrations; Max Faget already thinking beyond Mercury toward the moon.
Chapter 2 — “I could picture the astronauts looking down at it with binoculars”
Lines 1084–1420. Max Faget’s 1959 Dolley Madison House “blue-sky” seminar with Glennan, von Braun, Pickering, Silverstein; early lunar-landing design thinking; Silverstein ordering moon references stripped from George Low’s draft long-range plan.
Chapter 3 — “Those days were out of the Dark Ages”
Lines 1421–1936. First STG Cape contingent (June 1959) and Big Joe boilerplate heat-shield test; Hangar S rope-off workspace, sixteen-hour days, ammonia against mosquitoes; Air Force treating STG as low-priority amateurs; improvised Cape operations before modern clean-room culture.
Chapter 4 — “He would rather not have done it”
Lines 1937–2590. Bob Seamans’s gloomy fall 1960—Eisenhower budget cuts, Saturn second-stage casualty, Mercury-only future; Kennedy election and campaign “space gap” rhetoric; Kennedy’s pre-Gagarin ambivalence about manned spaceflight; Gilruth/Faget/Petrone later veneration vs. Seamans’s contemporary reading of presidential indifference.
Chapter 5 — “We’re going to the moon”
Lines 2591–2985. Kennedy’s April 1961 apogee shattered by Gagarin (Apr 12); political shock and congressional pressure; Wiesner/Webb/Johnson deliberations; path to May 25 speech and the decade deadline—wiki hinge for Kennedy commitment.
Chapter 6 — “The flight article has got to dominate”
Lines 2986–3525. Rocco Petrone’s summer 1961 Cape pivot—Heavy Space Vehicle Systems Office, site selection, mobile launcher and V.A.B. logic; “flight article dominates” as Cape design principle; constraints (explosive potential, downrange safety, labor pool, weather) shaping Kennedy Space Center expansion.
Chapter 7 — “We had more harebrained schemes than you could shake a stick at”
Lines 3526–4064. Gilruth on Kennedy’s word “safely”; reliability-number fights (Johnson, Piland, Faget, Gilruth, Walt Williams); direct ascent, earth-orbit rendezvous, lunar crasher, and other mode sketches before L.O.R. crystallized.
Chapter 8 — “Somewhat as a voice in the wilderness…”
Lines 4065–4508. Lunar-orbit rendezvous origins—Tom Dolan/Vought modular lander, Langley lunar-parking-orbit work, John Houbolt’s persistent lobbying to Abe Seamans; energy-budget logic and rendezvous risk as the central engineering controversy.
Chapter 9 — “What sonofabitch thinks it isn’t the right thing to do?”
Lines 4509–5356. Joe Shea’s January 1962 arrival; Langley mode briefings and Shea’s conversion to L.O.R.; hidden STG rethinking vs. public anti-rendezvous posture; Shea named ASPO chief; North American (C.S.M.) and Grumman (L.E.M.) prime contracts—eighteen months after Kennedy speech, NASA knew how it would go.
Chapter 10 — “It aged me, I’m sure”
Lines 5357–5777. F-1 engine combustion instability—June 28, 1962 test-stand destruction at Edwards; Rocketdyne/Marshall struggle to tame the 1.5-million-pound-thrust engine that made single-launch L.O.R. possible.
Chapter 11 — “It sounded reckless”
Lines 5778–6186. George Mueller’s all-up testing plan vs. German and N.A.C.A. incremental flight-test cultures; Shea’s “three tribes” (Peenemünde Germans, N.A.C.A. craftsmen, I.C.B.M. systems engineers); Mueller hired to impose schedule discipline across centers.
Chapter 12 — “Hey, it isn’t that complicated”
Lines 6187–6729. Shea in Houston (Nov 1963) finds no L.O.R.-compatible C.S.M. design; North American contract award controversy—Martin ranked first, North American selected after rescoring toward experimental-aircraft experience; Stormy Storms and the C.S.M. program’s troubled start.
Chapter 13 — “We want you to go fix it”
Lines 6730–7097. F-1 injector redesign finally tames combustion instability (Castenholz, Thomson); five-engine cluster test (Apr 1965); V.A.B. High Bay and crawler-transporter milestones; Shea’s accumulating stress as ASPO ramrod.
Chapter 14 — “Did he say ‘fire’?”
Lines 7098–7772. Apollo 1 (AS-204) pad fire, Jan 27, 1967—Before the Fire / After the Fire divide; Simpkinson’s reconstruction (scuffed cable, glycol fumes, pure-oxygen environment, flammable netting); Grissom, White, Chaffee; program history bisected by the catastrophe.
Chapter 15 — The Crucible
Lines 7773–8615. Leadership converges at K.S.C. after the fire; Shea moves into astronauts’ quarters; investigative panel (Borman over Schirra); Block II redesign, hatch, wiring, flammables; North American–NASA confrontation and the program’s forced maturation.
Chapter 16 — “You’ve got to start biting somewhere”
Lines 8616–9036. Shea’s breakdown and departure; George Low recruited to head ASPO (Mathews demurs; Webb “persuasion” charade); Low as “knitter of people” vs. Shea’s impatient charisma; recovery management through first post-fire flights.
Chapter 17 — “And then on launch day it worked”
Lines 9037–9630. Saturn V stages arriving at the Cape; stacking in the V.A.B.; Apollo 4 (AS-501) as Mueller’s first all-up test—November 9, 1967; Rigell/Petrone scale from Redstone hand-holding to million-pound-thrust operations.
Chapter 18 — “We’re going to put a guy in that thing and light it”
Lines 9631–10302. Manned Spacecraft Center’s deceptively bland campus; Flight Operations’ evolution from Mercury flight-test mindset toward real-time ground control; Glynn Lunney and the Operations Division inventing their role as the spacecraft circles the earth.
Chapter 19 — “There will always be people who want to work in that room”
Lines 10303–10802. Building 30 and the MOCR—Staff Support Rooms, SPAN, recovery coordination; Gemini shift to Houston control; CRT consoles, simulations, and the culture of controllers who endure headaches to work “in that room.”
Chapter 20 — “The flight director may take any necessary action”
Lines 10803–11153. Flight director’s sweeping mission-rule authority; Chris Kraft as model (piccolo theory vs. controllers’ awe at his technical depth); Gene Kranz and the flight-director corps; power, anonymity, and exposure.
Chapter 21 — “There was no mercy in those days”
Lines 11154–11851. Bill Tindall appointed “Chief of Apollo Data Priority Coordination” (Aug 1967)—Mission Techniques; who-does-what fights between astronauts, contractors, and controllers; Tindall meetings and simulation brutality as Apollo learns to fly its machines.
Chapter 22 — “You’ve lost the engines?”
Lines 11852–12327. Apollo 6 (Apr 4, 1968)—severe pogo and multiple S-II engine shutdowns amid national upheaval; Apollo engineers largely oblivious to Vietnam and politics; performance problems that feed George Low’s Apollo 8 gamble.
Chapter 23 — “It was darn scary”
Lines 12328–12915. George Low’s August 1968 proposal to send Apollo 8 circumlunar; Kraft, Bostick, Phillips, Paine, Mueller, Webb deliberations; compressing MPAD calculations and selling “C-prime” as schedule rescue and Soviet-race countermove.
Chapter 24 — “We … we’re go on that, Flight”
Lines 12916–13829. Lunar module as novel machine—Grumman’s flimsy materials, volatile propellants, hand-milled fittings; Apollo 9 L.E.M. checkout in earth orbit; rendezvous and docked DPS burns as prerequisites for lunar landing.
Chapter 25 — “Well, let’s light this sumbitch and it better work”
Lines 13830–14428. Apollo 11 landing night—E.V.A., Armstrong’s “one small step”; post-landing anomalies (1201/1202 alarms, switch breakage, engine-lift-off sensor) worked through MOCR, SPAN, MER, and contractor rooms while the world watched.
Chapter 26 — “I think we need to do a little more all-weather testing”
Lines 14429–15087. Apollo 12 launch (Nov 14, 1969)—Kapryan’s weather gamble, lightning strike twice during ascent, SCE-to-Aux workaround; Griffin’s first launch shift; Conrad’s exuberance and the program’s continuing anomaly culture.
Chapter 27 — “You really need to understand that the C.S.M. is dying”
Lines 15088–15972. Apollo 13 (Apr 1970)—Swigert replaces Mattingly; cryo stir and O2 Tank 2 explosion; Sy Liebergot’s EECOM console; Kranz’s White Team crisis opening; Glynn Lunney’s assessment of Flight Operations’ “crowning achievement.”
Chapter 28 — “You don’t have time to worry”
Lines 15973–16640. Lunney’s Black Team shift—power-down decisions, L.E.M. activation, consumables and navigation; Kranz/Tindall/MER coordination; improvised procedures under time pressure as Odyssey dies and Aquarius becomes lifeboat.
Chapter 29 — “I hope the guys who thought this up knew what they were doing”
Lines 16641–17596. L.E.M. lifeboat concept from Grumman specs (Kelly/Munier, 1961) through simulations; consumables math, carbon-dioxide scrubber hack, cold and sleep deprivation; re-entry after service-module jettison—Thirteen preserved, not yet saved.
Chapter 30 — “We drank the wine at the pace they handed it to us”
Lines 17597–18055. Kennedy’s Apollo as national boast with a deadline; Apollo 13 as last moment of public transfixion; fading space enthusiasm, spin-off defensiveness, and NASA bureaucratization; remaining flights (14–17) and program wind-down through 1972.
Epilogue. Twenty Years after the First Landing
Lines 18056–18689. 1989 retrospectives—Aaron’s “dominoes” uniqueness, family sacrifices (Cape/Houston divorce rates), gentlemen-engineers culture, aging veterans (Webb, Gilruth, Kraft, Houbolt, Petrone, etc.); Petrone on unreported “Renaissance” meaning; what Apollo symbolized vs. what the public remembers.
Notes
Lines 18690–19859. Endnotes tied to interview sources and technical references; back-matter book divisions and glossary/index repeats.
Coverage Guide
Space Task Group origins and Cape “Dark Ages” (wiki early manned space)
Chs. 1–3 + Prologue reactions: Langley/Hampton migration, Faget/Gilruth shop, Hangar S improvisations—foundation for 1958–61 NASA manned-flight pages.
Kennedy decision and political economy of commitment
Chs. 4–5: Eisenhower retrenchment, Seamans’s budget fears, Gagarin shock, May 25 1961 speech—pair with diplomatic histories for Cold War competition frame.
Mode, hardware, and center politics (wiki engineering core)
Chs. 6–13: L.O.R. (Houbolt/Shea), Saturn V/F-1, Mueller all-up, North American C.S.M. contract, Grumman L.E.M.—primary source for how Apollo was designed, not just flown.
Fire, recovery, and ASPO leadership transition
Chs. 14–16: Apollo 1 crucible, Block II, Shea→Low at ASPO—essential for 1967 hinge and contractor–NASA relationship pages.
Saturn V, Cape operations, and all-up testing
Chs. 17 + 6 + 10–11: V.A.B., crawler, F-1 instability, Apollo 4—launch-vehicle and K.S.C. infrastructure material.
Mission Control and flight operations (wiki operations spine)
Chs. 18–21 + 19–20: MOCR evolution, flight directors, Tindall Mission Techniques, simulations—densest ground-ops narrative in the period set.
Flight sequence: 6 → 8 → 9 → 11 → 12 → 13
Chs. 22–29: unmanned failures enabling Apollo 8 gamble; L.E.M. checkout; landing anomalies; lightning strike; Thirteen lifeboat—event-level mining for mission pages.
Program close and cultural aftermath
Ch. 30 + Epilogue: public attention fade, bureaucracy, family cost, veteran memory—use for late-Apollo/early-1970s cultural pages; Epilogue’s 1989 coda is period-gated spill for reflection only.

sources/nasaw-the-chief-hearst.title: [source] The Chief: The Life of William Randolph Hearst (Nasaw, 2000)
sources/nasaw-the-chief-hearst.content:
The Chief
Author: David Nasaw
Published: 2000 (Houghton Mifflin; 2nd printing packaging in working file)
Working text: Digital PDF via Anna’s Archive (hash abf8a051a2a9c556b27154729d695ce7)
Raw extract: wiki/raw/nasaw-the-chief-hearst.txt (pdftotext -layout)
Extract stats: 27,895 lines · ~295,490 words · 1,811,873 bytes
Deploy note: Full-text raw is not deployed — wiki/.gitignore ignores *.txt; Quartz ignorePatterns includes raw.
OCR note: Clean digital PDF extract; occasional ligature glyphs (ﬁ/ﬂ) in plain text.
Overview
The Chief is David Nasaw’s full-life biography of William Randolph Hearst, built with new access to Hearst Corporation materials, San Simeon oral histories, and Joseph P. Kennedy papers among many archives. Nasaw tracks the making of a self-fashioned media sovereign: mining-heir childhood; Harvard dropout turned Examiner proprietor; New York Journal spectacle and the Spanish-American War; Progressive-era candidacies and Congress; World War I neutrality/treason fights; 1920s studio, collecting, and Marion Davies Hollywood court; Depression finance crisis; Roosevelt support then anti–New Deal/anti-Communist crusades; European contacts including Hitler; the late-1930s fall; Citizen Kane; and managed old age until death in 1951.
For this United States 1946–89 wiki the book’s core is thin but real: Chapters 36 and Epilogue (post-1945 old age, estate, San Simeon gift path) plus late cultural afterlife of the Hearst myth. Parts I–VIII and most of IX are continuity from earlier U.S. period wikis—mine those fully in the 1866–1919 and 1920–45 sister pages. Period-gate hard on pre-1946 narrative except where needed to finish a story already open after 1945.
PDF structure: TOC; copyright/LC; Acknowledgments; Preface; Parts I–IX with Chapters 1–36; Epilogue; Notes; Index; About the Author.
Narrative Source Flow
Front matter / Acknowledgments / Preface
Lines 1–321. TOC; © 2000 Nasaw; acknowledgments (Randolph Hearst, Hearst Corp., San Simeon staff, Kennedy papers via Schlesinger, research army); Preface framing the biography.
PART I — Great Expectations
Lines 322–323. Part divider.
Chapter 1 — A Son of the West
Lines 324–1116. George Hearst pioneer myth vs. Will’s self-creation; California inheritance and western expectations.
Chapter 2 — To Europe Again and on to Harvard
Lines 1117–1764. European tours; Harvard years and dropout path.
Chapter 3 — “Something Where I Could Make a Name”
Lines 1765–2798. Search for a vocation and a name; lobbying for the Examiner.
PART II — Proprietor and Editor
Lines 2799–2800. Part divider.
Chapter 4 — At the Examiner
Lines 2801–3408. 1887 takeover of money-losing San Francisco Examiner; young proprietor vs. de Young’s Chronicle.
Chapter 5 — “I Can’t Do San Francisco Alone”
Lines 3409–3916. Limits of one-city success; drive toward a larger stage.
Chapter 6 — Hearst in New York: “Staging a Spectacle”
Lines 3917–5161. New York entry; Journal as staged spectacle journalism.
Chapter 7 — “How Do You Like the Journal’s War?”
Lines 5162–5866. Spanish-American War and yellow-press debate; Nasaw’s caution that war would have come without Hearst, even as Hearst claimed/received outsized blame and credit.
PART III — Publisher, Politician, Candidate, and Congressman
Lines 5867–5868. Part divider.
Chapter 8 — Representing the People
Lines 5869–6792. Populist/Democratic politics as “people’s” tribune.
Chapter 9 — “Candidate of a Class”
Lines 6793–7511. Class candidacy and presidential/municipal ambitions.
Chapter 10 — “A Force to Be Reckoned With”
Lines 7512–8150. National political weight of the Hearst press.
Chapter 11 — Man of Mystery
Lines 8151–8634. Steffens-era mystery of Hearst’s program and personality.
Chapter 12 — Party Leader
Lines 8635–9122. Independence League / party-leadership experiments.

Overview
The Snowball is Alice Schroeder’s authorized life of Warren Edward Buffett, built from years of interviews with Buffett, family, and associates, plus partnership letters and Berkshire archives. For this United States 1946–89 wiki the book is a spine for postwar value investing and Midwestern capital formation: Columbia/Graham-Newman, Omaha partnerships (1956–69), Dempster/American Express/Berkshire textile-to-holding-company turn, See’s Candies, Washington Post and GEICO, Buffalo News, 1970s–80s compounding, and the Rubicon into large negotiated deals—set against Susie’s departure and Astrid Menks’s Farnam Street role.

sources/sloan-my-years-with-general-moto.content:
My Years with General Motors
Author: Alfred P. Sloan, Jr. (edited by John McDonald with Catharine Stevens)
Published: 1964 (Doubleday & Company, Garden City, NY)
Working text: Digital EPUB via Anna’s Archive (hash 92f790472362294573bf9ee84eeb4730)
Raw extract: wiki/raw/sloan-my-years-with-general-motors.txt (EPUB via pandoc -t plain)
Extract stats: 17,902 lines · ~174,986 words · 1,064,902 bytes
Deploy note: Full-text raw is not deployed — wiki/.gitignore ignores *.txt; Quartz ignorePatterns includes raw.
Overview
My Years with General Motors is Alfred P. Sloan, Jr.’s first-person corporate history of GM, written from the vantage of twenty-three years as chief executive and forty-five years on the board and its committees. With Fortune editor John McDonald and Catharine Stevens—and consulting historian Alfred D. Chandler—Sloan reconstructs policy documents and managerial reasoning rather than a private life memoir. The book’s spine is organization and strategy: Durant’s opportunity versus Ford’s Model T philosophy; the 1920 collapse and Pierre S. du Pont rescue; the concept of decentralized divisions with coordinated control; product policy (a car for every purse and purpose); the copper-cooled engine failure as organizational lesson; committee coordination and financial controls; transformation of the mass market in the 1920s; annual model change, styling, dealers, and GMAC; overseas and nonautomotive lines; World War II and Cold War defense production; personnel, the UAW, and incentive compensation; and a closing statement on change and progress.
For this United States 1946–89 wiki the book covers GM management as Sloan presents it in the early 1960s: postwar dealer modernization, permanent defense contracting, seventeen years without an extended national strike after the 1945–46 ordeal, bonus/incentive philosophy, overseas scale circa 1962–63, and Sloan’s claim that his generation uniquely shaped the large corporation and the automobile’s transformation of American life. Pre-1946 chapters are essential continuity for how that order was built; mine wartime and postwar chapters (esp. 16, 18–24) as period core, with earlier chapters as institutional baseline beside Iacocca, Walton, and Welch.
EPUB structure: Table of Contents; title/editor/Doubleday 1964; Preface; Introduction; Chapters 1–24; Illustrations captions; Footnotes.
Narrative Source Flow
Front matter
Lines 1–77. TOC; title page (Sloan; edited by John McDonald with Catharine Stevens; Doubleday, Garden City, 1964).
Preface
Lines 78–192. Justifies GM story from Sloan’s policy focal point; credits McDonald (Fortune), Catharine Stevens, Alfred D. Chandler (MIT consulting historian), and Fortune/research collaborators (Seligman, Parker, Silberman, Walker Evans as picture editor, et al.).
Introduction
Lines 193–461. Progress of the world’s largest private industrial enterprise across the century and the earth; Chevrolet, Pontiac, Oldsmobile, Buick, Cadillac, GMC as roughly half U.S. passenger cars and trucks; frames engineering arts and modern corporation as the book’s subject.
Chapter 1 — The Great Opportunity—I
Lines 462–952. 1908 dual founding moment: Durant forms General Motors from Buick base; Ford announces Model T—two philosophies that will dominate successive industry periods.
Chapter 2 — The Great Opportunity—II
Lines 953–1868. Sloan’s entry path: born New Haven, 23 May 1875; father’s Bennett-Sloan wholesale move to New York/Brooklyn; Hyatt Roller Bearing and route into GM via United Motors / Durant orbit—personal bridge into the corporation.
Chapter 3 — Concept of the Organization
Lines 1869–2467. End-1920 crisis: vanished market, shut plants, high-priced inventory, cash shortage, confused product line; simultaneous external slump and internal management crisis demanding reorganization.
Chapter 4 — Product Policy and Its Origins
Lines 2468–2947. Need for a concept of the automobile business after 1908–10 and 1918–20 expansions; logical industry concept as competitive force; origins of GM’s graded product ladder.
Chapter 5 — The “Copper-Cooled” Engine
Lines 2948–3936. Painful departure from first principles for ~2½ years; copper-cooled engine program as organizational failure and lesson despite Executive Committee push and divisional resistance.
Chapter 6 — Stabilization
Lines 3937–4079. Spring 1923: Pierre S. du Pont resigns presidency; Sloan succeeds; end of first modern-corporation period; credit to du Pont for rescue and return of general stability after 1920–21.
Chapter 7 — Co-Ordination by Committee
Lines 4080–4726. Fall 1923 boom atmosphere (first four-million vehicle year prospect); reconciliation after copper-cooled conflict; committee coordination as discipline for the 1920s boom.
Chapter 8 — The Development of Financial Controls
Lines 4727–6036. Financial control coevolving with committee coordination from 1920 ruins; modern financial policies as major advance alongside organization and product policy.
Chapter 9 — Transformation of the Automobile Market
Lines 6037–6849. Mid-1920s: strategy known in the mind but little reflected in market results by end-1924; then transformation of demand and competitive structure through the decade.
Chapter 10 — Policy Creation
Lines 6850–7685. By 1929 market transformation essentially complete; Ford’s Model A as stubborn old concept vs. Chrysler’s GM-like policy; Ford’s nearly two million of five million 1929 units as splurge not trend.
Chapter 11 — Financial Growth
Lines 7686–8624. GM as growth company; after 1918 and especially under modern administration, faster than industry to number-one producer; stakeholders—employees, shareholders, dealers, consumers, suppliers, government.
Chapter 12 — Evolution of the Automobile
Lines 8625–9399. Early reliability goal; motorists as risk-capital source; engineering evolution from buggy-like machines to modern cars.
Chapter 13 — The Annual Model Change
Lines 9400–9772. Annual models as accepted American life; vast management effort behind them; contrast with foreign/special cars; competitive advanced engineering and styling each year.
Chapter 14 — The Technical Staffs
Lines 9773–10424. GM as engineering organization (~19,000 engineers/scientists; 17,000 in divisions, 2,000 on general technical staffs); continuous technological progress as policy.
Chapter 15 — Styling
Lines 10425–11030. Styling as organized staff activity pioneered by GM in late 1920s; continuous interaction with engineering since 1928 producing modern GM style.
Chapter 16 — Distribution and the Dealers
Lines 11031–11955. Turbulence when markets shift buyers’/sellers’; novelty in each cycle; evolution of the dealer distribution system; postwar dealer facility and training-center expansion into the 1950s–60s.
Chapter 17 — GMAC
Lines 11956–12368. Why GM owns a major consumer-finance institution; GMAC’s share of U.S. car-credit; business sought only through GM dealers.
Chapter 18 — The Corporation Overseas
Lines 12369–13480. Free-world vehicle absorption and GM overseas position circa 1962–63; Overseas Operations Division assets/employees; manufacturing/assembly in twenty-two countries.
Chapter 19 — Nonautomotive: Diesel Electric Locomotives, Appliances, Aviation
Lines 13481–14872. Diversification limits: durables connected with motors (~10% civilian sales); diesel locomotives, appliances, aviation engines, earth-moving; Durant-era expansion contrasted with later discipline.
Chapter 20 — Contributions to National Defense
Lines 14873–15435. Permanent defense establishment as fact of corporate life; GM defense sales $350–500 million/year (1959–62), ~3% of sales; wartime and Cold War production role.
Chapter 21 — Personnel and Labor Relations
Lines 15436–16097. More than seventeen years without extended national-issue strike as of writing; contrast with mid-1930s violence and 1945–46 postwar strike; labor peace without surrendering basic management responsibilities; inflation critique of contracts.
Chapter 22 — Incentive Compensation
Lines 16098–16986. Bonus Plan since 1918 as integral management philosophy; 1942 annual-report statement placing executives as if running their own businesses; incentive as progress and stability tool.
Chapter 23 — The Management: How It Works
Lines 16987–17239. Motivation (incentive) and opportunity (decentralization); thesis that good management reconciles centralization and decentralization.
Chapter 24 — Change and Progress
Lines 17240–17567. Unique historical opportunity of Sloan’s generation: new product (automobile) and new organization type (large-scale corporation); transformation of United States and world economy.
Illustrations / Footnotes
Lines 17568–17902. Picture captions (early roads, Mercedes, Flint, etc.); numbered footnotes supporting chapters (e.g., early GM presidents; Ethyl sale 1962; dealer training centers).
Coverage Guide
Founding rivalry and Sloan’s entry (continuity)
Chs. 1–2: Durant vs. Ford Model T philosophies; Hyatt/United Motors path into GM.
1920 crisis, organization, product policy (continuity → institutional baseline)
Chs. 3–7: reorganization, product ladder, copper-cooled failure, du Pont→Sloan succession, committee coordination—how the modern GM was built.
Financial controls, 1920s market, growth (continuity)
Chs. 8–11: control systems, market transformation, 1929 competitive map, financial growth to industry leadership.
Product, styling, distribution machine (bridge + wiki)
Chs. 12–17: engineering evolution, annual model, technical staffs, styling, dealers, GMAC—operating system still governing postwar Detroit; Ch. 16 dealer modernization is strong 1946–89 material.
Overseas, diversification, defense, labor, management creed (wiki core)
Chs. 18–24: 1960s overseas scale, nonautomotive lines, Cold War defense work, post-1945–46 labor peace, bonus plan, decentralization thesis, generational coda—primary pages for this wiki beside Iacocca’s later Ford/Chrysler story.

Overnight Success: Federal Express and Frederick Smith
Author: Vance H. Trimble
Published: 1993 (Crown Publishers, New York; first edition)
Working text: Digital PDF via Anna’s Archive (hash c12b4305840178217a4cf0367184a665)

Period-Overlap Note
Wiki core is Chapters “An Hour Most Desperate” through “The Flying Tiger Crisis” (1970s FedEx founding, 1974 crisis, profitability, Memphis hub scale-up, 1980s expansion)—inside United States 1946–89. Early family chapters (Cap’n Jim Buck / How to Make $17,000,000 / Perfect Baby / East Parkway / childhood flying) → sister page in United States 1920-45. Yale–Vietnam and Little Rock bridge into the FedEx story stay with this wiki. No copy to 1990–present (narrative closes on 1980s Flying Tiger pursuit; book written ~1990–93).
Overview
Overnight Success is Pulitzer-winning journalist Vance Trimble’s unauthorized-feeling biography of Frederick Wallace Smith and the creation of Federal Express—the Memphis hub overnight package system that made “FedEx it” a generic verb. Trimble (fresh from his Sam Walton book) reconstructs Smith’s Dixie Greyhound / Toddle House inheritance, Yale and Marine combat in Vietnam, Arkansas Aviation rescue, the hub-and-spoke brainstorm, Falcon jets and purple livery, venture-capital wooing (including Henry Crown), the May 1974 bank-forgery crisis and board ouster, jury trial, first July 1975 profit, midnight hub theater, high-tech misfires, esprit de corps worries, and the Flying Tiger global-cargo dream.
For this United States 1946–89 wiki the book is a spine for postwar logistics entrepreneurship and deregulation-era air cargo: overnight small-package networks, Memphis as national sort hub, CAB/aircraft constraints, venture finance, and the personal volatility of a founder under extreme leverage.
Book structure (from Contents; page numbers OCR-noisy): jacket/title/copyright; dedication; 21 narrative chapters (plus “How to Make $17,000,000” section on father Fred Smith’s fortune); Notes and Acknowledgments; Index.
Narrative Source Flow
Front matter / Contents
Lines 1–215. Jacket flap (six packages on day one; hub concept; forgery to save company; July 1975 first profit); title page; © 1993; LC catalog; dedication; Contents listing chapter titles through Notes/Index.
An Hour Most Desperate
Lines 216–475. May 15, 1974 Little Rock frame: age-thirty Smith fired as CEO, forged $2M Union National loan papers, FBI threat, suicidal visit to banker Herbert Hall McAdams II; compassion and Scripture; sets the crisis that the founding narrative will explain.
Cap’n Jim Buck’s Steamboat Life
Lines 476–872. Mississippi River steamboat world and Smith family transportation ancestry—continuity → 1920–45.
How to Make $17,000,000
Lines 873–1420. Father Fred Smith’s rise: Fisher’s trucks, Dixie Greyhound, Toddle House, Memphis fortune—continuity → 1920–45.
A Perfect Baby!
Lines 1421–2005. Charlotte Clark meets Fred Smith (Peabody Skyways, 1934); marriage politics; birth of Frederick Wallace Smith (1944)—continuity.
The House on East Parkway South
Lines 2006–2482. Memphis mansion childhood among siblings/stepsiblings; household chaos and privilege—continuity.
If I Die Flying…
Lines 2483–3054. Calvé-Perthes hip disease; childhood aviation obsession; early flying and “if I die flying” temperament.
Yale—And Scars of Guilt
Lines 3055–3564. Yale fall 1962; friend’s death and hospital guilt; path toward Marine Corps/Vietnam as expiation.
War and Love
Lines 3565–4332. Marine lieutenant in Vietnam (1967 jungle firefight); combat leadership; wartime marriage/love strand.
Little Rock Brainstorms
Lines 4333–4993. Home from Vietnam to rescue Arkansas Aviation / Adams Field fixed-base operation; stepfather Col. Fred Hook’s bad investment; seedbed for overnight air-freight idea.
That Damned Purple Airplane
Lines 4994–5793. Art Bass meeting; feasibility studies (A. T. Kearney / AAPG dual hire); Falcon fleet; designer Rick Runyon’s purple/plum livery chosen despite Smith’s “goddamned purple airplane” protest.
Put in All the Fruit Salad
Lines 5794–6593. 1972–76 operational grind; secretary Charlotte Curtis on Smith’s obsession; financing and early network build (“fruit salad” of pieces).
The Wooing of Colonel Crown
Lines 6594–7335. April–May 1973 New Court / Charles Lea; pitch to Henry Crown; big-money venture round to keep planes flying.
When Soul-Mates Split
Lines 7336–8090. March 12, 1974 Icarus Room (O’Hare Hilton) investor revolt day after forgery confession to Enterprise board; lenders’ $11.5M second-injection dread; Smith’s ouster politics.
We, the Jury, Find…
Lines 8091–8920. Memphis criminal defense via Lucius E. Burch, Jr.; trial over forged trust documents; jury outcome and personal reckoning.
Falling in Love Again
Lines 8921–9725. Post-crisis private-life shatter; CAB denial of DC-9s; Falcon “wing tip to wing tip” inefficiency; professional and marital strain.
Backwater Town Critic
Lines 9726–10328. Late-1970s–early-1980s wealth and public-company rise (IPO ~$24 → doubles); Smith as Memphis civic critic; Wall Street watching package growth not local speeches.
Drama at Midnight
Lines 10329–10792. Late 1980 midnight hub visits; Mike Fitzgerald and 90–100k package nights vs. early “station wagon” sort volumes.
Out of a High-Tech Brain
Lines 10793–11715. Around age forty: bold/failed side ventures; casting off early entrepreneurs (many left rich); keeping FedEx reins.
Esprit de Corps
Lines 11716–12238. Fear that billion-dollar scale would kill start-up spirit; decentralization worries; cultural defense amid hypergrowth.
In Search of Adventure
Lines 12239–12725. 1978 Rhodesia/Zimbabwe bush observation; combat fascination after Vietnam.
The Naked Madonna
Lines 12726–13239. Diane Smith’s nude Madonna-and-child portraits as Christmas gifts; Memphis gossip vs. private life.
The Flying Tiger Crisis
Lines 13240–14001. 1980s global ambition; 1984 approach to Tiger International / Flying Tigers; Gelco Express and overseas build when turned down.
Notes and Acknowledgments
Lines 14002–14541. Smith’s refusal to authorize a biography; Trimble’s 1990 turn from Walton to the “transportation Smiths”; source notes and thanks.
Coverage Guide
Memphis family fortune (continuity → 1920–45)
Cap’n Jim Buck; How to Make $17,000,000; Perfect Baby; East Parkway—brief background here.
Yale / Vietnam / Little Rock bridge (wiki core)
If I Die Flying (close); Yale; War and Love; Little Rock Brainstorms.
FedEx founding through 1980s scale (wiki core)
Purple Airplane through Flying Tiger Crisis: hub concept, capital, 1974 crisis/trial, profits, hub midnight drama, culture, global cargo bid.
