sources/turner-call-me-ted.title: [source] Call Me Ted (Turner with Burke, 2008)
sources/turner-call-me-ted.content:
Call Me Ted
Author: Ted Turner with Bill Burke
Published: 2008 (Grand Central Publishing / Hachette; first eBook November 2008)
Working text: Digital EPUB via Anna’s Archive (hash b2b0ddf22332740fd82dbd1e2f87e8c9)
Raw extract: wiki/raw/turner-call-me-ted.txt (EPUB via pandoc -t plain)
Extract stats: 12,954 lines · ~134,427 words · 751,108 bytes
Deploy note: Full-text raw is not deployed — wiki/.gitignore ignores *.txt; Quartz ignorePatterns includes raw.
Period-Overlap Note
Wiki core is Chapters 4–23 (billboards and father’s suicide through WTCG, Braves, SuperStation, America’s Cup, CNN launch, Goodwill Games, CBS/MGM fights, cable-operator partnership, Jane Fonda, Montana land)—inside United States 1946–89. Chapters 1–3 (1938 birth, WWII boarding, McCallie, Brown/Coast Guard) are brief continuity. Chapters 24–33 + Appendix (Gulf War, Cartoon Network/TNT expansion, Time Warner, UN Foundation gift, AOL merger, stepping away) belong primarily to 1990–present; sister page there mines those chapters first. No copy to 1920–45 (childhood before 1946 is thin).
Overview
Call Me Ted is Robert Edward “Ted” Turner III’s first-person life of media entrepreneurship and competitive sailing, written with Bill Burke and intercut with short “TED STORY” oral blocks from colleagues and family. It runs from Cincinnati childhood and Ed Turner’s billboard empire through UHF television, satellite SuperStation, CNN, sports ownership, America’s Cup, and the cable wars of the 1980s, then into Time Warner, the billion-dollar UN pledge, and the AOL disaster that pushed him aside.
For this United States 1946–89 wiki the book is a spine for postwar outdoor advertising into cable television and 24-hour news: Turner Advertising after 1963, Channel 17 / WTCG (“Watch This Channel Grow”), Braves purchase and UHF audience build, SuperStation satellite distribution, 1977 America’s Cup, CNN/Headline News, Fastnet 1979, early cable-operator alliances, failed CBS bid, MGM library purchase and debt, and the land/Jane Fonda turn at the period’s close.
EPUB structure: copyright/Contents; dedication; Preface; Chapters 1–33; Appendix (Eleven Voluntary Initiatives); Acknowledgments; photo credits.
Narrative Source Flow
Front matter / Contents / dedication
Lines 1–111. © 2008 Turner Works, LLC; Grand Central / Hachette imprint; ISBN 978-0-446-54336-1; Contents listing Preface through Acknowledgments; dedication to Turner’s children.
Preface
Lines 112–156. Why write now after stepping away; setbacks (father and sister, sailing near-death, Braves losing years, later wealth loss); philanthropy and five children; invitation to the ride.
Chapter 1 — Early Years
Lines 157–492. Birth 19 November 1938, Cincinnati; Ed Turner and Florence Rooney; sister Mary Jean (1941); father’s Navy service and four-year-old boarding school; postwar family moves; early nature passion and difficult father.
Chapter 2 — McCallie
Lines 493–907. Seventh-grade boarding at McCallie military academy, Chattanooga; youngest boarder; discipline, demerits, and competitive drive; father’s purse-string control of schooling.
Chapter 3 — College and the Coast Guard
Lines 908–1528. Senior-year college choice; Brown University; mischief with Peter Dames; Coast Guard service; father’s insistence on eventual takeover of the billboard company.
Chapter 4 — Billboards
Lines 1529–1913. Post-college Florida rebellion with Dames; return into Turner Advertising; learning outdoor sales and plant operations under Ed Turner’s expansion in the South.
Chapter 5 — Tragedy
Lines 1914–2094. Summer 1962 General Outdoor deal with Bob Naegele to make Turner the South’s largest billboard operator; father’s mounting stress and erratic behavior; suicide (gunshot), March 1963.
Chapter 6 — Picking Up the Pieces
Lines 2095–2320. Jimmy Brown first on the scene; warning signs and $50,000 check to stepmother Jane; holding the company together amid debt and competitor pressure.
Chapter 7 — On My Own
Lines 2321–2667. By end of March 1963 Turner as chairman/president; son Robert Edward Turner IV born May 1963; marriage to Judy failing; consolidating control of the billboard business.
Chapter 8 — Sailing Gets Serious
Lines 2668–3038. Mid-1960s sailing intensity alongside business; Flying Dutchman and yacht-club life; Ferrari anecdote; racing ladder that later leads to ocean racing and the Cup.
Chapter 9 — WTCG: “Watch This Channel Grow!”
Lines 3039–3619. Late-1960s radio holdings without Atlanta 24-hour outlet; billboard ad for UHF WJRJ Channel 17; purchase and rebranding push; movies, wrestling, counterprogramming against network affiliates.
Chapter 10 — The Braves
Lines 3620–4161. Braves telecasts as ratings and UHF-receiver catalyst (~100,000 estimated new converters); ballpark enthusiasm amid losing seasons; path toward franchise ownership to secure rights and identity.
Chapter 11 — The SuperStation
Lines 4162–4763. Growth ceiling in Atlanta vs. Big Three affiliates; satellite distribution leap—WTCG as national cable SuperStation; “bigger footprint” strategy and operator relationships.
Chapter 12 — The America’s Cup
Lines 4764–5212. Competitive sailing peak around SuperStation launch; campaign toward and winning the 1977 America’s Cup; “Captain Outrageous” public persona alongside media expansion.
Chapter 13 — Cable News Network
Lines 5213–5526. Cable partnership creed (“you run the wires, I’ll make them sing”—Bob Magness/TCI); 1978 decision to launch all-news channel himself after years of no one else doing it; naming and early planning for CNN.
Chapter 14 — Fastnet
Lines 5527–5872. 1979 Fastnet Race ordeal while CNN preparations advance; near-disaster at sea; return to intensify the nine-months-to-launch countdown.
Chapter 15 — CNN Launch
Lines 5873–6200. Country-club facility retrofit; Reese Schonfeld / Burt Reinhardt hiring surge; launching without enough capital to reach profitability; race against copycats and lenders’ skepticism.
Chapter 16 — A Dagger Pointed at Our Heart
Lines 6201–6661. 1980 America’s Cup defense attempt with Courageous vs. Dennis Conner while CNN is newborn; competitive and financial strain; “dagger” metaphor for threats to the young news network.
Chapter 17 — World Citizen
Lines 6662–6905. International travel and Cold War–era public diplomacy instincts; using media reach and sports for global visibility beyond U.S. cable homes.
Chapter 18 — The Goodwill Games
Lines 6906–7118. Post-Olympic-boycott alternative: Goodwill Games concept and Moscow staging; sports diplomacy brand alongside CNN’s international ambitions.
Chapter 19 — CBS
Lines 7119–7538. Mid-1980s scale logic—own broadcast network plus cable; exploratory pursuit of CBS; Big Three slow to enter cable; failed/blocked path that pushes other expansion routes.
Chapter 20 — MGM
Lines 7539–7903. Studio merger talks with Kirk Kerkorian / MGM-UA to secure film library against Hollywood leverage; purchase and debt load that reshape Turner’s balance sheet.
Chapter 21 — The Cable Operators
Lines 7904–8198. John Malone / TCI rescue and cable MSO equity alliance after MGM strain; shared fight against broadcast networks; accepting outside ownership to keep assets in the cable camp.
Chapter 22 — Meeting Jane Fonda
Lines 8199–8492. Courtship and marriage to Jane Fonda; public/political celebrity intersection with Turner’s media persona.
Chapter 23 — “Give Me Land, Lots of Land”
Lines 8493–8694. Montana Bar None then Flying D Ranch (~119,000 acres); bison pasture vision; land conservation turn that prefigures later philanthropy.
Chapter 24 — The Gulf War
Lines 8695–9058. Tom Johnson hired to lead CNN (1990); Gulf War coverage cementing CNN’s global news role—period gate → 1990–present.
Chapter 25 — Movies and Cartoons
Lines 9059–9466. 1990s strategy: own programming; TNT success; Cartoon Network and library exploitation under Time Warner board constraints.
Chapter 26 — Networking
Lines 9467–9857. Continued ABC/NBC/CBS merger feelers; Cap Cities/ABC Olympics talks; Jerry Levin blocking network purchase.
Chapter 27 — Time Warner Merger
Lines 9858–10188. Summer 1995: O.J. ratings spike; agreement to merge Turner into Time Warner.
Chapter 28 — The New Time Warner
Lines 10189–10674. Post-announcement Braves World Series 1995; integration politics inside the combined company.
Chapter 29 — Billion-Dollar Gift
Lines 10675–11023. Philanthropy seminar roots; $1 billion pledge to UN causes / UN Foundation.
Chapter 30 — Transitions
Lines 11024–11377. Jonathan Levin murder; personal and corporate transitions around the UN Foundation decision.
Chapter 31 — AOL: Phased Out and Fenced In
Lines 11378–11866. January 2000 AOL–Time Warner deal whirlwind; divorce from Jane same week; dilution and loss of influence.
Chapter 32 — Stepping Away
Lines 11867–12370. September 11 from CNN Center; final exit from corporate power.
Chapter 33 — Onward and Upward
Lines 12371–12864. Post-business focus on global problems, conservation, and energy; closing creed.
Appendix — Eleven Voluntary Initiatives
Lines 12865–12916. Pocket list of personal pledges (planet, weapons, UN, renewable energy/climate added 2008).
Acknowledgments
Lines 12917–12954. Mort Janklow; Hachette team; Debbie Masterson, Taylor Glover; Elizabeth Dewberry; Bill Burke; photo credits.
Coverage Guide
Childhood / schooling (continuity)
Chs. 1–3: Cincinnati–McCallie–Brown/Coast Guard—brief background.
Billboards through land / Jane (wiki core)
Chs. 4–23: father’s death, WTCG, Braves, SuperStation, Cup, CNN, Goodwill Games, CBS/MGM, cable MSOs, Fonda, Montana ranches.
Gulf War through AOL exit (forward → 1990–present)
Chs. 24–33 + Appendix: mine on the sister page.

sources/walton-made-in-america.title: [source] Sam Walton: Made in America — My Story (Walton with Huey, 1992)
sources/walton-made-in-america.content:
Sam Walton: Made in America
Author: Sam Walton with John Huey
Published: 1992 (Doubleday hardcover); Bantam edition June 1993
Working text: Digital EPUB via Anna’s Archive (hash f0b1e4a4a4aae6d9bd6e001119d817b5)
Raw extract: wiki/raw/walton-made-in-america.txt (pandoc plain from EPUB)
Extract stats: 10,020 lines · ~95,355 words · 528,857 bytes
Overview
Sam Walton: Made in America is Walton’s late-life autobiography of retail entrepreneurship from Depression-era Missouri childhood and Army service through Ben Franklin variety stores, the first Wal-Marts in northwest Arkansas and Oklahoma, national expansion, the 1970 public offering, partnership culture, distribution and computer systems, head-on competition with Kmart and other discounters, Sam’s Clubs, family wealth and philanthropy, and succession under David Glass. Huey structures the book as Walton’s continuous narrative intercut with short oral-history blocks from Helen Walton, Bud Walton, early managers, Wall Street figures, and competitors.
For this United States 1946–89 wiki the source is central to postwar mass retailing, small-town and Sun Belt consumer markets, franchise and independent merchant experience, the rise of discount stores, corporate partnership ideology, logistics and information systems as competitive weapons, and the social visibility of new retail fortunes in the 1980s. Chapters that open before 1946 (childhood, education, Army) and that close after 1989 (late illness, Medal of Freedom, co-author note) are kept for continuity; the commercial core of the book sits squarely inside the wiki period.
EPUB structure: front matter and publishing history; Contents; Acknowledgments; Foreword; Chapters 1–18; A Postscript (family); Co-Author’s Note (Huey); residual front/back matter.
Narrative Source Flow
Acknowledgments
Lines 153–221. Walton dedicates the book to Helen Robson Walton and their children Rob, John, Jim, and Alice, and to Wal-Mart associates and early managers who left larger chains for a Bentonville “one-horse outfit.” He names Bentonville Five and Dime opening associates (Inez Threet, Ruby Turner, Wanda Wiseman, Ruth Keller, August 1, 1951), early managers (Clarence Leis, Willard Walker, Charlie Baum, Claude Harris, Ferold Arend, Jack Shewmaker, and others), competitor Harry Cunningham of Kmart as designer of the modern discount store, and the later executive team under David Glass. Brother Bud Walton is singled out as retail partner from the third store onward.
Foreword
Lines 222–319. Walton introduces himself as founder and chairman of Wal-Mart Stores, claims growth from one northwest Arkansas store into the world’s largest retailing organization in about thirty years, and explains the book as an answer to myths about his finances and lifestyle after he declined publicity while building the company. Writing under cancer and family pressure, he frames the story as entrepreneurship, risk, hard work, and “traditional principles that made America great,” with competitive passion as the personal constant.
Chapter 1 — Learning to Value a Dollar
Lines 320–678. Opens with a former teacher’s reaction to Forbes naming Walton the richest man in America (October 1985) and Walton’s account of media intrusion in Bentonville, thrift, pickup truck and bird dogs, and refusal of solicitation. Moves into Depression-era family thrift, paper routes, competitive schooling and sports, marriage into the Robson family, Helen’s finance training, and the 1953 family partnership (later Walton Enterprises) modeled on L. S. Robson’s ranch partnership advice.
Chapter 2 — Starting on a Dime
Lines 679–1451. Ambition from childhood (Eagle Scout, paper routes, college hustling) through University of Missouri, J. C. Penney trainee experience, wartime marriage to Helen, Army service, and the rejected plan to buy a St. Louis Federated department store when Helen insisted on a town under 10,000. Purchase of a Ben Franklin variety store in Newport, Arkansas (1945), Butler Brothers franchise methods, early merchandising experiments, and the lesson of a short lease that cost him the store when the landlord refused renewal after Walton had built the business.
Chapter 3 — Bouncing Back
Lines 1452–2054. After Newport, spring 1950 search for a new store; choice of Bentonville for proximity to Helen’s family and quail hunting; ninety-nine-year lease hardball and L. S. Robson’s help; Walton’s Five and Dime on the Bentonville square (opened August 1, 1951) and expansion of a multi-store Ben Franklin / variety group across small Arkansas and nearby towns. Bud Walton’s partnership, airplane travel for store visits, early self-service and promotional tactics, and continuous experimentation while still inside the variety-store franchise world.
Chapter 4 — Swimming Upstream
Lines 2055–2805. Decision to go beyond Ben Franklin into true discounting after Butler Brothers refused to franchise Walton’s discount idea; Rogers and Springdale Wal-Marts and the small-town discount thesis against industry skepticism (including Bud’s early doubts). Everyday low prices versus selective price cuts, “stack it high and sell it cheap” promotions, early buyers and managers (Claude Harris, Phil Green, Charlie Cate), and the maverick identity Walton contrasts with his conservative civic habits.
Chapter 5 — Raising a Family
Lines 2806–3215. Helen’s plan for four children early; family life intertwined with store debt and openings; children’s work in stores; hunting, tennis, and church; tension between Walton’s absences and Helen’s community and family leadership. Family voices (Alice, Jim, Rob, John, Helen) describe dinner-table business talk, worry over debt, and the later structure of Walton Enterprises as the vehicle that kept ownership concentrated.
Chapter 6 — Recruiting the Team
Lines 3216–3730. Building a management cadre by hiring from competitors and promoting from within; Ferold Arend, Ron Mayer, Jack Shewmaker, David Glass, and other executives; resistance to large headquarters staff; preference for operators who could run stores and merchandise. Industry meetings (including NMRI) and relationships with other discounters; Walton’s habit of walking competitors’ floors and borrowing ideas.
Chapter 7 — Taking the Company Public
Lines 3731–4350. Capital constraints of debt-financed store growth; decision to take Wal-Mart public (1970); Bentonville and Wall Street culture clash; Stephens Inc. and early analyst coverage; family and employee ownership stakes; stock splits and the long rise in share value. Helen and family reactions to public scrutiny; Walton’s insistence on keeping operating control and a lean central office after the IPO.
Chapter 8 — Rolling Out the Formula
Lines 4351–4985. Systematic multi-state expansion from the Arkansas–Oklahoma–Missouri core; real-estate and small-town site selection; Saturday morning meetings; airplane supervision of managers; distribution growing from necessity as store count rose. Internal tables and recollections of store counts and sales growth; conflicts and turnover among top executives as the company professionalized.
Chapter 9 — Building the Partnership
Lines 4986–5630. “Associate” language, profit sharing, stock ownership for employees, open-door practices, and the claim that partnership ideology differentiated Wal-Mart from hierarchical chains. Truck drivers, hourly associates, and office staff in oral blocks; Helen’s views on people and community; limits and tests of the partnership idea as the workforce scaled into the hundreds of thousands.
Chapter 10 — Stepping Back
Lines 5631–6105. Walton’s partial steps back from day-to-day control, experiments with other managers in the chief executive role, and the turbulence around succession before David Glass’s lasting leadership. Personal habits—store visits, hands-on merchandising—continue even when titles shift; lessons about founders who cannot fully let go.
Chapter 11 — Creating a Culture
Lines 6106–6730. Saturday meetings, cheers, store visits, information sharing, and competitive games as deliberate culture-building. Resistance to bureaucracy; preference for communication over manuals; stories that became company legend. Culture presented as a cost advantage and a control system for a far-flung store network.
Chapter 12 — Making the Customer Number One
Lines 6731–7316. Credo that successful retailing means giving customers what they want—assortment, low prices, service, hours, parking, experience—learned in small-town markets where farm families and later working women shaped demand. Discussion of impact on main-street merchants; Walton’s sharper sympathy for capable specialty competitors (e.g. strong hardware operators) than for weak general merchandisers; satisfaction guarantee and service standards as stated policy.
Chapter 13 — Meeting the Competition
Lines 7317–7934. Strategic choice to confront rather than avoid national discounters; Kmart as both model and rival; Sears’s delay in recognizing discount competition; Sol Price, Fed-Mart, and Price Club as sources for the wholesale-club idea that became Sam’s Club. Territorial fights with regional chains (including Kuhn’s), acquisitions and head-to-head openings, and Walton’s lifelong store-espionage habit at home and abroad.
Chapter 14 — Expanding the Circles
Lines 7935–8271. Distribution centers, private trucking, and computer systems as capital investments sold internally against Walton’s skepticism about technology spend. David Glass’s automated DC vision; satellite and communications networks; logistics cast as a primary competitive advantage that enabled national roll-out while Kmart under-invested in systems in the late 1970s.
Chapter 15 — Thinking Small
Lines 8272–8988. Paradox of “thinking small” while becoming the largest retailer: personal store visits by air, delegation to strong managers, resistance to unwieldy centralization. 1960 local magazine quote that nine variety stores might be enough; subsequent decades of 30–70 percent growth years; fanaticism about getting buyers and managers into stores; fleet of propeller aircraft (one jet) as supervision infrastructure.
Chapter 16 — Giving Something Back
Lines 8989–9368. Opens with John D. Rockefeller, Jr. on rights and duties. Family wealth kept largely in Wal-Mart stock; dividend income as spendable philanthropy; refusal of random personal solicitations after the Forbes episode. Walton’s and the company’s stated giving priorities (education, community, children’s hospitals, associate-driven campaigns such as Children’s Miracle Network) and the argument that everyday low prices themselves “give something back” by saving customers money.
Chapter 17 — Running a Successful Company: Ten Rules That Worked for Me
Lines 9369–9552. Condensed management rules Walton says stayed relatively stable across forty-seven years in retailing: commit to the business; share profits and treat associates as partners; motivate and communicate; appreciate and celebrate; listen to people in the stores; exceed customer expectations; control expenses better than competition; swim upstream and ignore conventional wisdom. David Glass notes Walton’s habit of naming many different “keys” to success while actually holding them all at once.
Chapter 18 — Wanting to Leave a Legacy
Lines 9553–9826. Illness forces reflection on time away from family, pressure on partners, executive pay versus “servant leadership,” and whether Wal-Mart’s accomplishment will outlast him. Comparison (via Tom Peters) to Henry Ford as entrepreneur; defense of competitive free enterprise and criticism of management that takes care of itself first; hope that the associate-partner model and customer focus remain after he is gone.
A Postscript
Lines 9827–9917. Family account (from a child of Walton) of multiple myeloma from early 1990, experimental treatments, continued store flying, return to the book project in late 1991, and the Presidential Medal of Freedom ceremony in Bentonville with President and Mrs. Bush and Wal-Mart associates present. Records Walton’s death and the family’s sense of his priorities at the end.
Co-Author’s Note
Lines 9918–end. John Huey on how the book was made: Fortune assignment to the Ozarks (from late 1988), Bill Barry at Doubleday persuading Walton to write, editorial process, oral contributions from family and associates, and Huey’s role as shaper of Walton’s dictated and revised narrative rather than as invisible ghost.
Coverage Guide
Postwar small-town and Sun Belt retailing
Chapters 2–5 and 8 are the spine for 1945–1970 merchant life: Newport Ben Franklin, Bentonville variety stores, airplane supervision, family labor, and the jump into discounting in towns larger chains under-served. Use for main-street commerce, franchise variety chains, and the geography of early Wal-Mart.
Discount store revolution and competition
Chapters 4, 12–13, and parts of 6–8 cover the shift from variety stores to discounting, Kmart/Cunningham as template, Sears’s lag, regional discounters, and Sam’s Club via Sol Price. Core for 1960s–1980s retail structure.
Corporate form, capital markets, and ownership
Chapters 1, 5, 7, and 16 treat Walton Enterprises, the 1970 IPO, associate equity and profit sharing, and concentrated family ownership through stock. Useful for postwar private-to-public growth companies and 1980s wealth visibility.
Logistics, information systems, and scale
Chapters 8, 14–15 document distribution centers, trucking, computers, satellite communications, and the “think small” managerial counterweight to scale—key for 1970s–80s corporate modernization.
Culture, labor ideology, and philanthropy
Chapters 9, 11, 16–18 state Wal-Mart’s partnership language, Saturday culture, customer creed, charitable posture, and late reflections on executive pay and legacy. Treat as the company’s own ideology as of 1992, not as external verification.

Jack: Straight from the Gut
Author: Jack Welch with John A. Byrne
Published: 2001 (Warner Books)
Working text: Digital EPUB via Anna’s Archive (hash 73d9ad93adf2f039dd7c6ea2cfe83111)
Raw extract: wiki/raw/welch-straight-from-the-gut.txt (pandoc plain from EPUB)
Extract stats: 26,857 lines · ~142,068 words · 815,841 bytes
Overview
Jack: Straight from the Gut is Jack Welch’s first-person account, written with John A. Byrne, of a career at General Electric from the plastics pit through the chairmanship. Welch narrates childhood and education, early GE plastics entrepreneurship, the succession race to replace Reg Jones, and the CEO years defined by the no. 1 or no. 2 portfolio rule, delayering, “boundaryless” behavior, Crotonville teaching, Work-Out, differentiation of people, globalization, services, Six Sigma, and the late succession contest—ending as he leaves the company.
For this United States 1946–89 wiki the highest-value material is Welch’s formation and 1981–89 restructuring: GE culture before and after he takes the chair (April 1981), plant closings and “Neutron Jack” reputation, portfolio surgery in the early Reagan years, Crotonville as corporate university, and the emerging boundaryless/Work-Out ideology by the late 1980s. Childhood through plastics (1950s–70s) supply corporate-career social history. Chapters on 1990s services, NBC deal aftermath beyond the period edge, Six Sigma (1995+), Internet, and succession are post-1989 spill—use for continuity of 1980s doctrines, not as primary 1946–89 evidence.
EPUB structure: front matter; Acknowledgments; Introduction; numbered/named chapters across career arc (early life, plastics, CEO years, initiatives, succession); residual back matter. Some SECTION dividers in the extract are thin labels between chapter blocks.
Narrative Source Flow
Author’s Note
Lines 172–197. Author’s Note This may seem a strange way to begin an autobiography. A confession: I hate having to use the first person. Nearly everything I’ve done in my life has been accomplished with other people. Yet when you write a book like this, you’re forced to use the narrative “I” when it’s real y the “we” that counts. I wanted to mention the names of al the people who took this journey with me. My editors kept beating me up, trying to get the names out. We final y struck a compromise. That’s why the acknowledgments in the back of the book are somewhat long.
Prologue
Lines 198–550. Prologue I spent most of the Saturday morning after Thanksgiving 2000 waiting for the “New Guy.” That was the secret code for my successor, the future chairman and CEO of General Electric. On Friday night, the board had unanimously approved Jeff Immelt to succeed me. I cal ed him right away. “I have some good news. Can you and your family come to Florida tomorrow and spend the weekend?” Obviously, he knew what was going on. But we left it at that and went quickly to the arrangements to get him to Florida. On Saturday morning, I could hardly wait to see him. We both loved GE. He knew it had to change, and he thought I had the passion and the smarts to do it. I’m not sure he knew how much I wanted GE to change-but his support for al I did over 20 years never wavered. The competition to succeed Reg had been brutal, complicated by heavy politics and big egos, my own included.
SECTION I. EARLY YEARS
Lines 551–554. Part/section divider.
1 — Building Self-Confidence
Lines 555–1669. Building Self-Confidence It was the final hockey game of a lousy season. We had won the first three games in my senior year at Salem High School, beating Danvers, Revere, and Marblehead, but had then lost the next half dozen games, five of them by a single goal. So we badly wanted to win this last one at the Lynn Arena against our archrival Beverly High. As co-captain of the team, the Salem Witches, I had scored a couple of goals, and we were feeling pretty good about our chances. It was a good game, pushed into overtime at 2-2. We’d organize our own neighborhood basebal , basketbal , footbal , and hockey games, playing at the Pit, a dusty piece of flat land surrounded by trees and backyards off North Street. We’d sweep the gravel flat in the spring and summer, choose up sides and teams, even schedule our own tournaments. We’d play from early in the morning until the town whistle blew at quarter to nine. most inventors, was already on to the next project, becoming champion for a new thermoplastic cal ed PPO (polyphenylene oxide). He convinced me that PPO was going to be the next great thing. He described its unique ability to withstand high temperatures.
2 — Getting Out of the Pile
Lines 1670–1976. Getting Out of the Pile In 1961, I had been working at GE for a year as an engineer making 10,500 when my first boss handed me a 1,000 raise. I was okay with it-until I found out later that day that I got exactly what al four of us sharing an office received. I thought I deserved more than the “standard” increase. I talked to my boss, and the discussion went nowhere. Frustrated, I started looking for another job. I began scanning the “Help Wanted” ads in Chemical Week magazine and The Wal Street Journal, hoping to find a quick escape. He ran the earliest experiments on the new plastic in beakers. I designed the kettles to test the bigger batches and built them at a local machine shop. We constructed a pilot plant from scratch in a smal outbuilding in the back of our offices. Each day, we’d run several experiments, testing different processes. For someone just off a col ege campus, it was a real adventure.
3 — Blowing the Roof Off
Lines 1977–2598. Blowing the Roof Off Years before I was given the nickname Neutron Jack, I had actual y blown up a factory-for real. It was 1963, early in my GE career. I was 28 years old and had been with the company for al of three years. I can remember that spring day as if it were yesterday. It was one of the most frightening experiences of my life. I was sitting in my office in Pittsfield, just across the street from the pilot plant, when the explosion occurred. It was a huge blast that blew the roof off the building and knocked out al the windows on the top floor. Without naming him, I launched into that story the next morning in front of 170 of GE’s top executives. I used it as an example of how our company wasn’t getting what maximizing global intel ect is al about. I chal enged everyone in the room to look at themselves in the mirror to make sure they weren’t in the same boat. It would by no means be the last time this would happen. Even so, the family business continued to grow, and so did I. Once we had the Selkirk plant up and began sel ing Noryl, sales took off. We grew rapidly from 1965 to 1968 and then I got the next big break.
4 — Flying Below the Radar
Lines 2599–3279. Flying Below the Radar Life appeared to be perfect. There was only one regret. I could no longer share my success with my parents. My mother had died on January 25, 1965, which was the saddest day of my life. She was only 66 years old but had been suffering from heart trouble for many years. I had been an undergraduate at UMass in Amherst when she had her first heart attack. I was so upset then that after my aunt cal ed with the news, I literal y rushed out of the dorm and began running down the highway to Salem, about 110 miles away. Nevertheless, the future looked very bright. This was a time when forecasters believed that plastics would be the fastest-growing industry over the next decade-faster than computers and electronics. Even the movies were getting into it. In The Graduate, Dustin Hoffman was encouraged to get a career in “plastics!” We added marketing people and began promoting the plastics business as if it were Tide detergent. While the bureaucracy often frustrated me, I tried hard not to be a very visible critic of it-especial y not to the higher-ups. By the early 1970s, I had started to think about the possibility of running GE. I actual y said it in 1973 when I presumptuously wrote in my performance review that my long-range career objective was to become CEO.
5 — Getting Closer to the Big Leagues
Lines 3280–4075. Getting Closer to the Big Leagues During June of 1973, I got my next big break. Reuben Gutoff was promoted to head of strategic planning for the entire company, and I got his job as group executive. The promotion meant that I had to move to corporate headquarters. Besides the chemical and metal urgical division I already managed from Pittsfield, I was now responsible for a number of other businesses: medical systems in Milwaukee, appliance components in Fort Wayne, electronic components in Syracuse. It was a diverse portfolio of products with over $2 bil ion in annual sales. From my first days in plastics, I understood the importance of getting the right people. It was clear that when I found someone great, it made al the difference in the world. I learned a lot of this the hard way-by making some big mistakes. The inconsistency of my first hires was laughable. One of my most common errors was to hire on appearances. My promotion to Fairfield brought me to a new organizational layer as a “sector executive.” There was a hierarchy at GE, like any other large company, and I had been lucky to climb through it. Sometimes it felt like the civil service, with al its 29 levels and dozens of titles and promotions, from a lab to a unit to a subsection to a section to a department, then a division and a group.
6 — Swimming in a Bigger Pond
Lines 4076–5718. Swimming in a Bigger Pond Early one December morning in 1977, I drove past the security guard at the front gate of GE’s headquarters in Fairfield and up the winding driveway. Al the trees were bare and the grounds were covered with snow that day. I turned into the concrete underground garage, parked my car in an empty slot, got in the elevator, and went to the third floor of the west building. I walked down the wide hal way to a corner office with a glass door, the farthest office away from Chairman Reg Jones. During his presentation, he had been using a couple of terms that I was unfamiliar with. So I interrupted him to ask: “What’s the difference between ‘facultative’ and ‘treaty’ insurance?” After fumbling through a long answer for several minutes, an answer I wasn’t getting, he final y blurted out in exasperation, “How do you expect me to teach you in five minutes what it has taken me 25 years to learn!” I couldn’t believe our guests didn’t have a great time. They just couldn’t have faked it that much. I’d been to enough parties to know a good one. Just before noon, however, things changed. Reg came back to my office. “I want to talk,” he said.
SECTION II. BUILDING A PHILOSOPHY
Lines 5719–5722. Part/section divider.
7 — Dealing with Reality and Superficial Congeniality
Lines 5723–6575. Dealing with Reality and “Superficial Congeniality” On April 1, 1981, I was like the dog who caught the bus. I final y had the job. Despite al the experiences that had gotten me this far, I wasn’t nearly as sure of myself as I pretended to be. Outwardly, I had a pretty good dose of self-confidence, and those who knew me would have described me as self-assured, cocky, decisive, quick, and tough. Inwardly, I stil had plenty of insecurities. Whenever I had to get up in front of people, I struggled with my speech impediment. I fussed with a comb-over to disguise my receding hairline. 1 or No. 2 strategy, what they liked and disliked about GE, and what things we ought to change quickly. We spent time discussing the just-concluded planning sessions and how they could be improved. Creating an open dialogue was difficult. Only those I worked closely with were wil ing to let it rip. Most of the guys didn’t want to stick their necks out. Whether it was appliances in the late 1970s, nuclear in the early 1980s, or dot-coms at the turn of the century, getting people to face reality was the first step toward an eventual solution. When I became CEO, I inherited a lot of great things, but facing reality was not one of the company’s strong points.
8 — The Vision Thing
Lines 6576–7505. The Vision Thing My first time in front of Wal Street’s analysts as chairman was a bomb. I had been in the job for eight months when I went to New York City on December 8, 1981, to deliver my big message on the “New GE.” I had worked on the speech, rewriting it, rehearsing it, and desperately wanting it to be a smash hit. It was, after al , my first public statement on where I wanted to take GE. You know, the vision thing. However, the analysts arrived that day expecting to hear the financial results and the successes achieved by the company during the year. I drew three circles and divided our businesses into one of three categories: core manufacturing, technology, and services. Inside the core circle, for example, I put lighting, major appliances, motors, turbines, transportation, and contractor equipment. Any business outside the circles, I told Carolyn, we would fix, sel , or close. These businesses were the marginal performers, or were in low-growth markets, or just had a poor strategic fit. Employees in many of the traditional businesses were upset. The 2 bil ion divestiture of Utah didn't raise an eyebrow, but sel ing this 300 mil ion low-tech, tin- bending housewares business brought out unbelievable cries. I got my first blast of angry letters from employees.
9 — The Neutron Years
Lines 7506–8665. The Neutron Years In the early 1980s, you didn’t have to be in a GE business that was up for sale to wonder if Jack Welch knew what he was doing or where he was going. The turmoil, angst, and confusion were everywhere. The causes were the goal to be No. 1 or No. 2, the three circles, the outright sale of businesses, and the cutbacks now occurring in many parts of GE. Within five years, one of every four people would leave the GE payrol , 118,000 people in al , including 37,000 employees in businesses that were sold. The plant made metal irons when consumers already overwhelmingly favored plastic models. We had four plants, including one in North Carolina, making plastic irons. Ontario’s product line had to be discontinued. Closing the plant was uncomfortable for everyone, but it was the highest-cost plant in our system, and we were going to be competitive. In fairness to 60 Minutes, the program did point out that we had given our employees six months’ advance notice when the average then was only one week. Our lawyers design the work and plot the strategy, with the advantage of having an intimate knowledge of our company and its people. The outside law firms work much more closely with us. They are partners in our firm. Ironical y, I shouldn’t have agonized as long as I did on so many people who weren’t going to cut it.
10 — The RCA Deal
Lines 8666–9621. The RCA Deal I’l never forget the time I walked through a Japanese manufacturing plant. It was in the mid-1970s, after putting together a joint venture with Yokogawa Medical Systems. On a tour of a Yokogawa plant outside Tokyo, I watched in total amazement as ultrasound units were being assembled. The process was like nothing I had seen in the United States. When the machines were finished, a worker unbuttoned his shirt, dabbed some gel on his chest, and ran the ultrasound probes over his body for a quick quality test. The same guy then wrapped up the product, put it in a box, attached a shipping label, and got it on the loading dock. I’l never forget the kick we got looking out the windows through the fog and seeing the RCA sign il uminated on top of their building at Rockefel er Center. It was just three blocks away from ours. We could hardly wait to get the GE logo up there. We felt like hot stuff at the moment. ultimately negotiated a deal with SES, a Luxembourg company with 22 satel ites that reach 88 mil ion households. We sold our satel ite holdings to them for $5 bil ion, split almost equal y in cash and stock. The pending deal would give us a 27 percent stake in the new SES Group and make the entity a true global player.
11 — The People Factory
Lines 9622–10401. The People Factory After I became chairman, Joyce Hergenhan was the first officer I hired from outside the company, one of a handful of officers ever brought in from the outside. She was outspoken and tough as nails, a very smart MBA who was wel schooled in hard knocks. She had been Con Edison’s senior vice president for public affairs at a time when the utility was suffering power outages and generating more heat than light. Before we met, I had done a little background check and learned she was a sports trivia nut. Over dinner, for fun, I decided to throw her a high, hard one for my first question. Cs are likely to enervate rather than energize. They procrastinate rather than deliver. You can’t waste time on them, although we do spend resources on their redeployment elsewhere. The vitality curve is the dynamic way we sort out As, Bs, and Cs, the most important tool of the Session C. Ranking employees on a 20-70-10 grid forces managers to make tough decisions. My ex-wife, Carolyn, always reminded me that I worked in the company ten years before I ever knew who was chairman. The important thing I urged every GE manager to remember was that “they were the CEO” as far as their people were concerned.
12 — Remaking Crotonville to Remake GE
Lines 10402–11363. Remaking Crotonvil e to Remake GE Change has no constituency-and a perceived revolution has even less. In early January 1981, just two weeks after being named chairman-elect, I was in Florida for GE’s annual general management meeting. I had been going to this event at the Bel eview Biltmore in Clearwater since 1968. It was during a cocktail reception before dinner one evening that I searched out Jim Baughman. Jim was a bearded academic, a former Harvard Business School professor, who had consulted for GE over the years. He had been named the head of Crotonvil e, our management development center, a year earlier. We held three BMCs a year, with about 60 in each class, and one EDC a year for 35 to 50 of our most high-potential managers. Both these courses were three weeks long and were scheduled so that each class could present their recommendations in a two-hour session at the quarterly meetings of our Corporate Executive Council (CEC). Work-Out liberated many of them. From a simple idea hatched at Crotonvil e, Work-Out helped us to create a culture where everyone began playing a part, where everyone’s ideas began to count, and where leaders led rather than control ed. They coached-rather than preached-and they got better results.
13 — Boundaryless
Lines 11364–12482. Boundaryless: Taking Ideas to the Bottom Line I was sitting on the beach under an umbrel a in Barbados in December 1989 on a belated honeymoon with my second wife, Jane. My year-in-advance schedule had kept us from having a typical honeymoon when we were married in April. Now we were having our “romantic vacation” at last, but as usual I ended up talking about work-not what you’d cal pil ow talk. Work-Out had become a huge success. We were kicking bureaucracy’s butt with it. Ideas were flowing faster al over the company. I was groping for a way to describe this, something that might capture the whole organization-and take idea sharing to the next level. It wasn’t only fat cats. Boundaryless was paying off for everyone. Stock ownership changes behavior-and the compensation changes gave us momentum for the 1990 launch of boundaryless. Stil , it was only one piece of the puzzle. We needed more. We needed a way to surface the best ideas and move them quickly through the organization. loved the fact that we gave a Crotonvil e class a chal enge and it went out and found a great idea in the head of an army colonel in Pennsylvania. This was boundaryless behavior at its best. Our people real y were finding “a better way,” and it was making the difference between GE and the rest of the business world.
14 — Deep Dives
Lines 12483–12974. Deep Dives There are advantages to being the chairman. One of my favorite perks was picking out an issue and doing what I cal ed a “deep dive.” It’s spotting a chal enge where you think you can make a difference-one that looks like it would be fun-and then throwing the weight of your position behind it. Some might justifiably cal it “meddling.” I’ve often done this-just about everywhere in the company. I got involved in everything my nose told me to get involved in, from the quality of our X-ray tubes to the introduction of gem-quality diamonds. I was sure we could do more. Starting in 1992, I jokingly became its unofficial “project manager.” After we decided against an expensive acquisition to improve our competitive position, we launched our own internal development effort. I asked John Trani, the CEO of medical, to bypass al the typical reporting relationships and have the project report directly to him. They ranged from CFO of GE Plastics Japan, general manager of sales and marketing of GE Medical Systems Japan, marketing director of GE Consumer Finance Japan, to the heads of human resources for GE-Toshiba Silicones and GE Medical Systems. Jeff and I had never been with a more impressive young crowd.
SECTION III. UPS AND DOWNS
Lines 12975–12980. Part/section divider.
15 — Too Full of Myself
Lines 12981–13758. Too Ful of Myself For chrissakes, Jack, what are you going to do next? Buy McDonald’s?” The remark came from a foursome of guys across the seventh fairway at Augusta as I was teeing off from the third hole in April 1986. Four months after announcing the deal to buy RCA, I had just acquired Kidder, Peabody, one of Wal Street’s oldest investment banking firms. While the guys were only kidding, there were others who real y didn’t think much of our latest decision. At least three GE board members weren’t too keen on it, including two of the most experienced directors in the financial services business, Citibank Chairman Walt Wriston and J.P. When Si went through his first bonus exercise, he’d ask everyone at Kidder to give him a list of his or her accomplishments for the year. Inevitably, he’d have six people claiming credit for being the key player on the same deal. Every one of them believed they made the deal happen. The attitudes were symbolic of the problem: an entitlement culture where every player overvalued themselves. There are different amounts of it for different levels of performance, but everyone’s life raft is tied to the same boat. One culture, one set of values, one currency, doesn’t mean, however, one style-every GE business has its own personality. For the same reason-a big culture gap-I’ve passed up opportunities to acquire high-tech companies in Silicon Val ey that appeared to be a good strategic fit.
16 — GE Capital: The Growth Engine
Lines 13759–14981. GE Capital: The Growth Engine One night in June 1998, I was sitting on the couch at home, leafing through the “deal book” for the next day’s GE Capital board meeting. One of the ideas up for approval struck me as one of the wackiest I had seen in my 20 years on the board. The proposal was to buy $1.1 bil ion of auto loans in Thailand from a group of failed finance companies that had been seized by the government. I knew the country was in the worst recession in its history, and we were the only auto finance company stil standing. Over the years, we had a murderers row of talent-Larry Bossidy, Dennis Dammerman, Norm Blake, Bob Wright, Gary Wendt, and Denis Nayden. Every one of them would go on to become CEOs inside or outside the company. A perfect example of homegrown success was Denis Nayden, who started right out of the University of Connecticut in 1977 as marketing administrator for air-rail financing. The chart I like best is one that was shown by Jim Colica, the longtime head of risk management, at a GE board meeting in June 2001 (below). It captures the growth and breadth and risk containment of GE Capital Services.
17 — Mixing NBC with Light Bulbs
Lines 14982–16431. Mixing NBC with Light Bulbs When we announced the acquisition of RCA in December 1985, NBC looked great. The network was a $3 bil ion business with 8,000 employees that had a lot of juice. It was on the verge of being first in prime-time ratings, first in late night programming, and first in Saturday morning children’s programs. Led by The Cosby Show, the highest-rated series on TV, we had nine of the 20 most-watched TV programs, including Family Ties, Cheers, and Night Court. At the top of my mind was, How do we keep it going? I think I’ve told everyone that Andy was the most exciting person I ever interviewed for a job. He was total y different from any of the news leaders I had met. He was humorous, spontaneous, fil ed with energy, and total y comfortable with himself-traits by now you know I find appealing. He charmed the hel out of me. Bob’s vision to see NBC as more than just a network was a winner. The network audience has continued to erode, making his bets on cable television look even better. CNBC is the leader in financial news, and MSNBC is the top-rated cable news network on a 24-hour basis among 25 to 54-year-old viewers.
18 — When to Fight, When to Fold
Lines 16432–17624. When to Fight, When to Fold One of my strongest childhood memories is of climbing the stairs to my parents’ second-floor flat in Salem, Massachusetts, and hearing my mother crying. I was only nine years old in 1945. I had never heard my mother cry before. When I walked through the doorway, she was standing over an ironing board in the kitchen, pressing my father’s shirts. Tears were streaming down her face. “Oh, God,” she said. “Franklin Roosevelt has died.” I was stunned. I didn’t know why the president’s death would cause my mother such heartache. Al the employees caught up in this mess received detailed letters outlining our “concerns” or “al egations” based on our internal investigation. They had the opportunity to give their side of the story, with the help of lawyers they hired-at our expense. Bil came back with disciplinary recommendations for each employee. At one point during a two-month period, Bil , Brian, Ben, and I were on the phone nearly every day. only means that people must abide by the letter and spirit of the law, it also means doing the right thing and fighting for what you believe is right. On PCBs, we’ve assured ourselves that they are not harmful to our employees or our neighbors.
SECTION IV. GAME CHANGERS
Lines 17625–17787. SECTION IV GAME CHANGERS If you like business, you have to like GE. If you like ideas, you have to love GE. This is a place where ideas can flow freely from and through more than 20 separate businesses and more than 300,000 employees. Boundaryless behavior al ows ideas to come from anywhere. We formalize our freewheeling style in a series of operating meetings that blend one into another. We can be doing a Session C review of managers in power systems and someone wil come up with an idea on sourcing in Hungary. The next day we’re in medical, bragging about what power has just done in Hungary.
19 — Globalization
Lines 17788–18711. Globalization GE has always been a global trading company. In the late 1800s, Thomas Edison instal ed the 3,000-bulb electric lighting system at London’s Holborn Viaduct. At the turn of the century, GE built the largest power plant in Japan. Some of the company’s earliest CEOs traveled by boat for a month or two to look for business in Europe and Asia. I had an early start in globalization. Reuben Gutoff and I formed two joint ventures in plastics in the mid-1960s, one with Mitsui Petrochemical in Japan and the other with AKU, the chemical and fiber company in Hol and. He has a strong British accent.” “Oh no,” I said, “I forgot to tel anyone that Weinstock would be using Ed’s name as his code.” It probably looked to Weinstock as though we were playing it cool. Not that it helped. He was a cool customer himself, as shrewd, wily, and clever as anyone I ever met. I constantly reminded our business leaders, “Would you rather have three to four smart University of Tokyo graduates who know the country and the language, or a friend of yours from down the hal ?” Globalization took a big step forward with an exciting promotion that showed our efforts are paying off.
20 — Growing Services
Lines 18712–19116. Growing Services Like just about everything at GE, growing services was al about people. With the exception of our medical business, most of the people making the heavy hardware in the company thought of services as the “after market”-supplying spare and replacement parts for the aircraft engines, locomotives, and power generation equipment we sold. “After market”-the name itself puts it in the backseat. In our big-equipment businesses, the engineers liked to spend their time on the newest, the fastest, and the most powerful. They didn’t think much about the “after market.” They weren’t alone-our salespeople also focused primarily on the customers’ new equipment needs. It was an unprofitable operation that primarily serviced and overhauled Rol s-Royce engines, and British Airways wanted out of it. This shop was our first significant foray into servicing other manufacturers’ engines. In 1996, Bil , with Dennis Dammerman’s help, acquired Celma, a former state-owned service shop in Brazil that had been privatized. It gave us the capability to service Pratt & Whitney engines.
21 — Six Sigma and Beyond
Lines 19117–20042. Six Sigma and Beyond In 20 years as CEO, I missed only one Corporate Executive Council (CEC) meeting. It was in June 1995, one of the most important meetings we ever had. I had invited my friend and former col eague Larry Bossidy, then CEO of Al iedSignal, to come to Crotonvil e to talk about Six Sigma quality. There was a good excuse for my not being there. I was home in bed, recovering from open-heart surgery. After returning from India in late January, I couldn’t stop feeling tired al the time. I thought I’d just caught some kind of bug that was making me feel lousy. If there is a Six Sigma zealot, Harry’s the guy. We invited him to our annual officers meeting in Crotonvil e in October. I canceled our usual golf outing-a symbolic gesture if there ever was one-so that 170 of us could listen to Harry talk about his program. For four solid hours, he jumped excitedly from one easel to another, writing down al kinds of statistical formulas. The high probability is that Jeff Immelt’s successor wil be a Six Sigma Black Belt. At my Crotonvil e sessions in the last couple of years, I used to joke that the reason I was so slow on the uptake for e-business was that we were perfecting Six Sigma first.
22 — E-Business
Lines 20043–20698. E-Business The Internet revolution nearly passed me by-until Jane made me comfortable with it. She had been using the Net for years to keep up with friends. Many nights, I’d be going through my work papers while she would sit across from me, plugged in and typing away. Jane started buying and sel ing stocks online in 1997, keeping track of her portfolio on the Internet. She was doing so wel that I asked her to watch over mine. Wherever we went, Jane’s laptop came along with us. Whenever she tried to convince me to use a laptop on my own, I resisted, thinking my inability to type hardly made it worth it. On the sel side, the Net al owed us to improve service. We could fulfil faster. New and existing customers could get input on their shipments without multiple phone cal s. This was the end of the expediter falsely reassuring a customer that the order was on the way. Combined with Six Sigma, the Internet could help us give our customers better service.
